title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, along the Main Path, to the Sydney Region

plants.name: Corymbia 'Summer Red'
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre on your right is Corymbia ‘Summer Red’, a grafted eucalypt with dark green leathery foliage and attractive red new foliage, red fluffy flowers and beautiful bud formations (photo above).

plants.name: Eremophila nivea
plants.context: 2. Also on the right is Eremophila nivea, a small shrub with mauve tubular flowers and striking silverJgrey foliage covered in hairs (photo next page top left). This plant is found in the wild on the southern west coast of Western Australia.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Scarlet King'
plants.context: 3. On your right and left is Grevillea ‘Scarlet King’ an attractive cultivar with dark red toothbrush flowers contrasting with white stems and greyJ green divided foliage (photo above right).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Peaches and Cream'
plants.context: 4. Also on your right is Grevillea ‘Peaches and Cream’ with deeply divided attractive green leaves and large flower heads of pink and cream (photo above). This hybrid was developed in Queensland by Jan Glazebrook and Dennis Cox and patented in 2006.

plants.name: Syzygium australe
plants.context: 5. Cross the bridge, go past the café to see on your left Syzygium australe, or Scrub Cherry, a tall shrub with very shiny green leaves and white pow- derpuff flowers (photo above). The edible fruit ma- tures from December to February, and is a droop- ing pear shaped red or purple berry, known as a Riberry. This plant grows from southern New South Wales to central Queensland.

plants.name: Doryanthes palmeri
plants.context: 6. Bear left up the hill along the Main Path to see on your right Doryanthes palmeri or Spear Lily (photo below left). When in flower this is one of the most spectacular flowers in the Gardens, a huge nodding cluster of bright red flowers much visited by insects and hon- eyeaters. At present there are vigorous stalks and buds showing above the rosette of leaves which themselves can reach a length of about 3 m. The flowers grow on a stalk which may reach 5 m in height. This plant is found in nort

plants.name: Telopea 'Canberry Gem'
plants.context: 7. Further on your left is Telopea ‘Canberry Gem’ which forms another spectacular display (photo above right). Bright pink/red wa- ratah flowers on a large bush with dark green foliage.

plants.name: Banksia 'Birthday Candles'
plants.context: 8. Still on your left is Banksia ‘Birthday Can- dles’ just coming into flower, showing yellow brown brushes on a mound of green divided foliage (photo above). This cultivar was developed from Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa by Bill Molyneux of Austraflora Nurseries in Montrose, Victoria.

plants.name: Banksia pencillata
plants.context: 9. Again on your left is Banksia pencillata or Newnes Plateau Banksia. a small tree covered in short greenish yellow cones (photo below). This plant is found in a restricted area of the Blue Mountains, New South Wales.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Lady O'
plants.context: 10. Cross the road to see on your left and right Grevillea ‘Lady O’, a long blooming shrub with red flowers and bright green foliage (photo below). ‘Lady O’ is a cross between a Grevillea victoriae hybrid x Grevillea rhyolitica made by local plant breeder Peter Ollerenshaw and named for his mother.

plants.name: Banksia neoanglica
plants.context: 11. On your right is Banksia neoanglica, or New England Banksia, with silver backed dark green foliage with new slender green cones (photo below). This shrub grows along the east coast of Queensland and New South Wales.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Bonfire'
plants.context: 12. On your left is Grevillea ‘Bonfire’, a tall bush with fine dark green needle foliage and clusters of red flowers (photo below left). This plant is a hy- brid between Grevillea johnsonii and G. wilsonii.

plants.name: Grevillea manglesii subsp. ornithopoda
plants.context: 13. Again on your left is Grevillea manglesii subsp. ornithopoda, or Birdsfoot Grevillea, a large bush with frothy white terminal clusters of flowers and tripartite ‘birdsfoot’ foliage (photo above right). This plant is native to Western Australia near Perth.

plants.name: Hakea victoria
plants.context: 14. On your right is Hakea victoria or Royal Ha- kea with stemJclasping, green veined foliage with prickly edges (photo above). This plant is found in a restricted area on the south coast of Western Australia.

plants.name: Medicosma cunninghamii
plants.context: 15. Cross the road towards the Sydney Region Flora to see on your left Medicosma cunninghamii, a rainforest tree, called Pinkheart or Bonewood (photo above). This tree, with dark green foliage and white star flowers, is found in northern coastal New South Wales and south- eastern Queensland. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk along the Main Path to see some winter flowers

plants.name: Epacris purpurascens
plants.context: 1. On your right, in a pot, is Epacris purpurascens, a sparse, bush with close, pickly reddish leaves and pale pink star flowers with red stamens (photo above). This plant is found ion the coast from Sydney to Wollongong in New South Wales and is listed as vulnerable in the

plants.name: Epacris impressa 'Bega'
plants.context: 2. Still on your right is Epacris impressa ‘Bega’, a small bush with red tubular flowers (photo next page top left). This plant is found in southern New South Wales, near Bega.

plants.name: Pimelea physodes
plants.context: 3. Again on your right, in a pot and in the ground, is Pimelea physodes or Qualup Bell with greyJgreen foliage, reddish stems and pendant green bracts enclosing the small flower with dark red outer bracts (photo above right). This plant is found in southwestern Western Australia and is considered the most beautiful of the genus.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Scarlet King'
plants.context: 4. On your right is Grevillea ‘Scarlet King’, an attractive cultivar with dark red toothbrush flowers contrasting with white stems and greyJgreen divided foliage (photo above).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Peaches and Cream'
plants.context: 5. Again on your right is Grevillea ‘Peaches and Cream’ with deeply divided green leaves and large flower heads of pink and cream (photo above). This hybrid was developed in Queensland by Jan Glazebrook and Dennis Cox and patented in 2006.

plants.name: Anigozanthos 'Bush Pearl'
plants.context: 6. On your left is Anigozanthos ‘Bush Pearl’, a hybrid Kangaroo Paw with longJblooming bright pink flowers developed by Angus Stewart. (photo below)

plants.name: Eremophila subfloccosa subsp. subfloccosa
plants.context: 7. Further on your right, in a pot, is Eremophila subfloccosa subsp. subfloc- cosa, a low spreading shrub with furry silver foliage clasping the stem and green tubular flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to central and southern Western Australia and South Australia

plants.name: Correa baeuerlenii
plants.context: 8. Cross the bridge and go past the café to see on your left Correa baeuerlenii with long green bells and shiny aromatic foliage (photo above right). The calyx has an expanded base which looks like a chef's hat, resulting in the shrub's common name, Chef's Cap Correa. This plant is endemic to southern coastal New South Wales.

plants.name: Banksia 'Stumpy Gold'
plants.context: 9. Again on your left is Banksia ‘Stumpy Gold’ with fine, toothed linear foliage and short gold brushes with rusty red styles (photo below left). This plant is a dwarf cultivar of Banksia spinulosa var. collina that was selected by Richard Anderson of Merricks Nursery in Vic- toria from material collected on the New South Wales Central Coast.

plants.name: Epacris longiflora 'Nectar Pink'
plants.context: 10. Still on your left is Epacris longiflora ‘Nectar Pink’, a very floriferous small shrub covered in slender pink bells with white tips (photo above right).

plants.name: Acacia alata var. biglandulosa
plants.context: 11. On your right is Acacia alata var. biglandulosa or Winged Wattle, which has flattened phyllodes and many white fluffy ball flowers (photo below). This plant is native to Western Australia near Geraldton.

plants.name: Banksia ericifolia subsp. ericifolia
plants.context: 12. Continue up the hill on the Main Path and bear right to see on your left Banksia ericifolia subsp. ericifolia, a longJflowering, mediumJsized shrub with divided foliage and long orange inflo- rescences (photo below left). This plant is native to the central coast of New South Wales, but has naturalised in small numbers in Victoria.

plants.name: Banksia neoanglica
plants.context: 13. Also on your left is Banksia neoanglica, (B. spinulosa var. neoanglica) or New England Banksia, with silver backed dark green foliage with yellow brushes held upright (photo above right). This shrub grows along the east coast of Queensland and New South Wales

plants.name: Grevillea manglesii subsp. ornithopoda
plants.context: 14. Still on your left is Grevillea manglesii subsp. ornithopoda, or Birdsfoot Grevillea, a large bush with frothy white terminal clusters of flowers and tripartite ‘birdsfoot’ foliage (photo below left). This plant is native to Western Australia near Perth.

plants.name: Grevillea tripartita subsp. macrostylis
plants.context: 15. On your left is Grevillea tripartita subsp. macrostylis, an open, rangy plant with dark green, prickly, three lobed foliage and large single red and cream flowers with long showy red styles (photo above right). This plant is native to southern Western Australia, near Esperance A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will walk along the Main Path to see some winter flowers

plants.name: Pimelea physodes
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre look to your right to see, both in a pot and in the ground, Pimelea physodes, or Qualup Bell, with grey- green foliage close to reddish stems and pendant green bracts enclosing the small flower with dark red outer bracts (photo above). This plant is found in southwestern Western Australia and is considered to be the most beautiful of the genus.

plants.name: Pandorea sp. Mt. Maroon
plants.context: 2. Continue across the bridge and past the café to see on your right, in a pot, Pandorea sp. Mt. Maroon, a small trailing plant with cream bells with maroon centres and markings (photo next page top left). This plant is native to southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Robyn Gordon'
plants.context: 3. Bear right down the path to see on your right Grevillea ‘Robyn Gordon’ with deeply divided green foliage and red/pink flowers (photo above right). This plant is very popular and has been planted widely in Australia and other countries. It is a chance hybrid from the garden of the late David Gordon of Myall Park, Glenmorgan, Queensland and named after his daughter.

plants.name: Crowea saligna 'Rosy Glow'
plants.context: 4. On your left is Crowea saligna ‘Rosy Glow’ a small neat bush with pink star flowers (photo above).

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia 'Dwarf Orange'
plants.context: 5. Further on your right is Corymbia ficifolia ‘Dwarf Orange’, a small tree, with dark green foli- age with attractive red new growth (photo above). This grafted gum, originally from Western Australia, is one of the most spectacular when in full flower.

plants.name: Alyogyne 'West Coast Gem'
plants.context: 6. On your left is Alyogyne ‘West Coast Gem’ with a few clear purple ‘hibiscus’ style flowers which open for a short period only, but are prolific (photo below). The bush is medium sized with coarse green foliage.

plants.name: Phebalium verrucosum
plants.context: 8. Turn up to your left to see on your left, Phebalium verrucosum, (syn. Phebalium squamulosum subsp. verrucosum), a small shrub with masses of white heads of flowers (photo below). This plant is native to northeastern New South Wales

plants.name: Phebalium squamulosum subsp. verrucosum)
plants.context: 8. Turn up to your left to see on your left, Phebalium verrucosum, (syn. Phebalium squamulosum subsp. verrucosum), a small shrub with masses of white heads of flowers (photo below). This plant is native to northeastern New South Wales

plants.name: Eremophila maculata subsp. maculata
plants.context: 9. Turn sharp left up the hill to see on your right Eremophila maculata subsp. maculata, a small bush with light green foliage and yellow tubular flowers (photo below). This plant is found in the drier inland areas of all main- land states of Australia.

plants.name: Epacris calvertiana var. calvertiana
plants.context: 10. Continue up the hill, then left on Main Path and right on road to see on your right Epacris calvertiana var. calvertiana, with cream bells on dark green foliage (photo below). This small shrub is native to coastal New South Wales.

plants.name: Banksia aquilonia
plants.context: 11. On your left, somewhat hidden, is Banksia aquilonia, a tree to 8 metres tall, with long green leaves and tan young flowers which develop into pale yellow brushes (photo below). This plant is native to northern coastal Queensland.

plants.name: Grevillea sericea subsp. sericea
plants.context: 12. Continue along the road above the Rock Gar- den to see on your right Grevillea sericea subsp. sericea, an airy bush with light green foliage and white spider flowers (photo below left). This plant occurs naturally west of Sydney.

plants.name: Acacia parvipinnula
plants.context: 13. Turn left up the hill towards the Red Centre Garden to see on your right Acacia parvipinnula, or Silver Stemmed Wattle, a tree of dark green, ferny foliage and pale yellow, scented balls of flower. This wattle is native to central eastern New South Wales

plants.name: Acacia ulicifolia
plants.context: 14. Also on your right is Acacia ulicifolia, or Prickly Moses, with many pale yellow to white balls of flower on fine, dark green, prickly foliage (photo below left). This wattle grows along the eastern part of Australia from Queensland to Tasmania.

plants.name: Acacia oshanesii
plants.context: 15. On your left is Acacia oshanesii, a wattle native to coastal New South Wales and Queens- land (photo above right). This tree has fine, dark- green divided foliage with a few fluffy yellow ball flowers. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will walk up the hill to see some early wattles in flower

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk up the hill behind the café, along the road above the Rock Garden and return towards the Visitor Centre

plants.name: Eucalyptus caesia 'Silver Princess'
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre on your right is Eucalyptus caesia ‘Silver Princess’ with large, heart-shaped, leathery green leaves and dark red stems (photo above). This ornamental tree has a weeping habit, and will develop white branches, minni-ritchi bark with peeling curls, and large red flowers

plants.name: Guichenotia ledifolia
plants.context: 2. Low on your right is Guichenotia ledifolia, a small shrub with grey green foliage covered in drooping, dusty pink, 5-petalled flowers with maroon centres (photo top left next page. This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Epacris purpurascens var. purpurascens
plants.context: 3. Further on your right, in a pot, is Epacris purpurascens var. purpurascens, a sparse, drooping bush with prickly red leaves and mauve white flowers with red centres, found in coastal areas from Sydney to Wollongong in New South Wales (photo above right). This plant is listed as vulnerable in the wild.

plants.name: Pimelea physodes
plants.context: 4. Again on your right, both in a pot and in the ground, is Pimelea physodes. or Qualup Bell, with grey-green foliage held close to reddish stems and pendant green bracts enclosing the small flow- er with decorative dark red outer bracts (photo above). This plant is found in southwestern West- ern Australia and is considered the most beautiful of the genus.

plants.name: Anigozanthos 'Bush Pearl'
plants.context: 5. Still on your right is a group of Anigozanthos ‘Bush Pearl’, a hybrid Kangaroo Paw with long- blooming bright pink flowers developed by Angus Stewart (photo above).

plants.name: Grevillea rosmarinifolia 'Rosy Posy'
plants.context: 6. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see on your right Grevillea rosmarinifolia ‘Rosy Posy’, a compact bush with linear foliage and pendant racemes of pink and cream flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea bipinnatifida 'Jingle Bells'
plants.context: 7. Again on your right is Grevillea bipinnatifida ‘Jingle Bells’, a standard grevillea with deeply divided stiff, prickly foliage and many trusses of pink and orange flowers (photo below left).

plants.name: Hakea recurva
plants.context: 8. Continue up the hill, then turn right along the road above the Rock Garden to see on your right Hakea recurva, a large shrub with fearsomely prickly, grey-green needle foliage and some pinkish-yellow fragrant flowers beginning to open (photo above right). This plant is native to a band east from the area between Perth and Geraldton.

plants.name: Hakea constablei
plants.context: 9. Further on your right is Hakea constablei, a bushy shrub or small tree with very large brown nuts (photo below). This plant is endemic to the Blue Mountains near Sydney and was named after Ernest Constable, a plant collector for the Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney.

plants.name: Grevillea tripartita subsp. macrostylis
plants.context: 10. Still on your right is Grevillea tripartita subsp. macrostylis, an open, rangy plant with dark green, prickly, three lobed foliage and large single red and cream flowers with long showy red styles (photo below). This plant is native to southern Western Australia, near Esperance.

plants.name: Grevillea manglesii subsp. ornithopoda
plants.context: 11. Turn right down the hill to see on your right Grevillea manglesii subsp. ornithopoda, or Birdsfoot Grevillea, a large bush with frothy white terminal clusters of flowers and tripartite ‘birdsfoot’ foliage (photo below). This plant is native to Western Australia near Perth.

plants.name: Grevillea corrugata
plants.context: 12. Again on your right is Grevillea corrugata, a shrub with deeply lobed leaves, endemic to southwestern Western Australia (photo below left). This bush has prominent white buds which will open to white flowers August to September.

plants.name: Grevillea asteriscosa
plants.context: 13. Go past the turn along the Main Path and turn right along the next road to see on the corner Grevillea asteriscosa, or Star-leaf Grevillea,with small, dark green, prickly foliage and lipstick red flowers with long styles (photo above right). This plant is found in the wild in southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Banksia neoanglica
plants.context: 15. On your right is Banksia neoanglica, (syn. B. spinulosa var. neoanglica), or New England Banksia, with silver backed dark green foliage with yellow/gold brushes held upright (photo above right). This shrub grows along the east coast of Queensland and New South Wales. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will walk up the hill behind the café, along the road above the Rock Garden and return towards the Visitor Centre

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk up the Main Path to see some grevilleas in flower

plants.name: Anigozanthos manglesii
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre, on your right, in a pot, is Anigozanthos manglesii or Red and Green Kangaroo Paw, which is the floral emblem of Western Australia (photo above). This plant is one of the most spectacular of the Kangaroo Paws, with its green flowers with bright red bases on red furry stems. This plant grows along the southern part of the west coast of Western Australia.

plants.name: Acacia boormanii
plants.context: 2. Acacia boormanii, or Snowy River Wattle, on your left, has fine needle foliage and masses of golden ball flowers (photo next page top left). This plant is a medium-sized, suckering, multi- stemmed, copse-forming shrub, with a native range in the alpine country of southeastern Australia.

plants.name: Pandorea sp. Mt. Maroon
plants.context: 3. Cross the bridge and go past the café to see Pandorea sp. Mt. Maroon, on your right, in a pot, a small trailing plant with cream bells with maroon centres and markings (photo above right). This plant is found in southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Rhodanthe anthemoides
plants.context: 4. Also on your right is Rhodanthe anthemoides, a mound of grey-green foliage almost covered with white daisy flowers with gold centres (photo above). Also known as Chamomile Sunray, this plant is widespread on the mainland but listed as rare in Tasmania.

plants.name: Epacris longiflora 'Nectar Pink'
plants.context: 5. On your left is Epacris longiflora ‘Nectar Pink’, a very floriferous small shrub covered in slender pink bells with white tips (photo above).

plants.name: Acacia alata var. Biglandulosa
plants.context: 6. On your right is Acacia alata var. Biglandulosa, or Winged Wattle, with flat- tened phyllodes and masses of white fluffy ball flowers (photo below). This plant is native to Western Australia near Geraldton.

plants.name: Darwinia oldfieldii
plants.context: 7. Bear left up the Main Path to see on your left, in a pot, Darwinia oldfieldii, or Oldfield’s Darwinia, with narrow green foliage and bright pink flowers with long styles (photo below). This plant is native to the area around Geraldton, Western Australia.

plants.name: Grevillea monticola
plants.context: 8. Continue on the Main Path to see on your left Grevillea monticola, with prickly ‘holly- like’ foliage with many rusty orange buds which open to small white toothbrush flowers (photo below). This plant is endemic to south- western Western Australia.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Poorinda Adorning'
plants.context: 9. Grevillea ‘Poorinda Adorning’, on your right, is a low, prickly groundcover with bright red flowers with long styles (photo below). The series of Poorinda grevilleas were made from crosses by Leo Hodge at his property W Tree near Buchan, Victoria.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Coconut Ice'
plants.context: 10. On your right is Grevillea ‘Coconut Ice’ with large pink/orange spider flowers with long red styles (photo below). This hybrid plant is grown from seed collected from G. bipinnatifida. The male parent was G. banksii (white flowered form). The seedling was raised by Mr. M. Hodge of Queensland.

plants.name: Grevillea flexuosa
plants.context: 11. Turn right along the road to see on your right Grevillea flexuosa, or Zig-Zag Grevillea, with green, prickly divided foliage and large cream rods of flower which are sweetly scent- ed (photo below). This endangered shrub is found only in a small area east of Perth in Western Australia.

plants.name: Grevillea irrasa subsp. didymochiton
plants.context: 12. On your left is Grevillea irrasa subsp. didymochiton, a tall rangy bush with oblong green foliage and red spider flowers from the Moruya and Pambula areas of southeastern NSW (photo below left).

plants.name: Banksia neoanglica
plants.context: 13. Also on your left is Banksia neoanglica, or New England Banksia, with silver backed dark green foliage with yellow/gold brushes held upright (photo above right). This shrub grows along the east coast of Queensland and New South Wales

plants.name: Grevillea 'Sid Reynolds'
plants.context: 14. On your right is Grevillea ‘Sid Reynolds’ which arose as a seedling in the garden of Sid Reynolds and is thought to be a hybrid between Grevillea pinaster and G. commutate (photo below left). This medium sized shrub has fine foliage and red and yellow spider flowers in spring.

plants.name: Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa
plants.context: 15. Also on your right is Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa, or Hairpin Banksia, with long orange flowers, which is found in open forests and woodlands of the coasts and mountains of New South Wales and Queensland (photo above right). A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will walk up the Main Path to see some grevilleas in flower

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre up the hill behind the café and along the road above the Rock Garden

plants.name: Grevillea 'Peaches and Cream'
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre look down the steps to your right to see Grevillea ‘Peaches and Cream’ with deeply divided green leaves and large flower heads of pink and cream (photo above). This hybrid was developed in Queensland by Jan Glazebrook and Dennis Cox and patented in 2006.

plants.name: Guichenotia ledifolia
plants.context: 2. Low on your right is Guichenotia ledifolia, a small shrub with grey green foliage covered in drooping, dusty pink 5-petalled flowers with ma- roon centres (photo next page top left). This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Epacris longiflora
plants.context: 3. Still on your right is Epacris longiflora, with long thin tubular white flowers on a straggly light green bush (photo above right). This plant is found in the wild along the coast of New South Wales and Queensland.

plants.name: Epacris exserta
plants.context: 4. To the rear on your right is Epacris exserta, or South Esk Heath, a small erect bush with white flowers with maroon stamens (photo above). This riparian plant is endemic to northern Tasmania along three rivers, South Esk, North Esk and Supply and is considered threatened in the wild.

plants.name: Epacris impressa 'Bega'
plants.context: 5. Again on your right is Epacris impressa ‘Bega’, a small bush with vivid red tubular flowers (photo above). This plant is found in southern New South Wales, near Bega.

plants.name: Pimelea physodes
plants.context: 6. On your right, in a pot and in the ground, is Pimelea physodes or Qualup Bell with grey- green foliage, reddish stems and pendant green bracts enclosing a small flower with dark red outer bracts (photo below). This plant is found in southwestern Western Australia and is considered the most beautiful of the genus.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Scarlet King'
plants.context: 7. On your right and left is Grevillea ‘Scarlet King’, an attractive cultivar with dark red toothbrush flowers contrasting with white stems and grey-green divided foliage (photo below).

plants.name: Leptospermum variabile
plants.context: 8. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see on your right Leptospermum variabile, a large shrub with many branches, small leaves and numerous white ‘tea-tree’ flowers (photo below). This plant is native to northern NSW and Queensland.

plants.name: Hardenbergia violacea
plants.context: 9. Hardenbergia violacea, low on your right, is a vigorous vine with oblong leathery leaves and bright purple pea flowers (photo below). This plant is also known as False Sar- saparilla, or Purple Coral Pea and is found in eastern Australia from Queensland to Tasmania.

plants.name: Grevillea rosmarinifolia 'Rosy Posy'
plants.context: 10. Again on your right is Grevillea rosmarinifolia ‘Rosy Posy’, a compact bush with linear foliage and pendent racemes of pink and cream flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Chamelaucium 'Cascade Brook'
plants.context: 11. Continue up the hill then turn right along the road above the Rock Garden to see on your right Chamelaucium ‘Cascade Brook’, a form of Geraldton Wax, which is endemic to coastal areas of Western Australia between Perth and Geraldton (photo below). This plant is an open airy bush with masses of purplish-pink 5 petalled flowers with darker centres.

plants.name: Acacia ingramii
plants.context: 12. Continue olong the road and on your left is Acacia ingramii, a small tree with fine linear foli- age and masses of gold flower balls (photo below left). This plant grows in the wild near Armidale in northern New South Wales.

plants.name: Hakea recurva
plants.context: 13. On your right is Hakea recurva, a large shrub with fearsomely prickly, grey-green needle foliage and many pinkish-yellow fragrant flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to a band east from the area between Perth and Geraldton.

plants.name: Acacia cardiophylla
plants.context: 14. Acacia cardiophylla, or West Wyalong Wattle, on your left, has ferny, light green bipin- nate foliage and masses of yellow balls of flowers (photo above). This plant occurs in the wild in cen- tral and southern New South Wales.

plants.name: Grevillea vestita
plants.context: 15. Grevillea vestita, further on your right, is a large open bush with many starbursts of white flowers (photo above). This shrub is endemic to southwestern Western Australia A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre up the hill behind the café and along the road above the Rock Garden

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk around the car parks near the Visitor Centre to see some wattles in flower

plants.name: Philotheca myoporoides 'Winter Rouge'
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre go down the steps to your right, to see on your right Philotheca myoporoides ‘Winter Rouge’, a small shrub with green aromatic foliage, bright pink buds and white star flowers (photo above).

plants.name: Acacia ingramii
plants.context: 2. Also on your right is Acacia ingramii, a large bush or small tree with fine linear foliage and masses of gold ball flowers (photo next page top left). This wattle grows in the wild near Armidale in northern New South Wales.

plants.name: Anigozanthos 'Bush Pearl'
plants.context: 3. Still on your right is Anigozanthos ‘Bush Pearl’, a hybrid Kangaroo Paw with long-blooming bright pink flowers developed by Angus Stewart (photo above right).

plants.name: Xerochrysum bracteatum 'Dargan Hill Monarch'
plants.context: 4. At the botton of the steps, on your right, is Xerochrysum bracteatum ‘Dargan Hill Monarch’, a magnificent yellow paper daisy with gold centres and green foliage (photo above). Xerochrysum 'Dargan Hill Monarch' is a herbaceous form of the well known Everlasting or Straw flower which was found growing about one mile inland from Cunningham's Gap in southern Queensland in May 1961.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Scarlet King'
plants.context: 5. Turn left along the path to see on your left Grevillea ‘Scarlet King’ an attractive cultivar with dark red toothbrush flowers contrasting with white stems and grey-green divided foliage (photo above)

plants.name: Rhodanthe anthemoides
plants.context: 6. Cross the road and bear right down the path to see on your right Rhodanthe anthemoides also known as Chamomile Sunray, a mound of grey-green foliage almost covered with white daisy flowers with gold centres (photo below). This plant is widespread on the mainland but listed as rare in Tasmania.

plants.name: Thryptomene saxicola
plants.context: 7. On your right is Thryptomene saxicola making a strong display with airy arching sprays of tiny pink flowers on fine green foliage (photo below). This plant is found in granite outcrops and hills in southern Western Australia.

plants.name: Leptecophylla juniperina subsp. parvifolia
plants.context: 8. On your left is Leptecophylla juniperina subsp. parvifolia, a bush with dense, hard, prickly green leaves and tubular white bell flowers with a strong scent (photo below). This plant occurs in alpine and subalpine areas of Tasmania and this particular subspecies has shorter leaves than the other subspecies.

plants.name: Zieria smithii × cytisoides
plants.context: 9. Zieria smithii x cytisoides, also on the left, has masses of tiny white flowers with pinkish centres (photo below).

plants.name: Acacia filicifolia
plants.context: 10. On your right is Acacia filicifolia or Fern- leaf Wattle (photo below). This large tree has dark-green ferny foliage and pale yellow ball flowers and occurs naturally in southern Queensland and New South Wales. Cross at the zebra crossing and turn right up the hill, then left into the middle carpark.

plants.name: Acacia hakeoides
plants.context: 11. On your left is Acacia hakeoides, or Hakea Wattle, a small tree with linear green foliage, reddish stems, and clusters of large yellow flower balls (photo below). This plant is native to southern Australia.

plants.name: Acacia cardiophylla
plants.context: 12. On your right is Acacia cardiophylla, or West Wyalong Wattle, with ferny, light green bi- pinnate foliage and masses of yellow ball flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to central and southern New South Wales.

plants.name: Acacia williamsonii
plants.context: 13. On your left is Acacia williamsonii with yellow green linear foliage and yellow ball flowers (photo above right). Whirrakee Wattle is native to southern New South Wales and Victoria.

plants.name: Hardenbergia violacea
plants.context: 14. Go carefully across the road to see on your left Hardenbergia violacea, a vigorous vine with oblong leathery leaves and bright purple pea flowers, also known as False Sarsaparilla or Purple Coral Pea (photo below left). This plant is found in eastern Australia from Queensland to Tasmania.

plants.name: Pomaderris intermedia
plants.context: 15. Also on your left, intertwined with Hardenber- gia violacea, is Pomaderris intermedia, a large open shrub with smooth green foliage and striking yellow heads of flowers (photo above right). This plant grows in eastern Australia from Tasmania to northern New South Wales. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will walk around the car parks near the Visitor Centre to see some wattles in flower

plants.name: Pandorea pandorana 'Golden Showers'
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre look up to the left to see Pandorea pandorana ‘Golden Showers’, a vigorous twining vine with masses of tubular brown and gold flowers (photo above). This species is widespread in Australia down the east coast from Cape York to Flinders Island in Bass Strait and also occurs in central Australia.

plants.name: Anigozanthos manglesii
plants.context: 2. On your right, in a pot, is Anigozanthos manglesii or Red and Green Kangaroo Paw, which is the floral emblem of Western Australia (photo next page top left). This plant is one of the most spectacular of the Kangaroo Paws, with its green flowers and bright red bases on red furry stems. This plant grows along the southern part of the west coast of Western Australia.

plants.name: Acacia cognata 'Green Mist'
plants.context: 3. On your left is Acacia cognata ‘Green Mist’, a weeping shrub with green linear leaves and yellow balls of flower (photo above right). This cultivar is a dwarf form of the Bower Wattle, which is found in the wild in New South Wales and Victoria.

plants.name: Asterolasia 'Lemon Essence'
plants.context: 4. On your right is Asterolasia ‘Lemon Essence’, a compact shrub with many lemon star flowers (photo above). This plant was developed at the ANBG.

plants.name: Prostanthera ovalifolia 'Brundah Candy'
plants.context: 5. Also on your right is Prostanthera ovalifolia ‘Brundah Candy’, a medium sized shrub with highly aromatic leaves and masses of pink flowers (photo above). This plant was found by Noel and Sharon Cartwright at North Brundah School site, Brundah Hills, east of Grenfell, NSW.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Scarlet King'
plants.context: 6. Still on your right is Grevillea ‘Scarlet King’ an attractive cultivar with dark red toothbrush flowers contrasting with white stems and grey- green divided foliage (photo below).

plants.name: Chorizema cordatum - C. varium
plants.context: 7. Further on your right is Chorizema cordatum - C. varium (intermediate form), or Heart-leaved Flame Pea, a showy weeping shrub with vivid orange/pink flowers and bright green prickly foliage (photo below). This plant grows naturally in the moist southwestern parts of Western Australia.

plants.name: Xanthorrhoea glauca subsp. angustifolia
plants.context: 8. On your left, as you cross the bridge to the café, is Xanthorrhoea glauca subsp. angustifolia, a large grass tree with rippling, grey-green, linear foliage and many new flow- er spikes (photo below). This plant is found in the wild in Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland.

plants.name: Dracophyllum macranthum
plants.context: 9. Go past the café and bear right down the path to see on your right, in a pot, Dracophyl- lum macranthum with long spiky leaves and bright pink flowers. This plant occurs on the north coast of New South Wales and is listed as vulnerable in the wild.

plants.name: Phebalium squamulosum subsp. lineare
plants.context: 10. On your left is a group of Phebalium squamulosum subsp. lineare, a medium shrub with dull green, needle foliage and yellow star flowers (photo below). This plant is found in the wild in the upper Hunter Valley of New South Wales.

plants.name: Indigofera australis
plants.context: 11. On your left is Indigofera australis, or Austral Indigo, a small straggly bush with pinnate blue-green leaves and white flowers (photo below). This member of the pea family usually has pink flowers and is found from northern Queensland to Tasmania and also South Australia and Western Australia.

plants.name: Philotheca myoporoides subsp. myoporoides
plants.context: 12. On your right is Philotheca myoporoides subsp. myoporoides, beloved by bees and hover flies (photo below left). This plant forms a neat bush with dull green foliage, pink buds and white star flowers and is endemic to southeastern Australia.

plants.name: Alyogyne 'West Coast Gem'
plants.context: 13. On your left is Alyogyne ‘West Coast Gem’ with clear purple ‘hibiscus’ style flowers which open for a short period only, but are prolific (photo above right). The bush is medium sized with coarse foliage.

plants.name: Homoranthus montanus
plants.context: 14. Turn left up the path to see on your left Homoranthus montanus, or Mountain Mouse Bush, with dense green foliage and pink buds opening to lemon flowers, which is found in a small area in southeastern Queensland and is considered vulnerable in the wild (photo above).

plants.name: Chamelaucium floriferum
plants.context: 15. Also on your left is Chamelaucium floriferum, or Walpole Wax, a small bush with narrow aromatic leaves and many circular white flowers with maroon centres (photo above). This plant is native to extreme southwestern Western Australia. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Only a short walk today across the bridge to the café area, as there are so many plants in flower

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre up the hill behind the café and along the road above the Rock Garden

plants.name: Grevillea wilkinsonii
plants.context: 1. As you approach the Visitor Centre from the upper carpark, look to your right to see on your right Grevillea wilkinsonii, or Tumut Grevillea (photo above). This plant was first discovered in 1991 near Tumut, NSW, and is listed as endangered in the wild. The Tumut Grevillea is medium sized shrub with oblong, toothed leaves and mauve to purple toothbrush flowers.

plants.name: Prostanthera ovalifolia
plants.context: 2. On your right is Prostanthera ovalifolia, a medium sized shrub with highly aromatic leaves and masses of purple flowers (photo next page top left). This plant is native to the inland areas of New South Wales and southern Queensland.

plants.name: Zieria buxijugum
plants.context: 3. Also on your right is Zieria buxijugum, or Box Range Zieria, a small bush with grey-green leaves and many small white flowers with four petals and maroon centres (photo above right). This plant is restricted to a small area of southern coastal NSW, near Pambula.

plants.name: Hibbertia empetrifolia
plants.context: 4. On your left is Hibbertia empetrifolia, a low scrambling shrub with green leaves and wiry stems ending in bright yellow flowers (photo above). Also known as Tangled Guinea-flower, this plant is native to southeastern Australia.

plants.name: Thelychiton rex
plants.context: 5. On your left is Thelychiton rex, or Golden King Orchid, a large orchid which grows on trees or rocks with stiff leathery leaves and yellow star shaped flowers (photo above). This plant is found in southeastern Queensland

plants.name: Thelychiton speciosus
plants.context: 6. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see on your left Thelychiton speciosus, a popular and widely grown orchid previously known as Dendrobium speciosum (photo below). The Rock Lily or Rock Orchid has racemes of showy cream flowers with yellow buds and dark-green leaves. This orchid can grow on rocks or trees.

plants.name: Grevillea bipinnatifida 'Jingle Bells'
plants.context: 7. . On your right is Grevillea bipinnatifida ‘Jingle Bells’ a standard grevillea with deeply divided stiff, prickly foliage and many trusses of pink and orange flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Indigofera australis
plants.context: 8. On your left is Indigofera australis, or Aus- tral Indigo, a small straggly bush with pinnate blue green leaves and pink flowers (photo below). This member of the pea family is found from northern Queensland to Tasmania and also in South Australia and Western Australia.

plants.name: Chamelaucium 'Cascade Brook'
plants.context: 9. Turn right along the road above the Rock Garden to see on your right Chamelaucium ‘Cascade Brook’, or Geraldton Wax which is endemic to coastal areas of Western Australia between Perth and Geraldton (photo below). This plant forms an open, airy bush with mass- es of purplish-pink 5 petalled flowers with dark- er centres.

plants.name: Telopea speciocissima 'Corroboree'
plants.context: 10. On your right is Telopea speciocissima ‘Corroboree’, a tall shrub with an upright habit and bright red/pink ‘waratah’ flowers (photo below). This cultivar was selected in 1974 by Nanette Cuming from seedlings of Telopea speciosissima purchased from Breakoday Nursery, Box Hill, Victoria.

plants.name: Grevillea monticola
plants.context: 11. Also on your right is Grevillea monticola, with prickly ‘holly-like’ foliage with many rusty orange buds which open to small white tooth- brush flowers (photo below). This plant is endemic to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Acacia havilandiorum
plants.context: 12. On your left is Acacia havilandiorum, a small bush with arching stems of grey-green nee- dle foliage and gold ball flowers (photo below). This plant is native to New South Wales, Victoria and South Australia.

plants.name: Hakea macraeana
plants.context: 13. On your right is Hakea macraeana, or Needle -wood, a small tree with fine drooping foliage and white flowers along the stems, native to eastern Australia (photo below left).

plants.name: Acacia fimbriata
plants.context: 14. On your left is Acacia fimbriata, or Brisbane Golden Wattle, a small tree or shrub with profuse fluffy yellow ball flowers and narrow green leaves (photo above right). This plant occurs in Queensland and NSW.

plants.name: Kunzea affinis
plants.context: 15. On your left is Kunzea affinis, an open bush with purplish-pink flowers and small, crowded, green leaves (photo above). This plant is native to the southwestern coast of Western Australia near Esperance. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre up the hill behind the café and along the road above the Rock Garden

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will take only a short walk to the café area as there are so many plants in flower

plants.name: Dendrobium × delicatum
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre look across to your left to see Dendrobium x delicatum where many clusters of white flowers with oblong green foliage cover a rock (photo above). This plant is native along the Great Dividing Range in south- eastern Queensland, as a lithophyte (a plant that grows on rock).

plants.name: Stylidium bulbiferum
plants.context: 2. On your right, in a pot, is Stylidium bulbiferum, or Circus Triggerplant, mat-forming, with evergreen, linear leaves and short spikes of apricot ‘trigger’ flowers (photo next page top left). These plants grow in the wild in Western Austral- ia near Perth on granite outcrops in woods and on heaths.

plants.name: Stylidium adnatum
plants.context: 3. Also on your right, in a pot, is Stylidium adnatum, or Common Beaked Triggerplant, with bright-green foliage and soft pink clusters of flowers in spring (photo above right). This plant grows in the wild in southwestern Western Australia along the coast.

plants.name: Stylidium armeria
plants.context: 4. Again on your right, in a pot, is Stylidium armeria, or Thrift-leaved Triggerplant, with tufts of narrow leaves at the base and erect dark pink- magenta flowers (photo above). This plant is native to New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania, and Victoria.

plants.name: Eremophila nivea
plants.context: 5. On your left is Eremophila nivea, a small shrub with mauve tubular flowers and striking silver-grey foliage covered in hairs (photo above). This plant is found in the wild on the southern west coast of Western Australia.

plants.name: Pultenaea pedunculata 'Burnt Orange'
plants.context: 6. In a pot, on your right, is Pultenaea pedunculata ‘Burnt Orange’, a creeping plant with green foliage and orange and yellow pea flowers (photo below). This plant species occurs from Sydney south around the coast to South Australia, including Tasmania.

plants.name: Dampiera linearis 'Violet Princess'
plants.context: 7. On your right, in a pot, is Dampiera linearis ‘Violet Princess’, a small plant with soft, linear green leaves and dark purple flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Actinodium cunninghamii
plants.context: 8. Again, on your right, in a pot, is Actinodium cunninghamii with stem- clasping green foliage and pink daisy flowers with darker pink centres (photo below). The centres are fertile while the lighter flowers around the circumference are sterile. This plant is found in southwestern Western Aus- tralia and is named after the botanist Alan Cunningham.

plants.name: Telopea 'Braidwood Brilliant'
plants.context: 9. On your right are many newly planted Telopea ‘Braidwood Brilliant’, a hardy waratah which is a hybrid developed between Telopea speciosissima and T. mongaensis at the ANBG in 1962 (photo below). This plant is more frost tolerant than most waratahs, and has many brilliant red flowers.

plants.name: Xanthorrhoea glauca subsp. glauca
plants.context: 10. On your right is Xanthorrhoea glauca subsp. glauca, a large grass tree with rippling grey-green linear foliage and long stalks of small white flowers, dripping nectar, attracting much attention from birds, bees and butterflies (photo below left). This plant is found in the wild in coastal New South Wales and Queensland.

plants.name: Brachyscome diversifolia var. maritima
plants.context: 11. Just before you cross the bridge to the café, on your left, in a pot, is Brachyscome diversifolia var. maritima, with large white daisy flowers with gold centres (photo above right). This plant is native to Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia

plants.name: Daviesia horrida
plants.context: 12. Cross the bridge, go past the café to see on your left Daviesia horrida with grey, spiky linear foliage, yellow buds and small pea flowers of orange and red (photo below). This shrub is endemic to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Alyogyne huegelii 'Karana'
plants.context: 13. Bear right down the path to see on your left Alyogyne huegelii ‘Karana’ with masses of mauve flowers and coarse green foliage (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Bonfire'
plants.context: 14. Further on your left is Grevillea ‘Bonfire’, a tall bush with fine dark green needle foliage and many clusters of bright red flowers (photo below left). This plant is a hybrid between Grevillea johnsonii and G. wilsonii.

plants.name: Boronia 'Purple Jared'
plants.context: 15. Boronia ‘Purple Jared’, on your left, has green foliage and deep purple bell flowers (photo above right). This plant is a cross between Boronia megastima and B. heterophylla. For those of you (75%) who can smell boronias, it has a glorious scent. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will take only a short walk to the café area as there are so many plants in flower

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre up the road behind the café and along the road above the Rock Garden

plants.name: Anigozanthos viridis
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre look to your right to see in a pot Anigozanthos viridis, or Green Kangaroo Paw, with bright green furry flowers and red stems (photo above). This plant is found along the West Australian coast both north and south of Perth

plants.name: Anigozanthos 'Bush Blitz'
plants.context: 2. Further on your right is Anigozanthos ‘Bush Blitz’ with dark orange flowers with burgundy highlights in late spring and summer (photo next page top left). This cultivar, bred by Angus Stewart, flowers a little later than other Bush Gems but has an outstanding, long lasting display.

plants.name: Hibbertia stellaris
plants.context: 3. On your left, in a pot, is Hibbertia stellaris, or Orange Stars, with masses of orange star flowers on wiry foliage (photo above right). This brilliantly flowering ground cover from southern Western Australia grows naturally in swamps.

plants.name: Orthrosanthus multiflorus
plants.context: 4. Also on your left is Orthrosanthus multiflorus, or Morning Iris, a clumping plant with grass-like foliage and true blue flowers (photo below left). Each flower only lasts a day but they are produced in profusion during spring and summer. This plant is native to coastal southern and western Australia.

plants.name: Xanthorrhoea glauca subsp. angustifolia
plants.context: 5. On your right is Xanthorrhoea glauca subsp. angustifolia, a large grass tree with rippling, grey- green, linear foliage and an amazing nine flowering stalks with white flowers, dripping nectar, beloved by birds, bees and butterflies (photo above right). This plant is found in the wild in Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland.

plants.name: Olearia argophylla
plants.context: 7. Also on your left is Olearia argophylla, or Native Musk, a tall shrub or small tree with felt- ed grey leaves and many heads of white, strongly scented ‘daisy’ flowers with gold centres (photo below). This plant grows on the east coast in New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania.

plants.name: Callicoma serratifolia
plants.context: 8. On your left look up to see Callicoma serratifolia, a small tree with dark brown bark, with many fluffy white flowers with a strong scent and oval green leaves (photo be- low). This plant grows along the NSW coast north as far as southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Homoranthus papillatus
plants.context: 9. On your right is Homoranthus papillatus, or Mouse Bush, a compact shrub with fine green foliage and pale yellow-green flowers (photo below). This plant is listed as vulnerable in the wild and occurs only in the Granite Belt of Queensland north of Brisbane.

plants.name: Leptospermum 'Tickled Pink'
plants.context: 10. Also on your right is Leptospermum ‘Tickled Pink’ showing masses of pink ‘tea- tree’ flowers with green centres (photo below left). This plant is one of the cultivars developed at Bywong Nursery, Bungendore, New South Wales and is a hybrid between Leptospermum polygaolum 'Cardwell' and L. 'Rhiannon'.

plants.name: Hymenosporum flavum
plants.context: 11. On your left is Hymenosporum flavum, a small tree with highly-scented cream flowers aging to gold. This tree grows along the eastern Australia coast from the Hunter River in New South Wales north to Queensland and extending into New Guinea.

plants.name: Conostylis seorsiflora subsp. seorsiflora
plants.context: 12. Further on your right is Conostylis seorsiflora subsp. seorsiflora, a common species along coastal Western Australia between Albany and Cape Arid east of Esperance (photo below left). This plant is mat-forming, spreading by stolons, with many solitary yellow blooms.

plants.name: Chamelaucium 'Cascade Brook'
plants.context: 13. Turn left along the road above the Rock Garden to see on your right Chamelaucium ‘Cascade Brook’, or Geraldton Wax, which is endemic to coastal areas of Western Australia between Perth and Geraldton, an open airy bush with masses of purplish-pink, five-petalled flowers with darker centres (photo above right).

plants.name: Leptospermum polygalifolium subsp. montanum
plants.context: 14. On your left is Leptospermum polygalifolium ssp. montanum, also known as Tantoon Tea Tree or Mountain Tea Tree, a small tree covered in white five-petalled flowers with green centres (photo below left). This tree is native from the south coast of New South Wales to Cape York in far north Queensland

plants.name: Grevillea 'Mason's Hybrid'
plants.context: 15. On your right is Grevillea ‘Mason’s Hybrid’, a spreading bush with large spider blooms of pink, red and orange (photo above right). This hybrid arose from seed collected from an upright glaucous form of Grevillea bipinnatifida. The other parent is presumed to be G. banksii. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre up the road behind the café and along the road above the Rock Garden

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will visit the Rock Garden

plants.name: Callistemon subulatus
plants.context: 1. Go past the café and turn left up the road towards the Brittle Gum Lawn to see on your right Callistemon subulatus with bright red brushes and a low spreading habit (photo above). This plant is native to New South Wales and Victoria where it grows along the banks of watercourses.

plants.name: Doryanthes excelsa
plants.context: 2. Continue up the hill towards the Rock Garden, enter and walk up the steps to see on your right and left Doryanthes excelsa, or Gymea Lily (photo next page top left). This plant is indigenous to the coastal areas of New South Wales near Sydney and has sword-like leaves more than a metre long, and flower spikes 2-4 metres high.

plants.name: Eremaea pauciflora var. pauciflora
plants.context: 3. On your left is Eremaea pauciflora var. pauciflora, a small sprawling shrub with bright orange flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Verticordia plumosa var. plumosa
plants.context: 4. On your right is Verticordia plumosa var. plumosa, or Plumed Feather-flower, a small plant with many pink-purple flowers (photo above). This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Xanthorrhoea johnsonii
plants.context: 5. Turn right to see on your right Xanthorrhoea johnsonii, or Grass Tree, which has been burned to stimulate new growth (photo above). This plant is found in eastern parts of Queensland and New South Wales and the trunk can grow up to 5 metres tall.

plants.name: Verticordia galeata
plants.context: 6. Turn right to see on your right Verticordia galeata with bright gold, honey scented flow- ers in profusion (photo below). This plant occurs naturally near Geraldton, Western Australia.

plants.name: Grevillea whiteana
plants.context: 7. Go left across the plank bridge to see on your right Grevillea whiteana, a tall rangy bush with dark green linear leaves and creamy -white racemes of flowers (photo below). This plant occurs in the wild in southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Labichea lanceolata subsp. lanceolata
plants.context: 8. Turn right down the steps to see on your left Labichea lanceolata subsp. lanceolata, a large bush with bright green foliage and yellow flowers with a red throat (photo below). This plant is found in southwestern Western Australia, and is named after Jean Jacques Labiche (1748-1819), a second lieutenant on Freycinet's voyage around the world 1817-20.

plants.name: Verticordia pennigera
plants.context: 9. On your left, in a pot, is Verticordia pennigera, showing bright pink terminal clusters of fringed flowers on tiny grey-green foliage (photo below). Verticordia in Latin means ‘turner of hearts’. This beautiful genus comes mostly from southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Alyogyne huegelii 'West Coast Gem'
plants.context: 10. On your left is Alyogyne huegelii ‘West Coast Gem’ with clear purple ‘hibiscus’ style flowers which open for a short period only, but are prolific (photo below). The bush is medium sized with coarse foliage.

plants.name: Eremophila bignoniiflora × E. polyclada
plants.context: 11. Also on your left is Eremophila bignoniiflora x E. polyclada with linear green foliage and large tubular lilac-tinged white flowers with spotted throats (photo below).

plants.name: Alyogyne huegelii 'Misty'
plants.context: 12. Again on your left is Alyogyne huegelii ‘Misty’, a very attractive selection of A. huegelii with pale mauve flowers with maroon centres and green foliage (photo below left).

plants.name: Hibbertia pedunculata
plants.context: 13. On your right is Hibbertia pedunculata with bright yellow flowers on fine creeping foliage (photo above right). The species name ‘pedunculata’ refers to the flower having a peduncle or long stalk.

plants.name: Callistemon recurvus
plants.context: 14. At the bottom of the steps on your left is Callistemon recurvus, or Tinaroo Bottlebrush, with bright red brushes and occasionally leaves with the edges curved under (photo above). This plant is endemic to northern coastal Queensland.

plants.name: Callistachys lanceolata
plants.context: 15. On your left is Callistachys lanceolata, a small tree with green leaves and orange pea flowers with red accents (photo above). Commonly known as the Wonnich or Native Wil- low, this plant is native to southwestern Western Australia. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will visit the Rock Garden

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will take a short walk to the café, as there are many plants in flower

plants.name: Pandorea jasminoides
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre look up to your left to see Pandorea jasminoides covered in scented pink trumpet flowers with attractive mid-green foliage (photo above). This woody vine, also known as Bower of Beauty, is native to New South Wales and Queensland, and forms large pointed pods filled with papery seeds.

plants.name: Jasminum suavissimum
plants.context: 2. On the opposite wall is Jasminum suavissimum, or Forest Jasmine, with its five starry white petals and its lovely scent (photo next page top left). This plant is native to northeastern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Decaspermum struckoilicum
plants.context: 3. On your right as you walk towards the bridge is Decaspermum struckoilicum, or Mount Morgan Myrtle, a small tree with shiny olive-green leaves and many tiny white flowers (photo below right). This plant is considered endangered in the wild and occurs in only a very few localities near Mount Morgan in southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Dietes robinsoniana
plants.context: 4. On your left is Dietes robinsoniana, or Wedding Lily, with long strappy foliage and sweetly scented white flowers, with a gold fleck in the centre, held high on wiry stems (photo below left). This plant is found in the wild only on Lord Howe Island where it grows on cliff faces, often in exposed situations.

plants.name: Actinotus helianthi
plants.context: 5. Further on your right, in a pot, is Actinotus helianthi, or Flannel Flower, in full bloom with white star flowers with yellow grey centres and silver-grey divided foliage (photo above right). These plants are native to the coast and mountains of New South Wales and southern Queensland.

plants.name: Corymbia 'Summer Red'
plants.context: 6. On your right is Corymbia ‘Summer Red’, a grafted eucalypt with dark green leathery leaves and attractive orange-red new foliage and beautiful bud formations (photo below).

plants.name: Isopogon 'Little Drumsticks'
plants.context: 7. On your left is Isopogon ‘Little Drum- sticks’, or Broad-leaved Drumsticks, a low bushy shrub with well displayed yellow cone flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Homoranthus prolixus
plants.context: 9. On your left, in a pot, is Homoranthus prolixus, showing an attractive contrast between the layered grey-green foliage and acid yellow flowers (photo below). This plant is listed as vulnerable in the wild and only occurs in areas near Inverell and Bendemeer, New South Wales.

plants.name: Lomatia polymorpha
plants.context: 10. Cross the bridge to see on your right, Lomatia polymorpha, or Mountain Guitar Plant, a shrub or small tree with white heads of flowers and linear green leaves (photo below). This plant is endemic to Tasmania.

plants.name: Melaleuca liniarifolia 'Seafoam'
plants.context: 11. On your far right is Melaleuca liniarifolia ‘Seafoam’ in full bloom with white, soft, fluffy flowers attracting a wide variety of insects (photo below). This paperbark has twisted branches and green needle foliage.

plants.name: Xanthorrhea
plants.context: 12. On your left, in full flower, is Xanthorrhea or Grass Tree, with many creamy-white flowers dripping with nectar attracting insects and birds (photo below left).

plants.name: Callistemon 'Little John'
plants.context: 13. Further on your left is Callistemon ‘Little John’ a dwarf form of Callistemon viminalis (photo above right). This plant shows a stunning contrast between deep red bottlebrush flowers and green/blue foliage.

plants.name: Alyogyne 'Blue Heeler'
plants.context: 14. Low on your right is Alyogyne ‘Blue Heeler’, a low mound of textured green foliage with purple ‘hibiscus’ flowers that bloom over a long period (photos above).

plants.name: Alyogyne huegelii 'Misty'
plants.context: 15. Also on your right is Alyogyne huegelii ‘Misty’, a very attractive selection of A.huegelii with pale mauve flowers with maroon centres and green foliage (photo above). A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will take a short walk to the café, as there are many plants in flower

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk up the road behind the café into the Lamiaceae Section

plants.name: Anigozanthos flavidus
plants.context: 1. On your right after you leave the Visitor Centre is Anigozanthos flavidus, in pink and green shades (photo above). All kangaroo paws are endemic to Western Australia, and the flowers are bird pollinated.

plants.name: Grevillea leptobotrys
plants.context: 2. Also on your right, in a pot, is Grevillea leptobotrys with small racemes of lilac-pink flow- ers buried in prickly dark green foliage with red new growth (photo next page top left). Grevillea leptobotrys is known as the Tangled Grevillea and is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia 'Precious Pearl'
plants.context: 3. Still on your right is Corymbia ficifolia ‘Precious Pearl’ with masses of pink buds which will open to pale pink fluffy flowers (photo above right). This small and compact cultivar of the West Australian flowering gum, Corymbia ficifolia, is a grafted form.

plants.name: Clerodendron floribundum var. attenuatum
plants.context: 5. Bear left behind the café to see high on your left Clerodendron floribundum var. attenuatum, or Lolly Bush, a small rainforest tree in full bloom with clusters of strongly scented white bell flowers against dark green foliage (photo above). The green fruits of this tree will develop into black drupes, which appear glossy and succulent, giving rise to the common name. This plant is native across the northern half of Australia.

plants.name: Lomatia myricoides
plants.context: 6. Bear right past the depot to see on your right Lomatia myricoides, a medium shrub to small tree with linear green leaves and white clusters of flowers (photo below). This plant is found in southeastern New South Wales and northeastern Victoria.

plants.name: Callistemon 'Little John'
plants.context: 7. Bear left up the hill to see on your left Callistemon ‘Little John’, a dwarf form of Callistemon viminalis (photo below) .This plant shows a stunning contrast between deep red bottlebrush flowers and green-blue foliage.

plants.name: Baeckea gunniana
plants.context: 8. Also on your left is Baeckea gunniana, a small bush with tiny green leaves and white flowers with maroon centres (photo below). This plant commemorates both Abraham Baeck (1713-95), a physician and good friend of Linnaeus, and Ronald Campbell Gunn, pioneer botanist of Tasmania. This plant is native to alpine regions of ACT, Victoria and Tasmania.

plants.name: Elaeocarpus reticulata 'Prima Donna'
plants.context: 9. Further on your left is Elaeocarpus reticulata ‘Prima Donna’, a small dense tree with shiny green leaves and pink, fringed bell flowers (photo below). Blue berries follow the flowers which are attractive to seed eating birds.

plants.name: Myoporum parvifolium
plants.context: 10. Low on your right is Myoporum parvifolium, or Creeping Boobialla, a hardy, spreading groundcover with white flowers (photo below). This plant is found in South Australia, Victoria and southwestern New South Wales.

plants.name: Prostanthera lithospermoides
plants.context: 11. Turn right along the road signposted Family Lamiaceae to see on your left Prostanthera lithospermoides, an open bush with light green leaves and pairs of white flowers (photo below). This plant is native to northern NSW and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Lasiopetalum macrophyllum
plants.context: 12. Look right to see Lasiopetalum macrophyllum, or Shrubby Velvet Bush, with grey-green leaves with attractive bronze new growth (photo below left). This plant is native to the forests of NSW, Victoria and Tasmania.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Coconut Ice'
plants.context: 13. Further on your right Grevillea ‘Coconut Ice’ has large pink/orange spider flowers with long red styles (photo above right). This hybrid plant is grown from seed collected from G. bipinnatifida and the male parent was G. banksii (white flowered form). The original seedling was raised by Mr. M. Hodge of Queensland.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Lady O'
plants.context: 14. On your left is Grevillea ‘Lady O’, a long blooming shrub with red flowers and bright green foliage (photo below left). ‘Lady O’ is a cross be- tween a Grevillea victoriae hybrid and Grevillea rhyolitica made by local plant breeder Peter Ollerenshaw and named for his mother.

plants.name: Lomatia arborescens
plants.context: 15. Further on your right is Lomatia arborescens, or Tree Lomatia, a small tree with oblong serrated leaves and clusters of white flowers native to the forests of northeastern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland (photo above right). A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will walk up the road behind the café into the Lamiaceae Section

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk across the bridge past the café to the new Banksia Garden

plants.name: Pandorea jasminoides
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre look up to your left to see Pandorea jasminoides covered in scented pink trumpet flowers with attractive mid-green foliage (photo above). This woody vine, also known as Bower of Beauty, is native to New South Wales and Queensland, and forms large pointed pods filled with papery seeds.

plants.name: Grevillea insignis subsp. insignis
plants.context: 2. On your left is Grevillea insignis subsp. insignis, an open, rather straggly bush with blue -green prickly holly-like leaves and large terminal pink blooms with dark red stamens (photo next page top left). This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Homoranthus porteri
plants.context: 3. Go across the bridge past the café to see on your right, in a pot, Homoranthus porteri, a slight bush with bright green foliage and dark pink bells with protruding styles (photo above right). This plant is listed as vulnerable and is found in northern Queensland near Cooktown.

plants.name: Alyogyne huegelii 'Karana'
plants.context: 4. Further on your right is Alyogyne huegelii ‘Karana’ with masses of mauve flowers and coarse green foliage (photo above).

plants.name: Babingtonia virgata 'White Cascade'
plants.context: 5. On your left is Babingtonia virgata ‘White Cascade’ a medium-sized bush with green weep- ing foliage and masses of small white, 5-petalled flowers with maroon centres (photo above). This cultivar arose as a chance seedling of Baeckea (Babingtonia) virgata at Wirreanda Nursery in Ingleside, New South Wales.

plants.name: Scaevola ramosissima
plants.context: 6. On your right, in a pot, is Scaevola ramosissima with purple 5-part flowers with white centres and green leaves without stems (photo below left). This plant is found along the eastern coastal areas of Australia as far north as southern Queensland.

plants.name: Banksia victoriae
plants.context: 7. Continue straight ahead to the Banksia Garden, turn down to your right to see, in a pot, on your right, Banksia victoriae or Woolly Orange Banksia, with attractive grey-green toothed foliage and large orange brushes (photo above right). This plant is found around Geraldton and Perth in Western Australia.

plants.name: Banksia baxteri
plants.context: 8. On your left is Banksia baxteri, or Bird’s Nest Banksia, with tall spires of stiff, triangular pink-tipped foliage and yellow green flowers (photo above). This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia between Albany and Esperance.

plants.name: Banksia speciosa
plants.context: 9. Again on your left is Banksia speciosa, or Showy Banksia, with green triangular leaves and pale yellow flowers (photo below). This tall shrub is native to the area around Esperance, Western Australia.

plants.name: Banksia pilostylis
plants.context: 10. Still on your left is Banksia pilostylis, another tall shrub with linear serrated leaves and pale yellow flowers native to the area around Esperance, Western Australia (photo below).

plants.name: Banksia sceptrum
plants.context: 11. On your left is Banksia sceptrum, or Sceptre Banksia, with oblong green leaves and yellow flowers including the pistils (photo below). This plant is native to the area near Geraldton, Western Australia.

plants.name: Banksia menziesii
plants.context: 12. On your right is Banksia menziesii, or Menzies Banksia, a small tree or shrub with oblong, toothed, green leaves and deep pink to red flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to the south coast of Western Australia, around Perth.

plants.name: Banksia ashbyi
plants.context: 13. On your left is Banksia ashbyi with green toothed foliage (photo above right). This plant is native to the central west coast of Western Australia and has showy terminal bright orange flowers.

plants.name: Banksia occidentalis
plants.context: 14. On your right is Banksia occidentalis, or Red Swamp Banksia, a tall shrub or small tree with whorled, linear green leaves and green buds developing into red flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to the south coast of Western Australia.

plants.name: Banksia robur
plants.context: 15. Continue right around the curve to see on your left Banksia robur, or Swamp Banksia, with long egg-shaped leaves which are shiny on top and dull underneath (photo above right). This plant grows along the eastern mainland coast of Australia usually in sandy or swampy conditions. The brushes are bluish green when young, developing into yellow green and then rusty brown as they age. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will walk across the bridge past

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk past the rear of the café up the hill almost to the Red Centre Garden

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia 'Precious Pearl'
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre look to your right to see Corymbia ficifolia ‘Precious Pearl’ with masses of pink buds which will soon open to pale pink fluffy flowers (photo above). This compact cultivar of the southwestern West Australian flowering gum, Corymbia ficifolia, is a grafted form.

plants.name: Melaleuca decora
plants.context: 2. Turn left past the rear of the café and then bear right to see on your right three Melaleuca decora, a small tree with brownish papery bark, light green leaves and spikes of sweetly scented white flowers (photo next page top left). This tree is very popular with insects and is native to coastal areas of New South Wales and south- eastern Queensland.

plants.name: Babingtonia 'Howie's Feathertips'
plants.context: 3. Further on your left is Babingtonia ‘Howie’s Feathertips’, a large bush of dense light green foliage with masses of tiny white flowers (photo above right).

plants.name: Babingtonia pluriflora 'White Cascade'
plants.context: 4. Again on your left is Babingtonia pluriflora ‘White Cascade’, a medium-sized bush with green weeping foliage and masses of small white, 5-petalled flowers with maroon centres (photo above). This cultivar arose as a chance seedling of Baeckea virgata at Wirreanda Nursery in Ingleside, New South Wales.

plants.name: Eremophila decipiens subsp. decipiens
plants.context: 5. Turn left up the hill of see on your right Eremophila decipiens ssp. decipiens, a small shrub with red tubular flowers which is native to southwestern Western Australia (photo above).

plants.name: Eremophila maculata
plants.context: 6. Again on your right is Eremophila maculata with bright pink tubular flowers on a small bush (photo below). This plant is widespread in the drier inland areas of all mainland states of Australia.

plants.name: Eremophila longifolia
plants.context: 7. Still on your right is Eremophila longifolia, a large bush or small tree with long, narrow grey-green leaves, light green fruits and dusty pink tubular flowers (photo below). This plant is found across all the drier areas of mainland Australia.

plants.name: Eremophila psilocalyx (pachyphylla
plants.context: 8. On your right is Eremophila psilocalyx (pachyphylla), an upright broom-like shrub with small glossy green leaves and mauve tubular flowers (photo below). This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Westringia glabra
plants.context: 9. Turn right along the road labelled Family Lamiaceae to see on your left Westringia glabra, or Violet Westringia, a small bush with grey-green leaves and mauve flowers (photos below). This plant is native to New South Wales and Victoria.

plants.name: Stenocarpus angustifolius
plants.context: 10. Further on your left is Stenocarpus angustifolius, a medium sized bush with clusters of cream umbel flowers opening from green buds in attractive contrast to the lance-shaped light green foliage (photo below). This plant is native to the Townsville area of coastal Queensland.

plants.name: Banksia serrata
plants.context: 12. On your right is Banksia serrata, a small tree with very large greenish brushes, ovate serrated leaves and a wrinkled trunk (photo below left). The trunk wrinkles more with age leading to its common name of Old Man Banksia. Banksia serrata is a widespread species in eastern Australia.

plants.name: Triplarina nowraensis
plants.context: 13. Again on your right is Triplarina nowraensis, or Nowra Heath Myrtle, a small drooping bush with creamy-white tea-tree flowers which occur in pairs (photo above right). This plant is listed as endangered in the wild and only occurs in the Nowra area, New South Wales.

plants.name: Podolobium aciculiferum
plants.context: 14. Still on your right is Podolobium aciculiferum , with gold 3-part flowers with sharp- ly pointed dark green foliage (photo below). This plant is native to coastal New South Wales and Queensland.

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia
plants.context: 15. Look to your left before the entrance to the Red Centre Garden, to see Corymbia ficifolia, a showy small tree, with dark red fluffy blooms and dark green leathery foliage (photo below). This gum, from southwestern Western Australia, is one of the most spectacular when in full flower. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Today we will walk past the rear of the café up the hill almost to the Red Centre Garden
