title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, right behind the depot, then up to the Wattle section

plants.name: Guichenotia ledifolia
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre, on your right is Guichenotia ledifolia, a small shrub with grey-green foliage covered in drooping, dusty pink 5-petalled flowers with maroon centres (photo above). This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Coronidium sp
plants.context: 2. On your right is Coronidium sp., commonly known as the White Paper Daisy or Tall Everlasting, a compact shrub with silvery-grey leaves and many white paper daisies with gold centres, native to the open forests of eastern Australia (photo next page top left).

plants.name: Geleznowia verrucosa
plants.context: 3. On your left, in a pot, is Geleznowia verrucosa with close grey-green foliage and bright yellow terminal flowers (photo above right). This genus was described by Ukrainian- Russian botanist Nicolai Stepanovitch Turczaninow in 1849 and its only species is Geleznowia verrucosa, native to the weat coast of Western Australia north of Perth.

plants.name: Epacris longiflora 'Nectar Pink'
plants.context: 4. Again on your left is Epacris longiflora ‘Nectar Pink’, a very floriferous small shrub covered in slender pink bells with white tips (photo below).

plants.name: Pimelea physodes
plants.context: 5. On your right, both in the ground and in a pot, is Pimelea physodes, or Qualup Bell, with grey-green foliage close to reddish stems with pendant green bracts enclosing the small flowers and dark red outer bracts (photo below). This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia and is considered the most outstanding of the genus.

plants.name: Banksia spinulosa var. collina
plants.context: 6. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see on your right Banksia spinulosa var. collina, with fine linear foliage and slender, dull gold flowers (photo below left)). This shrub, commonly known as Hill Banksia or Golden Candlesticks, is native to the east coast of Australia in Queensland and New South Wales.

plants.name: Acacia covenyi
plants.context: 7. Bear right behind the depot, to see on your right, Acacia covenyi, commonly known as Blue Bush, which has magnificent silver-grey foliage and masses of contrasting bright lemon ball flowers (photo above right) . This plant is rare in the wild and is confined to Deua National Park in southeastern New South Wales.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Legacy Flame
plants.context: 9. Turn left up the hill, to see on your left, Grevillea ‘Legacy Flame’, a small grevillea, bred locally by Bywong Nursery, which commemorates 100 years of Legacy Australia with flame-like orange-red flowers which resemble the Legacy torch (photo below left).

plants.name: Correa 'Lemon Twist'
plants.context: 10. Also on your left is Correa ‘Lemon Twist’, a hybrid between C. reflexa var. nummularia and C. alba which occurred in the gardens of Native Plant Wholesalers in Mount Gambier (photo above right). ‘Lemon Twist’ forms a spreading shrub, 20cm high x 1m wide, with shiny foliage and well displayed lemon flowers over a long period.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Bloodline'
plants.context: 11. Again on your left is Grevillea ‘Bloodline’, a new grevillea bred at Bywong Nursery by Peter Ollerenshaw, a similar long flowering variety to Grevillea ‘Lady O’, but with a slightly arching habit (photo above).

plants.name: Brachychiton rupestris
plants.context: 12. On your right is Brachychiton rupestris, or Queensland Bottle Tree, a small tree with a trunk swollen with water, endemic to central Queensland and northern New South Wales (photo below left).

plants.name: Rhodanthe anthemoides
plants.context: 13. Turn right in front of the waterfall to see, on your right, in a pot, Rhodanthe anthemoides also known as Chamomile Sunray, a mound of grey-green foliage almost covered with maroon buds opening to white daisy flowers with gold centres (photo above right). This plant is widespread on the mainland but listed as rare in Tasmania.

plants.name: Acacia ingramii
plants.context: 14. Turn left along the road above the Rock Garden, to see on your right, Acacia ingramii, a large bush or small tree with fine linear foliage and masses of gold ball flowers. This plant is native to areas near Armidale in northern New South Wales.

plants.name: Acacia amoena
plants.context: 15. Also on your right is Acacia amoena, or Boomerang Wattle, a small bush with tough yellow-green leaves and golden ball flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to New South Wales and northern Victorian tablelands. title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, down the stairs to the right, then up the hill behind the café to the Acacia section

plants.name: Acacia aphylla
plants.context: 1. Three cheers for Wattle Day, 1 September. As you leave the Visitor Centre took right to see Acacia aphylla, or Leafless Rock Wattle, with large gold ball flowers on leathery, leafless, grey- green stems (photo above). This plant is native to the area around Perth, Western Australia.

plants.name: Isopogon cuneatus
plants.context: 2. Walk down the steps to your right, to see on your right, Isopogon cuneatus, an upright shrub with floppy branches of flat bright green leaves, often tinged with red, and large pink heads of drumstick flowers (photo next page top left). This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Philotheca myoporoides 'Winter Rouge'
plants.context: 3. Also on your right is Philotheca myoporoides ‘Winter Rouge’, a small shrub with green aromatic foliage, bright pink buds and white star flowers (photo above right).

plants.name: Acacia leprosa 'Scarlet Blaze'
plants.context: 4. On your left is Acacia leprosa ‘Scarlet Blaze’ with weeping green foliage and many striking reddish fluffy ball flowers (photo below). The cultivar ‘Scarlet Blaze’ has attracted attention because of a flower colour unique among wattles. The cultivar arose from a single red-flowered specimen discovered by bushwalkers in a Victorian state forest northeast of Melbourne. The original plant has since died.

plants.name: Acacia pycnantha
plants.context: 5. Turn left at the bottom of the steps, to see on your left Acacia pycnantha or Golden Wattle, the floral emblem of Australia (photo below). This small tree has curved green phyllodes with large yellow ball flowers and is native to southeastern mainland Australia.

plants.name: Westringia fruticosa 'Wunderbar'
plants.context: 6. Also on your left is Westringia fruticosa ‘Wunderbar’ or ‘Double Wonder’, a small dense shrub with grey-green foliage and pale mauve or pink semi-double flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Bloodline'
plants.context: 7. Again on your left is Grevillea ‘Bloodline’, a relatively new Grevillea bred at Bywong Nursery by Peter Ollerenshaw, a similar long flowering variety to Grevillea ‘Lady O’, but with a slightly arching habit (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Scarlet King'
plants.context: 8. Still on your left is Grevillea ‘Scarlet King’ an atttractive cultivar with dark red toothbrush flowers contrasting with white stems and grey-green divided foliage (photo below).

plants.name: Acacia leprosa 'Just Peachy'
plants.context: 9. Continuing on your left is Acacia leprosa ‘Just Peachy’, a hardy shrub with peach-coloured flowers in spring (photo below).

plants.name: Acacia cognata
plants.context: 10. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, on your right, Acacia cognata, a graceful weeping tree with green linear leaves and plenty of flowers (photo below). This plant is known as Bower Wattle and is native to southeastern main- land Australia.

plants.name: Acacia longifolia var. sophorae hybrid
plants.context: 11. Turn right along the road above the Rock Garden to see, on your left, Acacia longifolia var. sophorae hybrid, or Coastal Wattle, which is widespread along the eastern and southeastern coast of Australia (photo below). The lemon rod flowers are well displayed on leathery dark green phyllodes.

plants.name: Acacia fimbriata
plants.context: 12. Again on your left, is Acacia fimbriata, or Brisbane Golden Wattle, a small tree with profuse fluffy yellow ball flowers and narrow green leaves (photo below left). This plant is native to the table- lands of Queensland and NSW.

plants.name: Acacia phasmoides
plants.context: 13. On your right is Acacia phasmoides, or Phantom Wattle, a spreading wispy wattle, native to Dora Dora State Forest, near Holbrook, with grey-green linear foliage and bright yellow ball flowers (photo above right).

plants.name: Acacia muelleriana
plants.context: 14. Turn left up the hill to see, on your right, Acacia muelleriana, a bushy, many-stemmed shrub or tree with dark green pinnate leaves and cream ball flowers (photo below). This plant is native to eastern Queensland, as well as to the western slopes of NSW.

plants.name: Acacia ingramii
plants.context: 15. On your left and right are clumps of Acacia ingramii, small trees with fine, linear foliage and masses of gold ball flowers (photo below). This plant is native to areas near Armidale in northern New South Wales. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will take a very short walk from the Visitor Centre up the path towards the Rainforest Gully

plants.name: Boronia 'Purple Jared'
plants.context: 1. On your right as you leave the Visitor Centre is a pot containing two boronias, Boronia megastima ‘Lutea’ (photo above left) a small neat bush with yellow bell flowers, and Boronia ‘Purple Jared’ (photo above right) with green foliage and deep purple bell flowers, a cross between Boronia megastima and B. heterophylla. For those of you (75%) who can smell boronias, they have a glorious scent.

plants.name: Pandorea pandorana 'Golden Showers'
plants.context: 2. Look up to your left to see Pandorea pandorana ‘Golden Showers’, a vigorous twining vine with masses of tubular brown and gold flowers (photo next page top left). This species is widespread in Australia down the east coast from Cape York to Flinders Island in Bass Strait and also occurs in central Australia.

plants.name: Acacia pubescens
plants.context: 3. Down to your right is Acacia pubescens or Downy Wattle, with gold ball flowers and fringed foliage (photo above right). This endangered wattle is native to the Sydney Basin in central New South Wales. Much of its habitat has vanished with the growth of the city of Sydney.

plants.name: Philotheca myoporoides 'Profusion'
plants.context: 4. On your left is Philotheca myoporoides ‘Profusion’, a small shrub with green aromatic foliage that smells of apples when crushed, bright pink buds and white star flowers (photo above).

plants.name: Coronidium sp
plants.context: 5. On your right is Coronidium sp., commonly known as the White Paper Daisy or Tall Everlasting, a compact shrub with silvery leaves and many white paper daisies with gold centres, native to open forests in eastern Australia (photo above).

plants.name: Acacia cognata 'Green Mist'
plants.context: 6. On your left is Acacia cognata ‘Green Mist’, a weeping shrub with green linear leaves and yellow ball flowers (photo below). This cultivar is a dwarf form of the Bower Wattle, native to New South Wales and Victoria.

plants.name: Asterolasia 'Lemon Essence'
plants.context: 7. On your right is Asterolasia ‘Lemon Essence’, a compact shrub with masses of lemon yellow star flowers (photo below). This plant was developed at the ANBG.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Lana Maree'
plants.context: 8. Bear left up the path to see, in a pot on your left, Grevillea ‘Lana Maree’, a shrub with divided foliage and rich pink, bird attracting flowers bred by Richard Tomkin, Changers Green Nursery, Gin Gin, Queensland from the same cross as ‘Billy Bonkers’ – G. nana ssp. abbreviata x G. ‘Majestic’ (photo below).

plants.name: Pandorea sp. Mt. Maroon
plants.context: 9. Also on your left is Pandorea sp. Mt. Maroon, a small trailing plant with cream bells with maroon centres and markings, native to southeastern Queensland (lphoto below).

plants.name: Acacia pravissima 'Kuranga Cascade'
plants.context: 10. Again on your left is Acacia pravissima ‘Kuranga Cascade’, a weeping or prostrate wattle with triangular grey-green phyllodes and masses of golden ball flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Acacia fimbriata
plants.context: 11. Still on your left is Acacia fimbriata, or Brisbane Golden Wattle, a small tree with profuse fluffy yellow ball flowers and narrow green leaves (photo below). This plant is native to the tablelands of Queensland and NSW.

plants.name: Casuarina glauca prostrate form
plants.context: 12. Again on your left is Casuarina glauca prostrate form or Swamp Oak (photo below left). This plant has hard, long, green foliage which can fall attractively to soften edges in the garden and is a prostrate fine-leaf form of the common she-oak seen growing throughout eastern Australia mainly around moist gullies, streams and waterways.

plants.name: Hibbertia empetrifolia
plants.context: 13. On your right is Hibbertia empetrifolia, a low scrambling shrub with green leaves and wiry stems ending in bright yellow flowers (photo above right). Commonly known as Tangled Guinea-flower, this plant is native to southeastern Australia.

plants.name: Phebalium speciosum
plants.context: 14. Again on your right is Phebalium speciosum, a showy shrub with narrow elliptical leaves, dark green on top with dense silver-star hairs, and rusty hairs and silver scales below (photo below left). White to pale pink flowers are held in stalkless clusters of four to eight flowers. This plant is critically endangered and has a restricted distribution on the far north coast of New South Wales in Yabbra State Forest and National Park.

plants.name: Lagostrobus franklinii
plants.context: 15. On your left is Lagostrobus franklinii, or Huon Pine, a slow-growing, but long-lived tree with some living specimens in excess of 2,000 years old, native to the wet southwestern corner of Tasmania (photo above right). intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre up the hill above the Rock Garden finishing with some Hakeas in flower

plants.name: Grevillea wilkinsonii
plants.context: 1. As you near the Visitor Centre, on the right is Grevillea wilkinsonii, or Tumut Grevillea (photo above). This species was first discovered in 1991 near Tumut, NSW, and is listed as endangered in the wild. The Tumut Grevillea is an upright shrub with oblong, toothed leaves and mauve to purple toothbrush flowers that smell somewhat of old socks

plants.name: Prostanthera rotundifolia 'Mini Pink'
plants.context: 2. On your right is Prostanthera rotundifolia ‘Mini Pink’, with deliciously scented dark green rounded foliage and many pink flowers (photo next page top left).

plants.name: Pomaderris walshii
plants.context: 3. Also on your right is Pomaderris walshii, or Carrington Falls Pomaderris, a large, spreading shrub which is critically endangered and grows only in one location near Carrington Falls in the southern highlands of NSW, near Robertson (photo above right). The young stems have silvery to rusty hairs, the foliage is dark green, and the flower heads are cream to yellow.

plants.name: Grevillea petrophiloides subsp. remota
plants.context: 4. Again on your right, in a pot, is Grevillea petrophiloides ssp. remota, an erect and open shrub with long stems of pink flowers held above the divided foliage (photo above). This grevillea is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Hibbertia empetrifolia
plants.context: 5. On your left is Hibbertia empetrifolia, a low scrambling shrub with green leaves and wiry stems ending in bright yellow flowers (photo above). Also known as Tangled Guinea-flower, this plant is native to southeastern Australia.

plants.name: Eremophila nivea
plants.context: 6. On your right is Eremophila nivea, a shrub with mauve tubular flowers and striking, silky, silver-grey foliage covered in hairs (photo below). This plant is native to the southern west coast of Western Australia.

plants.name: Thelychiton epiphyticus
plants.context: 7. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, on your left, Thelychiton epiphyticus, Rock Lily or Rock Orchid, with racemes of showy cream flowers with yellow buds and dark-green leaves (photo below). This orchid can grow on rocks or trees and is native to coastal eastern Australia from Victoria to northern Queensland.

plants.name: Ranunculus collinus
plants.context: 8. Turn right behind the depot to see, on your left, Ranunculus collinus , a low green groundcover with bright yellow flowers, native to southeastern Australia (photo below).

plants.name: Westringia fruticosa 'Wunderbar'
plants.context: 9. As you turn left up the hill, on your left is Westringia fruticosa ‘Wunderbar’ or ‘Double Wonder’, a small dense shrub with grey-green foliage and pale mauve or pink semi-double flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Philotheca myoporoides subsp. myoporoides
plants.context: 10. Behind the Westringia, also on your left, is Philotheca myoporoides subsp. myoporoides, beloved by bees and hover flies (photo below). This plant forms a neat bush with dull green foliage, pink buds and white star flowers and is endemic to southeastern Australia.

plants.name: Indigofera australis
plants.context: 11. As you turn right in front of the waterfall, on your left is Indigofera australis, or Austral Indigo, a small straggly bush with pinnate blue green leaves and pink flowers (photo below). This member of the pea family is native from northern Queensland to Tasmania and also to South Australia and Western Australia.

plants.name: Alyogyne huegelii 'West Coast Gem'
plants.context: 12. On your left again is Alyogyne huegelii ‘West Coast Gem’ with coarse foliage and clear purple ‘hibiscus’ style flowers which open for a short period only, but are prolific (photo below left).

plants.name: Hakea drupacea
plants.context: 13. Turn right along the road above the Rock Garden to see, on your right, many bushes of Hakea drupacea, commonly known as Sweet Hakea, an open tree or shrub with green, sharp- pointed leaves and white pincushion flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Hakea macraeana
plants.context: 14. Also on your right is Hakea macraeana, or Needle-wood, a small tree with fine drooping foliage and white flowers along the stems, native to eastern Australia (photo below).

plants.name: Hakea horrida
plants.context: 15. Still on your right is Hakea horrida, a stiff shrub with extremely prickly, intricate needle foliage and strongly scented creamy-white fluffy flowers (photo below). This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia. title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre up the hill behind the café and along the road above the Rock Garden

plants.name: Oxylobium ellipticum
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre, on your left is Oxylobium ellipticum, or Common Shaggy-pea, with dense clusters of gold pea flowers with red flashes and elliptical leaves (photo above). This species is native to southeastern Australia.

plants.name: Eremophila mackinlayii subsp. spathulata 'Big John'
plants.context: 2. On your right, in a pot, is Eremophila mackinlayii subsp. spathulata ‘Big John’ with grey green leaves and large purple flowers (photo next page top left). This plant is a chimera, with two different groups of plant cells growing as one plant, E. mackinlayii and Myoporum insulare combined, with the outer skin of Eremophila and the inner genotype of Myoporum.

plants.name: Telopea 'Essie's Gift'
plants.context: 3. Also on your right is Telopea ‘Essie’s Gift’, with long green leaves and spectacular dark pink flowers (photo above right). 'Essie's Gift' is a recent selection of waratah and is named in honour of the late Essie Huxley who was devoted to the genus Telopea.

plants.name: Epacris longiflora
plants.context: 4. Still on your right is Epacris longiflora, or Native Fuchsia, with thin, tubular, white flowers on a small prickly bush (photo above). This plant belongs to the heath family whose native range extends from the central coast of New South Wales to southern Queensland.

plants.name: Asterolasia 'Lemon Essence'
plants.context: 5. Again on your right is Asterolasia ‘Lemon Essence’, a compact shrub with masses of lemon yellow star flowers (photo above). This plant was developed at the ANBG.

plants.name: Myoporum bateae
plants.context: 6. Still on your right is Myoporum bateae named for the collector of the type specimen, Miss Mary Bate and native to a restricted area in southeastern NSW (photo below left) This pyramidal, sweet-smelling shrub has horizontal branches carrying fine, drooping, aromatic leaves and pink flowers olong the top of the branches.

plants.name: Olearia phlogopappa
plants.context: 7. Again on your right is Olearia phlogopappa, or Alpine Daisy Bush, with grey foliage and mauve flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to southeastern New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania. The plant has a musky odour, but the flowers themselves have a light, pleasant scent.

plants.name: Olearia argophylla
plants.context: 8. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see on your left Olearia argophylla or Native Musk, a tall shrub or small tree with felted grey leaves and many heads of white, strongly scented ‘daisy’ flowers with gold centres (photos above). This plant is native to the east coast in New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania.

plants.name: Thelychiton epiphiticus
plants.context: 9. Also on your left is Thelychiton epiphiticus, Rock Lily or Rock Orchid, with racemes of showy, cream flowers with yellow buds and dark -green leaves (photo below). This orchid can grow on rocks or trees and is native to coastal eastern Australia from Victoria to northern Queensland.

plants.name: Nematolepsis squamea subsp. squamea
plants.context: 10. Still on your left is Nematolepsis squamea ssp. squamea a small tree with light green leaves and white fluffy flowers, native to southeastern Australia, including Tasmania (photo below).

plants.name: Leptospermum grandifolium
plants.context: 11. As you turn right along the road above the Rock Garden, on your left is Leptospermum grandifolium, or Mountain Teatree or Woolly Teatree, a small tree native to southeastern mainland Australia (photo below). This plant has broad greyish-green leaves with a sharp point at the tip and profuse white flowers.

plants.name: Leptospermum 'Love Affair'
plants.context: 12. Still on your left is Leptospermum ‘Love Affair’, a hardy evergreen shrub with pink ‘tea-tree’ flowers with green centres (photo below left)

plants.name: Homoranthus flavescens
plants.context: 13. On your right is Homoranthus flavescens, a neat bush with green needle foliage and bright acid yellow flowers in layers on top of the foliage (photo above right). This plant is native to northern NSW and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Grevillea wilkinsonii
plants.context: 14. Also on your right is Grevillea wilkinsonii, or Tumut Grevillea. This plant was first discovered in 1991 near Tumut, NSW, and is listed as endangered in the wild (photo below). . The Tumut Grevillea is a shrub with oblong, toothed leaves and mauve to purple toothbrush flowers, which smell somewhat of old socks.

plants.name: Telopea speciocissima 'Corroboree'
plants.context: 15. Still on your right is Telopea speciocissima ‘Corroboree’, a tall shrub with upright habit with bright red/pink ‘waratah’ flowers (photo below). A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre up the hill behind the café and along the road above the Rock Garden

plants.name: Doryanthes palmeri
plants.context: 1. High on your left after you leave the Visitor Centre is Doryanthes palmeri or Spear Lily (photo above). This is one of the most spectacular flowers in the Gardens, a huge nodding cluster of bright red flowers much visited by insects and honeyeaters. The rosette of leaves can reach a length of about 3m and the flowers grow on a stalk which may reach 5m in height. This species is native to northeastern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Pimelea ferruginea 'Magenta Mist'
plants.context: 2. On your right is Pimelea ferruginea ‘Magenta Mist’ with bright pink heads of flower on neat green foliage (photo next page top left).

plants.name: Melaleuca fulgens
plants.context: 3. Also on your right is Melaleuca fulgens, a small bush with narrow grey leaves and reddish-orange ‘bottlebrush’ flowers with gold stamens, which is native to the west coast and southwest of Western Australia, as well as parts of South Australia and the Northern Territory (photo above right).

plants.name: Orthrosanthus multiflorus
plants.context: 4. On your left is Orthrosanthus multiflorus, or Morning Iris, a clumping plant with grass-like foliage and true blue flowers (photo above). Each flower lasts only a day but they are produced in profusion during spring and summer. This plant is native to coastal southern and western Australia.

plants.name: Vesselowskya rubifolia
plants.context: 5. Also on your left is Vesselowskya rubifolia, a large shrub with serrated green leaves and fluffy cattails of pink and cream (photo above). This plant is a rainforest species with a restricted distribution in north- eastern New South Wales. The common name is Mountain Marara or Dorrigo Southern Marara.

plants.name: Libertia paniculata
plants.context: 6. Walk across the bridge and past the café to see on your left Libertia paniculata, with light green strappy foliage and small white flowers held high (photo below). These plants are native to the coast and adjacent ranges from southeastern Queensland to eastern Victoria.

plants.name: Blechnum cartilagineum
plants.context: 7. Also on your left is Blechnum cartilagineum or Gristle Fern, an erect fern with broad pinnate fronds arising from a central clump (photo below). The new fronds are pink, maturing to pale green. This fern is native to eastern Australia.

plants.name: Alyogyne huegelii 'White Gem'
plants.context: 8. On your right is Alyogyne huegelii ‘White Gem’, a bee and butterfly-attracting rounded shrub with ‘hibiscus-like’ white flowers and deep green lobed foliage (photos below).

plants.name: Carpobrotus rossii
plants.context: 9. Also on your right is Carpobrotus rossii or Native Pigface, a fast-growing succulent groundcover, with vivid pink flowers over a long period and edible leaves and fruit (photo below). This plant is native to southern Australia.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Loopy Lou'
plants.context: 10. Still on your right is Grevillea ‘Loopy Lou’, a compact shrub with divided foliage and large flowers in shades of peach, yellow and pink (photo below).

plants.name: Alyogyne 'Aussie Purple'
plants.context: 11. Again on your right is Alyogyne ‘Aussie Purple’ a hybrid between Alyogyne huegelii and A. hakeifolia, with bright purple flowers over a long period (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea rhyolitica
plants.context: 12. Further on your right is Grevillea rhyolitica, ‘Deua Flame’, a shrub with arching stems of glossy green foliage and coral red spider flowers (photo below left).

plants.name: Telopea 'Essie's Gift'
plants.context: 13. Still on your right is Telopea ‘Essie’s Gift’, with long green leaves and spectacular dark pink flowers (photo above right). 'Essie's Gift' is a new selection of waratah and is named in honour of the late Essie Huxley who was devoted to the genus Telopea.

plants.name: Verticordia chrysantha
plants.context: 14. On your left, in a pot, is Verticordia chrysantha, or Golden Feather Flower, a slow-growing, small shrub with bright yellow flowers, native to southwestern WA (photo above).

plants.name: Epacris breviflora
plants.context: 15. Low on your right is Epacris breviflora, or Drumstick Heath, endemic to southeastern Australia (photo above). This erect shrub has egg-shaped leaves with a sharp-pointed tip and clusters of white flowers near the end of the branches. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Just a short walk today from the Visitor

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, along the road above the Rock Garden, then into the Sydney Gully Region

plants.name: Grevillea 'Peaches and Cream'
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre look down to your right to see Grevillea ‘Peaches and Cream’ with deeply divided green leaves and large flower heads of pink and cream (photo above). This hybrid was developed in Queensland by Jan Glazebrook and Dennis Cox.

plants.name: Doryanthes palmeri
plants.context: 2. Look up to your left to see Doryanthes palmeri or Spear Lily (photo next page top left). This is one of the most spectacular flowers in the Gardens, a huge nodding cluster of bright red flowers much visited by insects and honeyeaters. The rosette of leaves can reach a length of about 3m and the flowers grow on a stalk which may reach m in height. This plant is native to northeastern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Prostanthera lasianthos
plants.context: 3. Also on your left is Prostanthera lasianthos, with dense, dark-green foliage and white flowers with dark pink centres (photo above right). This plant is native to southeastern Australia, including eastern Tasmania.

plants.name: Isopogon 'Little Drumsticks'
plants.context: 4. Down to your left is Isopogon ‘Little Drumsticks’, a low bushy shrub with intricate lobed foliage and well displayed yellow cone flowers (photo above).

plants.name: Eremophila mackinlayii subsp. spathulata 'Big John'
plants.context: 5. In a pot, on your right, is Eremophila mackinlayii subsp. spathulata ‘Big John’, a large shrub with grey-green leaves and many blue-purple flowers (photo above), thought to be a chimera, when the plant is Myoporum on the inside and Eremophila on the outside, which gives it extra vigour.

plants.name: Hymenosporum flavum
plants.context: 6. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, high on your left, Hymenosporum flavum, a small tree with highly-scented cream flowers aging to gold (photo below). This tree is native to the eastern Australian coast from the Hunter River in New South Wales north to Queens- land and extending into New Guinea.

plants.name: Callistemon subulatus
plants.context: 7. Turn right along the road above the Rock Garden to see, on your left, Callistemon subulatus with bright red brushes and a dense spreading habit (photo below). This plant is native to New South Wales and Victoria where it grows along the banks of watercourses.

plants.name: Homoranthus flavescens
plants.context: 8. Look down to your right to see Homoranthus flavescens, a neat bush with fresh green needle foliage and bright acid yellow flowers in layers on top of the foliage (photo below). This plant is native to northern NSW and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Leptospermum rotundifolia 'Julie Ann'
plants.context: 9. Again on your right is Leptospermum rotundifolia ‘Julie Ann’ with pink flowers with green centres aging to white (photo below). This cultivar is a prostrate form from the Jervis Bay area of New South Wales.

plants.name: Hakea commutata
plants.context: 10. Further on your right is Hakea commutata, a small shrub with stiff green foliage and yellow curled flowers with an unpleasant scent (photo below). This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Hakea archaeoides
plants.context: 11. Also on your right is Hakea archaeoides, a shrub with oblong leaves and pendulous dark red flowers followed by clusters of grey woody nuts (photos below). This plant is native to the north coast of New South Wales and is listed as vulnerable in the wild.

plants.name: Melaleuca wilsonii
plants.context: 12. On your left is Melaleuca wilsonii, or Wilson’s Honey Myrtle, an evergreen shrub with narrow leaves and reddish pink flowers in clusters along the stems, native to South Australia and central Victoria (photo below left).

plants.name: Grevillea whiteana
plants.context: 13. On your right is Grevillea whiteana, a tall rangy bush with dark green, linear leaves and creamy-white racemes of flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Jacksonia scoparia
plants.context: 14. On your left is Jacksonia scoparia, or Dogwood, a shrub or small tree with leafless, pendulous, grey-green branches and profuse yellow and red pea flowers in spring, native to the coastal NSW and southeastern Queensland (photo above).

plants.name: Grevillea caleyi
plants.context: 15. Also on your left is Grevillea caleyi, an open bush of divided grey-green foliage and red toothbrush flowers (photo above). This plant is endangered in the wild as it is native to a very restricted area of Sydney near Mona Vale. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, u

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, along the road above the Rock Garden, then back towards the café

plants.name: Jasminum simplicifolium subsp. suavissimum
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre, look left to see the vine Jasminum simplicifolium ssp. suavissimum, or Forest Jasmine, with five starry white petals and a delicate scent (photo above). This plant is native to northeastern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Pandorea jasminoides
plants.context: 2. Turn back towards the café to see, on your left, Pandorea jasminoides covered in scented pink trumpet flowers with attractive mid-green foliage (photo next page top left). This woody vine, also known as Bower of Beauty, is native to New South Wales and Queensland, and forms large pointed pods filled with papery seeds.

plants.name: Decaspermum struckoilicum
plants.context: 3. On your right is Decaspermum struckoilicum, or Mount Morgan Myrtle, a small tree with shiny olive-green leaves and many tiny white flowers (photo above right). This plant is considered endangered in the wild and occurs in only a very few localities near Mount Morgan in southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Dietes robinsoniana
plants.context: 4. On your left is Dietes robinsoniana, or Wedding Lily, with long strappy foliage and sweetly scented white flowers, with a gold fleck in the centre, held high on wiry stems (photo above). This plant is endemic to Lord Howe Island where it grows on cliff faces, often in exposed situations.

plants.name: Alyogyne 'Aussie Purple
plants.context: 5. On your right is Alyogyne ‘Aussie Purple’ a hybrid between Alyogyne huegelii and A. hakeifolia, with bright purple flowers over a long period (photo above).

plants.name: Anigozanthos 'Bush Pearl'
plants.context: 6. Also on your right, in a pot, is Anigozanthos ‘Bush Pearl’, a hybrid Kangaroo Paw with long-lasting bright pink flowers, developed by Angus Stewart (photo below left).

plants.name: Cuttsia viburnea
plants.context: 7. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, on your left, Cuttsia viburnea, a bushy tropical tree to 15m high which has toothed, shiny green leaves and flat clusters of strongly scented white flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to northeastern NSW and southeastern Queensland. C. viburnea is the only species assigned to the genus Cuttsia.

plants.name: Doryanthes palmeri
plants.context: 8. Also on your left is Doryanthes palmeri or Spear Lily (photo above). This is one of the most spectacular flowers in the Gardens, a huge nodding cluster of bright red flowers much visited by insects and honeyeaters. The rosette of leaves can reach a length of about 3m and the flowers grow on a stalk which may reach 5m in height. This plant is native to northeastern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Melaleuca armillaris
plants.context: 9. Bear right along the road above the Rock Garden to see, on your right, Melaleuca armillaris, or Bracelet Honey Myrtle, a tall shrub with spirally arranged leaves and white ‘bottlebrush’ flowers, native to South Australia, Victoria and Tasmania (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Mason's Hybrid'
plants.context: 10. Further on your right is Grevillea ‘Mason’s Hybrid’, a spreading bush with many spider blooms of pink, red and orange (photo below). This hybrid arose from seed collected from an upright glaucous form of Grevillea bipinnatifida with the other parent presumed to be G. banksii.

plants.name: Scaevola albida
plants.context: 11. Still low on your right is Scaevola albida, a prostrate shrub native to a range of habitats in Queensland, NSW, Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia (photo below). This plant has mauve fan flowers on light green groundcover foliage.

plants.name: Grevillea wilsonii × tripartita
plants.context: 12. Turn right downhill to see, on your right, Grevillea wilsonii x tripartita, a tall, rangy bush with prickly foliage and large pink spider flowers with red styles (photo below left).

plants.name: Grevillea asteriscosa
plants.context: 13. Turn right along the road to see, on your right, Grevillea asteriscosa or Star-leaf Grevillea with small, dark green, prickly foliage and lipstick red flowers with long styles (photo above right). This plant is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Lambertia formosa
plants.context: 14. Further on your left is Lambertia formosa, or Mountain Devil, with red flowers with long stamens and sepals (photo below left). The common name comes from the horned, woody seed follicles, which were used to make small devil-figures. This plant is endemic to the coast and ranges of New South Wales.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Coconut Ice'
plants.context: 15. Also on your left is Grevillea ‘Coconut Ice’ with large pink and orange spider flowers with long red styles (photo above right). This hybrid plant was grown from seed collected from G. bipinnatifida and the male parent was G. banksii (white flowered form). The seedling was raised by Mr. M. Hodge of Queensland. title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, turn right behind the depot, then uphill towards the Red Centre Garden

plants.name: Pandorea jasminoides
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre look up to your left to see Pandorea jasminoides covered in scented, pink trumpet flowers with attractive mid-green foliage (photo above). This woody vine, also known as Bower of Beauty, is native to New South Wales and Queensland, and forms large pointed pods filled with papery seeds.

plants.name: Banksia serrata
plants.context: 2. Further on your right is Banksia serrata, a small tree with very large greenish brushes, ovate serrated leaves and a wrinkled trunk (photo next page top left). The trunk wrinkles more with age leading to its common name of Old Man Banksia. Banksia serrata is a widespread species in eastern Australia, extending from southern Queensland to Victoria's south coast, across to northern Tasmania, and as far inland as the Great Dividing Range.

plants.name: Melaleuca nesophila 'Narrow Ness'
plants.context: 3. Bear left behind the café, then right behind the depot, then left again up the hill to see, on your left, Melaleuca nesophila ‘Narrow Ness’, an upright shrub with purplish-pink pom-pom flowers fading to white, giving it a two-tone appearance (photo above right). The narrow habit makes it suitable for smaller gardens.

plants.name: Leptospermum trinervium
plants.context: 4. On your right is Leptospermum trinervium (syn. Gaudium trinervium), commonly known as Flaky-barked Tea-tree, Slender Tea-tree or Paperbark Tree, a species of shrub or small tree, with grey-green foliage and white flowers, that is endemic to eastern mainland Australia (photo above).

plants.name: Cordyline stricta
plants.context: 5. Further on your left is Cordyline stricta, or Narrow-leaved Palm Lily, with long sprays of violet flowers (photo above). The glossy green foliage is linear and up to half a metre long. This plant is native to the coast of northeast- ern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Brachychiton rupestris
plants.context: 6. On your right is Brachychiton rupestris, or Queensland Bottle Tree, a small tree with a trunk swollen with water, endemic to central Queensland and northern New South Wales (photo below).

plants.name: Prostanthera williamsii
plants.context: 7. Turn right to see, on your left, Prostanthera williamsii, a small plant with aromatic foliage and pale mauve flowers fading to white, native to the northern tablelands of NSW, near Wollomombi Gorge (photo below).

plants.name: Banksia canei
plants.context: 8. On your right is Banksia canei commonly known as the Mountain Banksia, a species endemic to southeastern NSW and eastern Victoria. This shrub has narrow leaves, attrac- tive smooth bark and cream to yellow flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Banksia attenuata
plants.context: 9. Also on your right is Banksia attenuata, commonly known as the Slender Banksia, with narrow, serrated leaves and bright yellow flowers, native to southwestern WA (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Coconut Ice'
plants.context: 10. Further on your right is Grevillea ‘Coconut Ice’ with large pink/orange spider flowers with long red styles (photo below). This hybrid plant was grown from seed collected from G. bipinnatifida and the male parent was G. banksii (white flowered form). The seedling was raised by Mr. M. Hodge of Queensland.

plants.name: Lomatia myricoides
plants.context: 11. Still on your right is Lomatia myricoides, a medium shrub or small tree with linear green leaves and white clusters of flowers (photo below). This plant is native to southeastern New South Wales and northeastern Victoria.

plants.name: Grevillea whiteana
plants.context: 12. Turn left up the hill, to see on your left, Grevillea whiteana, a tall rangy bush with dark green linear leaves and creamy-white racemes of flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Leptospermum polygalifolium subsp. transmontanum
plants.context: 13. Also on your left is Leptospermum polygalifolium subsp. transmontanum, a light airy bush with white ‘tea-tree’ flowers with gold centres, native to the northern part of New South Wales and Queensland (photo above right).

plants.name: Hakea salicifolia subsp. salicifolia
plants.context: 14. On your right is Hakea salicifolia ssp. salicifolia, or Willow Hakea, a fast growing, bushy plant with long, narrow leaves and white flowers in axillary clusters. The nuts have round protuberances with black blister like warts on the surface. This plant is native to coastal NSW.

plants.name: Triplarina nowraensis
plants.context: 15. Still on your right is Triplarina nowraensis, or Nowra Heath Myrtle, a small drooping bush with creamy-white tea-tree flowers which occur in pairs (photo below). This plant is listed as endangered in the wild and only occurs in the Nowra area, New South Wales. title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk up the hill behind the café, along the road above the Rock Garden and finish at the waterfall at the lower entry to the Rock Garden

plants.name: Eremophila cuneifolia × E. fraseri
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre, on your right, in a pot, is Eremophila cuneifolia x E. fraseri, the most spectacular of all the E. cuneifolia hybrids, forming a shrub 2m high and wide with large green leaves, purple flowers with spotted throats, and very large pink sepals (photo above).

plants.name: Banksia robur
plants.context: 2. Further on your right, also in a pot, is Banksia robur (purple leaf form), or Swamp Banksia, with long egg-shaped leaves which are shiny on top and dull underneath (photo next page top left). The flowers are bluish-green when young, devel- oping into yellow-green and then rusty-brown with age. The new leaf growth is velvety reddish purple. This plant is native to the eastern mainland coast of Australia usually in sandy or swampy conditions.

plants.name: Banksia serrata
plants.context: 3. Still on your right is Banksia serrata, a small tree with very large greenish flowers, ovate serrated leaves and a wrinkled trunk (photo above right). The trunk wrinkles more with age leading to its common name of Old Man Banksia. Banksia serrata is a widespread species in eastern Australia, extending from southern Queensland to Victoria's south coast, across to northern Tasmania. The plant occurs as far inland as the Great Dividing Range.

plants.name: Spyridium burragorang
plants.context: 4. Again on your right is Spyridium burragorang, a long-flowering shrub with unusual white bracts surrounding a central cluster of flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to the Lake Burragorang district in the Blue Mountains of New South Wales and it is considered rare in the wild.

plants.name: Grevillea leptobotrys
plants.context: 5. Still on your right, in a pot, is Grevillea leptobotrys, or Tangled Grevilla, with small racemes of lilac-pink flowers buried in prickly dark green foliage with red new growth (photo above right). Grevillea leptobotrys is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Crinum pedunculatum
plants.context: 6. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, on your right, Crinum pedunculatum with long green strappy leaves and striking terminal clusters of white perfumed flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to the tidal flats of coastal Queensland and New South Wales.

plants.name: Hibiscus divaricatus
plants.context: 7. On your left is Hibiscus divaricatus, with pure yellow flowers contrasting with maroon centres and stamens on a straggly bush (photo above right). This hibiscus is found in Queensland, the Northern Territory, and in northern parts of Western Australia. Usually a shrub, this plant can reach the size of a small tree, up to about 5m tall.

plants.name: Doryanthes palmeri
plants.context: 8. Further on your left is Doryanthes palmeri or Spear Lily (photo above). This is one of the most spectacular flowers in the Gardens, a huge nodding cluster of bright red flowers much visited by insects and honeyeaters. The rosette of leaves can reach a length of about 3m and the flowers grow on a stalk which may reach 5m in height. This plant is found in northeastern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Leptospermum subglabratum
plants.context: 9. On your right is Leptospermum subglabratum with masses of 5-petalled white star flowers on small green foliage (photo below). This plant is native to Budawang Range, southeastern NSW.

plants.name: Anigozanthos 'Landscape Pink Pastel'
plants.context: 10. Also on your right as you turn right along the road above the Rock Garden, is Anigozanthos ‘Landscape Pink Pastel’ one of the ‘Landscape Line’ bred by Angus Stewart from Anigozanthos flavidus, or Tall Kangaroo Paw, which come in many colours (photo below). All Kangaroo Paws are native to Western Australia and the flowers are bird pollinated.

plants.name: Anigozanthos flavidus
plants.context: 11. Still on your right is Anigozanthos flavidus or Tall Kangaroo Paw in rusty orange and yellow shades (photo below).

plants.name: Acacia craspedocarpa
plants.context: 12. On your left is Acacia craspedocarpa, or Hop Mulga, a bush with yellow rod flowers and grey foliage native to south-central Western Australia (photo below left).

plants.name: Melaleuca nesophila
plants.context: 13. Turn right down the Main Path to see, on your right, Melaleuca nesophila, an upright shrub with purplish-pink pom-pom flowers fading to white, giving it a two-tone appearance (photo above right). This plant is native to the area near Albany, Western Australia.

plants.name: Callistemon comboynensis
plants.context: 14. Also on your right is Callistemon comboynensis, or Cliff Bottlebrush, with bright red flowers (photo below). This plant is native to coastal southern Queensland and northern New South Wales. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Today we will walk up the hill behind the café, along the road above the Rock Garde

plants.name: Babingtonia 'Howie's Feathertips'
plants.context: 15. Go past the waterfall to see, on your left, Babingtonia ‘Howie’s Feathertips’ a large bush of dense light green foliage with masses of tiny creamy-white flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Rhododendron (viriosum) lochiae
plants.context: 1. On your left as you approach the Visitor Centre is Rhododendron (viriosum) lochiae with magnificent coral bells on shiny dark green leaves (photo above). This is one of the few representatives of this genus in Australia and is native to the high mountains of tropical northern Queensland.

plants.name: Blandfordia grandiflora
plants.context: 2. On your right, in a pot, is Blandfordia grandiflora, or Christmas Bells, with large fluted red bells tipped with yellow on thin stems above linear foliage, native to southeastern Australia (photo next page top left).

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia 'Dwarf Orange'
plants.context: 3. On your left is Corymbia ficifolia ‘Dwarf Orange’ a small tree, with brilliant orange, fluffy blooms and dark green foliage (photo above right). This grafted gum, originally from Western Australia, is one of the most spectacular when in full flower.

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia
plants.context: 4. Also on your left is Corymbia ficifolia, a grafted gum with dark green leathery foliage and clusters of white fluffy flowers (photo above)

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia 'Precious Pearl'
plants.context: 5. On your right is Corymbia ficifolia ‘Precious Pearl’ with masses of pink buds opening to pale pink fluffy flowers mobbed by bees. This small and compact cultivar is a grafted form of the West Australian flowering gum, Corymbia ficifolia.

plants.name: Callistemon subulatus 'Brogo Overflow'
plants.context: 6. Continue across the bridge towards the café, then bear right to see, on your right Callistemon subulatus ‘Brogo Overflow’ with bright red brushes and a low spreading habit (photo below left).

plants.name: Pelargonium sp. striatellum
plants.context: 7. On your left is Pelargonium sp. striatellum, commonly known as Omeo Stork's-bill, an undescribed species listed as endangered in New South Wales and vulnerable in Victoria (photo above right). Omeo Storks-bill has leaves in basal rosettes with pale pink flowers marked in darker crimson stripes. The fruit is elongated and shaped like a stork's bill, hence the plant's common name. This plant is known from only four locations in lake beds in the Monaro region and from Lake Omeo, Victoria.

plants.name: Anigozanthos flavidus
plants.context: 8. On your right is Anigozanthos flavidus or Tall Kangaroo Paw in rusty red shades (photo above). All Kangaroo Paws are native to Western Australia and the flowers are bird pollinated.

plants.name: Scaevola humilis 'Sitting Pretty'
plants.context: 9. On your left is Scaevola humilis ‘Sitting Pretty’, with a spreading habit, green leaves and pink fan flowers, bred by Peter Abell (photo below).

plants.name: Callistemon 'Injune'
plants.context: 10. On your right is a clump of Callistemon ‘Injune’ an evergreen shrub with masses of pale pink flowers, which fade to white, both colours on the shrub at the same time (photo below).

plants.name: Actinotus helianthi
plants.context: 11. Low on your left is Actinotus helianthi or Flannel Flower with white star flowers with yellow grey centres and silver-grey divided foliage (photo below). These plants are native to the coast and mountains of New South Wales and southern Queensland.

plants.name: Poa labillardieri
plants.context: 12. Turn sharp left to see, on your left, Poa labillardieri or Common Tussock Grass, a soft, weeping fine-leaved grass native to southern and eastern Australia, including Tasmania (photo below left). The grey-green foliage can turn straw coloured and plume-like flower heads extend above the foliage to 1m high.

plants.name: Grevillea rhyolitica 'Deua Flame'
plants.context: 13. Also on your left is Grevillea rhyolitica ‘Deua Flame’, a shrub with arching stems of glossy green foliage and coral red spider flowers (photo above right).

plants.name: Alyogyne 'Aussie Purple'
plants.context: 14. Still on your left is Alyogyne ‘Aussie Purple’ a hybrid between Alyogyne huegelii and A. hakeifolia, with bright purple flowers over a long period (photo above). A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Just a short walk today from the Visitors Centre to the environs of the Café.

plants.name: Babingtonia plurijuga
plants.context: 15. On your right is Babingtonia plurijuga ‘White Cascade’ a medium-sized bush with green weeping foliage and masses of small white, 5-petalled flowers with green centres (photo above).

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk up the hill behind the café, past the entrance to the Rock Garden towards the Red Centre Garden

plants.name: Backhousia citriodora
plants.context: 1. After leaving the Visitor Centre look up to your left to see Backhousia citriodora, or Lemon Ironwood, a small tree with shiny green leaves and large, white, fluffy heads of flowers with prominent bracts (photo above). This plant is endemic to the tropical rainforest areas of Queensland between Brisbane and Mackay. The leaves of this plant are strongly lemon scented.

plants.name: Banksia serrata
plants.context: 2. On your right is Banksia serrata, a small tree with very large greenish brushes, ovate serrated leaves and a wrinkled trunk (photo next page top left). The trunk wrinkles more with age leading to its common name of Old Man Banksia. Banksia serrata is a widespread species in eastern Australia.

plants.name: Grevillea barklyana subsp. barklyana
plants.context: 3. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, on your left Grevillea barklyana subsp. barklyana, or Gully Grevillea, a large bush with pink toothbrush flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to a restricted area of Victoria along the upper Bunyip River.

plants.name: Westringia fruticosa 'Wunderbar'
plants.context: 4. Bear right behind the depot to see on your left as you turn left up the hill Westringia fruticosa ‘Wunderbar’ or ‘Double Wonder’, a small dense shrub with grey-green foliage and pale mauve or pink semi-double flowers (photo above).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Legacy Flame'
plants.context: 5. Also on your left is Grevillea ‘Legacy Flame’, a small grevillea, bred locally by Bywong Nursery, which commemorates 100 years of Legacy Australia with flame-like orange-red flowers which resemble the Legacy torch (photo above).

plants.name: Crowea 'Little Rockstar'
plants.context: 6. Further on your left is Crowea ‘Little Rockstar’, a compact form of Crowea, reaching only 60-80cm high, from a seedling variant growing at the ANBG (photo below). This plant has many pink star flowers.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Bloodline'
plants.context: 7. Still on your left is Grevillea ‘Bloodline’, a new Grevillea bred at Bywong Nursery by Peter Ollerenshaw, similar to the long flowering variety Grevillea ‘Lady O’, but with a slightly arching habit (photo below).

plants.name: Callistemon brachyandrus
plants.context: 8. Again on your left is Callistemon brachyandrus, with grey-green linear foliage and red flowers with gold tipped stamens (photo below). The common name of this plant is Prickly Bottlebrush and it does live up to its name. This species is native to western New South Wales, Victoria and South Australia.

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia 'Little Sweetie'
plants.context: 9. Turn right in front of the waterfall to see, on your left, Corymbia ficifolia ‘Little Sweetie’, a grafted gum with dark green leathery foliage and clusters of pink fluffy flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Lythrum salicaria
plants.context: 10. Also on your left is Lythrum salicaria or Purple Loosestrife, with terminal spikes of purple flowers on light green foliage with red stems (photo below). This interesting species is native not only to southeastern Australia but widespread in Europe, Asia and North America.

plants.name: Hakea constablei
plants.context: 11. Turn right along the road above the Rock Garden to see, on your right, Hakea constablei, a bushy shrub or small tree with very large brown nuts (photo below). This plant is endemic to the Blue Mountains near Sydney and was named after Ernest Constable, a plant collector for the Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney.

plants.name: Grevillea triloba
plants.context: 12. Further on your right is Grevillea triloba, a spreading shrub with white starburst flowers (photo below left). This grevillea is native to the Geraldton area in Western Australia.

plants.name: Banksia aemula
plants.context: 13. Turn left up the hill to see on your right Banksia aemula or Wallum Banksia, a small, gnarled tree with knobby bark and large squat green cones (photo above right). This plant is native to Queensland and New South Wales, in coastal, heath, and sandy soil areas.

plants.name: Acacia longissima
plants.context: 14. Aso on your right, is Acacia longissima, a spreading, graceful shrub with pale flowers in slender rods (photo above). This hardy wattle is both long flowering and late flowering, native to coastal Queensland and NSW. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Today we will walk up the hill behind the café, past the

plants.name: Leptospermum squarrosum
plants.context: 15. Also on your right is Leptospermum squarrosum, or Peach Blossom Tea Tree, a bushy, upright shrub, native to sandstone areas of the coast and adjacent plateaus of mid-New South Wales (photo above). The leaves are stiff, triangular and sharply pointed, being held alternatively and at right angles to the stem, with white flowers with green centres.

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, along the road above the Rock Garden, then back by the Main Path

plants.name: Crowea saligna
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre look right to see, in a pot, Crowea saligna, a small shrub with large pink flowers and aromatic foliage (photo above). Native bees and butterflies are attracted to this plant, which is native to the central coastal area of NSW.

plants.name: Crinum pedunculatum
plants.context: 2. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, on your left, Crinum pedunculatum with long green strappy leaves and striking terminal clusters of white perfumed flowers (photo next page top left). This plant is native to the tidal flats of coastal Queensland and New South Wales.

plants.name: Macrozamia communis
plants.context: 3. Also on your left is Macrozamia communis or Burrawang, with arching, shiny, yellow- green foliage (photo above right). The Burra- wang is a cycad native to the east coast of New South Wales.

plants.name: Beaufortia sparsa
plants.context: 4. Turn right along the road above the Rock Garden to see, on your right, Beaufortia sparsa, a small bush with neat, green foliage and luminous red/orange ‘bottlebrush’ flowers, native to the extreme southwestern corner of Western Australia (photo above).

plants.name: Calothamnus tuberosus
plants.context: 5. Further on your right is Calothamnus tuberosus, a stiff upright bush with spiky grey -green linear foliage and bright red fluffy flowers (photo above). This plant is endemic to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Acacia fulva
plants.context: 6. Further on your left is Acacia fulva, Velvet or Soft Wattle, named for its velvety, young leaves and seed pods, with rods of yellow ball flowers (photo below). This plant is rare and native from Gloucester to Mt. Yengo in Howes Valley, NSW.

plants.name: Grevillea leptobotrys
plants.context: 7. Turn right downhill, then bear right again along the Main Path to see, on your left, in a pot, Grevillea leptobotrys, or Tangled Grevilla, with small racemes of lilac-pink flowers buried in prickly, dark green foliage with red new growth (photo below). Grevillea leptobotrys is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Grevillea manglesii subsp. ornithopoda
plants.context: 8. Further on your right is Grevillea manglesii subsp. ornithopoda, or Birdsfoot Grevillea, a large bush with frothy, white terminal clusters of flowers and tripartite ‘birdsfoot’ foliage (photo below). This plant is native to Western Australia near Perth.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Lady O'
plants.context: 9. Again on your right is Grevillea ‘Lady O’, a long-blooming shrub with red flowers and bright green foliage (photo below). ‘Lady O’ is a cross between a Grevillea victoriae hybrid x Grevillea rhyolitica made by local plant breeder Peter Ollerenshaw and named for his mother.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Coconut Ice'
plants.context: 10. Turn right along the road to see, on your left, Grevillea ‘Coconut Ice’ with large pink/orange spider flowers with long red styles (photo below). This hybrid plant was grown from seed collected from G. bipinnatifida and the male parent was G. banksii (white flowered form). The seedling was raised by Mr. M. Hodge of Queensland.

plants.name: Banksia robur
plants.context: 11. Also on your left is Banksia robur, or Swamp Banksia, with long egg-shaped leaves which are shiny on top and dull underneath (photo below). This plant is native to the eastern mainland coast of Australia usually in sandy or swampy conditions. The flowers are bluish green when young, developing into yellow green and then rusty brown as they age.

plants.name: Banksia conferta
plants.context: 12. Still on your left is Banksia conferta, an attractive, tall bush with elliptical leaves and yellow -green flowers, native to the Lamington Plateau and Glasshouse Mountains in Queensland and adjacent northeastern NSW (photo below left).

plants.name: Banksia canei
plants.context: 13. Again on your left is Banksia canei, or Mountain Banksia, a species endemic to south- eastern NSW and eastern Victoria (photo above right). This shrub has narrow leaves, attractive smooth bark and cream to yellow flowers.

plants.name: Banksia integrifolia subsp. compar
plants.context: 14. On your left is Banksia integrifolia subsp. compar or Coast Banksia, a small tree with long yellow flowers and dark green leaves with silver backs (photo below left). This tree is native to the east coast of Queensland A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill

plants.name: Banksia aemula
plants.context: 15. On your right is Banksia aemula or Wallum Banksia, a small, gnarled tree with knobby bark and large squat green cones (photo above right). This plant is native to Queensland and New South Wales, from Bundaberg to Sydney, in coastal, heath, and sandy soil areas.

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, bear left behind the café and right behind the depot, then left up the hill towards the Rock Garden, pass in front of the Rock Garden, then left along the road above the Rock Garden to complete the circle

plants.name: Acacia binervia 'Sterling Silver'
plants.context: 1. As you approach the Visitor Centre on your left is Acacia binervia ‘Sterling Silver’, a hardy mounding plant, tolerant of windy sites and almost any well-drained soil, with beautiful silver-grey foliage and showy yellow rod flowers (photo above).

plants.name: Eremophila subfloccosa subsp. subfloccosa
plants.context: 2. Also on your left is Eremophila subfloccosa subsp. subfloccosa, a low, spreading shrub with furry, silver foliage clasping the stem and green tubular flowers (photo next page top left). This plant is native to central and southern Western Australia and South Australia.

plants.name: Pilidiostigma rhytispermum
plants.context: 3. To the right of the door to the Visitor Centre, in a pot, is Pilidiostigma rhytispermum, or Small-leaved Plum Myrtle, a woody shrub with small leaves and cream cup flowers with prom- inent yellow stamens (photo above right). This plant has black fruits which are attractive to many fruit eating birds and is native to the coast of southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Peaches and Cream'
plants.context: 4. After the Visitor Centre look down to your right to see Grevillea ‘Peaches and Cream’ with divided green leaves and large flower heads of pink and cream (photos above). This hybrid was developed in Queensland by Jan Glazebrook and Dennis Cox and patented in 2006.

plants.name: Syzygium 'Cascade'
plants.context: 5. On your left is Syzygium ‘Cascade’, a cultivated hybrid between Syzygium luehmannii (a NSW/Qld species) and S. wilsonii (a northern Qld species) (photo above). New growth is an attractive bronze- pink colour and the flowers are pink.

plants.name: Corymbia 'Summer Red'
plants.context: 6. On your right is Corymbia ‘Summer Red’, a grafted eucalypt with dark green leathery foliage, attractive new red foliage and beautiful bud formations (photo below).

plants.name: Crowea 'Little Rockstar'
plants.context: 7. Bear left behind the café, then right behind the depot, then left uphill towards the Rock Garden, to see on your left, Crowea ‘Little Rockstar’, a compact form of Crowea, reaching only 60-80cm high, from a seedling variant growing at the ANBG (photo below). This plant has many pink star flowers.

plants.name: Correa alba
plants.context: 8. Further on your left is Correa alba, or White Correa, with grey-green leaves with silver backs and white star flowers (photo below). This correa is a popular and reliable plant in the garden, native to eastern coastal regions of Australia, first formally described by Henry Cranke Andrews in 1798.

plants.name: Callistemon recurvus
plants.context: 9. Further on your left is Callistemon recurvus, or Tinaroo Bottlebrush, with bright red flowers and some leaves with the edges curved under (photo below). This plant is endemic to coastal northern Queensland.

plants.name: Callistemon pachyphyllus 'Smoked Salmon'
plants.context: 10. Still on your left is Callistemon pachyphyllus ‘Smoked Salmon’, with pink brushes on stiff foliage (photos below). This plant is a selected, naturally occurring, pink flowered form of C. pachyphyllus found growing amongst the normal red flowered form in the Runaway Bay area of the Gold Coast, brought into cultivation in 1976 by Mrs Joan Barton.

plants.name: Acacia cognata
plants.context: 11. Turn right in front of the waterfall, follow the Main Path to the road, then sharp left to see, on your left, Acacia cognata, or Bower Wattle, a graceful, weeping tree with green linear leaves, native to southeastern mainland Australia (photos below).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Mason's Hybrid'
plants.context: 12. Also on your left is Grevillea ‘Mason’s Hybrid’, a spreading bush with large spider blooms of pink, red and orange (photo below left).

plants.name: Brachyscome multifida 'Country Lights'
plants.context: 13. Bear left down the hill to see, low on your right, Brachyscome multifida ‘Country Lights’, a mounding daisy with fine green foliage and dark purple flowers with gold centres (photo above right).

plants.name: Callistemon viminalis
plants.context: 14. Callistemon viminalis, on your left, is a tree with drooping foliage and brilliant red flowers (photos above). This plant, also known as Weeping Bottlebrush, is native to New South Wales and Queensland. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, bear left behind the café a

plants.name: Callistemon montanus
plants.context: 15. On your right is Callistemon montanus, with bright red flowers with gold tips (photos above). This plant is a haven for both birds and butterflies and is native to northern New South Wales and southern Queensland.

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre up the hill behind the depot towards the Red Centre Garden

plants.name: Corymbia 'Summer Red'
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre, on your right is Corymbia ‘Summer Red’, a grafted eucalypt with dark green leathery foliage, attractive new red foliage, red fluffy flowers with yellow centres and beautiful bud formations (photo above).

plants.name: Alocasia brisbanensis
plants.context: 2. Bear left up the hill behind the café, to see on your left, Alocasia brisbanensis, or Spoon Lily or Cunjevoi, with large, veined leaves and bunches of green rounded fruits (photo next page top left). This plant can grow up to 1.5m tall and is native to rainforests of eastern mainland Australia.

plants.name: Scaevola 'Pink Fusion'
plants.context: 3. Bear right behind the depot to see, low on your right, Scaevola ‘Pink Fusion’, a low- growing, wide-spreading, cushion-like plant with many pink, fan flowers over a long period (photo above right).

plants.name: Westringia fruticosa 'Wunderbar'
plants.context: 4. Turn left up the hill to see, on your left, Westringia fruticosa ‘Wunderbar’ or ‘Double Wonder’, a small dense shrub with grey-green foliage and pale mauve or pink semi-double flowers (photo above).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Legacy Flame'
plants.context: 5. Also on your left is Grevillea ‘Legacy Flame’, a small grevillea, bred locally by Bywong Nursery, which commemorates 100 years of Legacy Australia with flame-like, orange-red flowers which resemble the Legacy torch (photo above).

plants.name: Crowea 'Little Rockstar'
plants.context: 6. Further on your left is Crowea ‘Little Rockstar’, a compact form of Crowea, reaching only 60-80cm high, from a seedling variant growing at the ANBG (photo below). This plant has many pink star flowers.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Bloodline'
plants.context: 7. Also on your left is Grevillea ‘Bloodline’, a plant bred at Bywong Nursery by Peter Ollerenshaw, like the long flowering variety Grevillea ‘Lady O’, but with a slightly arching habit (photo below).

plants.name: Cordyline stricta
plants.context: 8. Still on your left is Cordyline stricta, or Narrow-leaved Palm Lily, with long sprays of shiny black berries (photo below). The glossy green foliage is linear and up to half a metre long. This plant is native to the coast of north- eastern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Metal Red'
plants.context: 9. Again on your left is Grevillea ‘Metal Red’, a hardy shrub with metallic-red flowers held above soft, divided green foliage. a hybrid between G. banksii 'prostrate' x G. 'Bronze Rambler' (photo below left).

plants.name: Phebalium woombye
plants.context: 10. Once more on your left is Phebalium woombye, a bushy shrub with slender leaves, silver on the reverse, and clusters of starry, pink flowers, native to southeastern Queensland and northeastern NSW coastal regions (photo above right).

plants.name: Correa alba
plants.context: 11. Further on your left is Correa alba, commonly known as White Correa, with grey-green leaves with silver backs and white star flowers (photo above). This correa is a popular and reliable plant in the garden, native to eastern coastal regions of Australia from northern NSW to Tasmania and eastern South Australia. This species was first formally described by Henry Cranke Andrews in 1798.

plants.name: Eucalyptus macrocarpa
plants.context: 12. Turn right in front of the waterfall to see, on your left, Eucalyptus macrocarpa, or Mottlecah, with magnificent silver- grey, sword-like foliage (photo below left). This sprawling mallee is native to southwestern Western Australia.

plants.name: Callistemon comboynensis
plants.context: 13. Again on your left is Callistemon comboynensis, or Cliff Bottlebrush, with bright red flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to coastal southern Queensland and northern New South Wales.

plants.name: Backhousia myrtifolia
plants.context: 14. Turn left, then right uphill towards the Red Centre Garden to see, on your right Backhousia myrtifolia, or Grey Myrtle, a rainforest tree with cream star flowers and cinnamon scented leaves, native to subtropical rainforests of eastern Australia (photo below left). A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Today we

plants.name: Swainsona formosa
plants.context: 15. Look straight ahead to see Swainsona formosa, or Sturt’s Desert Pea, with pale green leaves and bright red pea flowers with shiny black centres or bosses (photo above right). This iconic plant, the floral emblem of South Australia, is named for the English botanist Isaac Swainson and is native to all mainland states except Victoria.

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will take a short walk from the Visitor Centre to the Banksia Garden

plants.name: Grevillea 'Peaches and Cream'
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre look down to your right to see Grevillea ‘Peaches and Cream’ with deeply divided green leaves and large flower heads of pink and cream (photo above). This hybrid was developed in Queensland by Jan Glazebrook and Dennis Cox and patented in 2006.

plants.name: Doryanthes palmeri
plants.context: 2. Look up to your left to see Doryanthes palmeri or Spear Lily (photo next page top left). When in flower this is one of the most spectacular flowers in the Gardens, a huge nodding cluster of bright red flowers much visited by insects and honeyeaters. At present the enormous seed pods are clearly visible on the spent flower. This plant is native to northeastern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Epacris longiflora
plants.context: 3. Further on your left is Epacris longiflora ‘Nectar Pink’, a very floriferous small shrub covered in slender pink bells with white tips (photo above right).

plants.name: Corymbia 'Summer Red'
plants.context: 4. On your right is Corymbia ‘Summer Red’, a grafted eucalypt with dark green leathery foliage, attractive new red foliage, red fluffy flowers and beautiful bud formations (photo above).

plants.name: Anigozanthos 'Bush Pearl'
plants.context: 5. Also on your right is Anigozanthos ‘Bush Pearl’, a hybrid Kangaroo Paw with long- blooming bright pink flowers developed by Angus Stewart (photo above).

plants.name: Crowea 'Little Rockstar'
plants.context: 6. Again on your right is Crowea ‘Little Rockstar’, a compact form of Crowea, reaching only 60-80cm high, from a seedling variant growing at the ANBG (photo below left). This plant has many pink star flowers.

plants.name: Banksia integrifolia
plants.context: 7. Cross the bridge and skirt the café to see, on your left, Banksia integrifolia, a small tree with oblong, green, silver-backed leaves and greenish flowers (photo above right). This banksia, commonly known as the Coast Bank- sia, is native to the eastern coast of Australia from Victoria to Queensland.

plants.name: Banksia menziesii
plants.context: 8. As you enter the Banksia Garden, on your right is Banksia menziesii, Firewood Banksia or Menzies Banksia, a small tree or shrub with oblong, toothed, green leaves and deep pink to red flowers (photo above). This plant is native to the west coast of Western Australia, around Perth.

plants.name: Banksia epica
plants.context: 9. On your left is Banksia epica, a bushy shrub without a lignotuber, with large creamy-yellow flowers and iridescent lime-green buds (photo below). This species is native to the Great Australian Bight, WA.

plants.name: Banksia hookeriana
plants.context: 10. On your right is Banksia hookeriana, or Hooker’s Banksia, with upright, slender, green, toothed foliage and bright orange flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to the area between Perth and Geraldton in Western Australia.

plants.name: Banksia brownii
plants.context: 11. Also on your right is Banksia brownii or Feather-leaved Banksia, named after Robert Brown, (1773-1858), Scottish born botanist who accompanied Flinders to Australia in 1801 (photo above right). This shrub with soft, linear, whorled leaves and gold flowers is native to the south coast of Western Australia from Albany to the Stirling Ranges.

plants.name: Banksia spinulosa 'Birthday Candles'
plants.context: 12. Down to your right is Banksia spinulosa ‘Birthday Candles’ a dense, bright-green bush with attractive needle foliage and short yellow flowers with reddish styles (photo below left). ‘Birthday Candles’ is a dwarf cultivar of Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa developed by Bill Molyneux of Austraflora Nurseries in Montrose, Victoria.

plants.name: Banksia neoanglica
plants.context: 13. On your right is Banksia neoanglica, or New England Banksia, with silver-backed, dark-green foliage with gold flowers held upright (photo above right). This shrub is native to the eastern tablelands of Queensland and New South Wales.

plants.name: Banksia paludosa
plants.context: 14. Again on your right is Banksia paludosa, or Marsh Banksia, with young ginger-coloured cones which develop into gold flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to central and southeastern New South Wales with an outlying population on the north coast near Kempsey. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Toda
