plants.context: 12. On your right is Alyogyne ‘Aussie Purple’, a hybrid between Alyogyne huegelii and A. hakeifolia, with bright purple flowers over a long period (photo below).

plants.name: Scaevola sp
plants.context: 13. Also on your right is Scaevola sp., a low-growing, spreading, cushion-like plant with many pink fan flowers over a long period (photo below).

plants.name: Prostanthera magnifica
plants.context: 14. On your left is Prostanthera magnifica, or Magnificent Mint-bush, with pink to mauve flowers with showy purple to red calyces and shiny leaves with wavy margins (photo below left). This plant is native to the central western coast of WA. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Today we will take a short walk from

plants.name: Callistemon 'Injune'
plants.context: 15. Further back to your right is Callistemon ‘Injune’, an evergreen shrub with many pale-pink flowers, which fade to white, both colours on the shrub at the same time (photo above right).

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the depot, cut through on the Main Path, then uphill again ending in the Rock Garden

plants.name: Jasminum simplicifolium subsp. suavissimum
plants.context: 1. Follow your nose to high to your right as you approach the Visitor Centre to see Jasminum simplicifolium ssp. suavissimum, or Forest Jasmine, with five starry white petals and a strong scent (photo above). This plant is native to northeastern NSW and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Banksia serrata
plants.context: 2. Further on your right is Banksia serrata, a small tree with large greenish flowers, ovate serrated leaves and a wrinkled trunk (photo next page top left). The trunk wrinkles more with age leading to its common name of Old Man Banksia. Banksia serrata is a widespread species in eastern Australia, as far inland as the Great Dividing Range.

plants.name: Orthrosanthus multiflorus
plants.context: 3. On your left is Orthrosanthus multiflorus, or Morning Iris, a clumping plant with grass-like foliage and true- blue flowers, native to coastal southern and western Australia (photo above right). Each flower only lasts one day but they are produced in profusion.

plants.name: Actinotus helianthi
plants.context: 4. On your right, in a pot, Is Actinotus helianthi or Flannel Flower, with white, star flowers with yellow-grey centres and silver- grey divided foliage (photo above). These plants are native to the coast and mountains of NSW and southern Queensland.

plants.name: Scaevola 'Pink Fusion'
plants.context: 5. Bear left up the hill, then right behind the depot, to see on your right Scaevola ‘Pink Fusion’, a low-growing, wide-spreading, cushion-like plant with many pink, fan flowers over a long period (photo above).

plants.name: Prostanthera lasianthos 'Kallista Pink'
plants.context: 6. Also on your right is Prostanthera lasianthos ‘Kallista Pink’, an erect, tall shrub, with dark green aromatic foliage and sprays of well-displayed pink flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Elaeocarpus reticulata 'Prima Donna'
plants.context: 7. Turn left uphill to see, on your left, Elaeocarpus reticulata ‘Prima Donna’, a dense tree with green leaves and pink, fringed bell flowers (photo below). Blue berries follow the flowers which are attractive to seed-eating birds.

plants.name: Cordyline stricta
plants.context: 8. Also on your left is Cordyline stricta, or Narrow-leaved Palm Lily, with long sprays of violet flowers, shiny black berries and glossy, green linear foliage up to half a metre long (photo below). This plant is native to the coastal northeastern NSW and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Grevillea robusta
plants.context: 9. Turn left along the Main Path to see, on your right, Grevillea robusta or Silky Oak, a large tree with divided foliage and golden-yellow flowers dripping with nectar (photo below). This plant is native to northeastern NSW and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Hibiscus divaricatus
plants.context: 10. Turn right uphill to see, on your left, Hibiscus divaricatus with pure yellow flowers contrasting with maroon centres and stamens on a straggly bush (photo below). This hibiscus is native to Queensland, the NT and northern parts of WA. Usually a shrub, this plant can reach the size of a small tree, up to about 5m tall.

plants.name: Doryanthes palmeri
plants.context: 11. Further on your left is Doryanthes palmeri or Spear Lily (photo below). This is one of the most spectacular flowers in the Gardens, a huge nodding cluster of bright red flowers much visited by insects and honeyeaters. The rosette of leaves can reach 3m long, flowers on a stalk which can be 5m in height. This plant is found in northeastern NSW and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Callistemon viminalis
plants.context: 12. Further on your right is Callistemon viminalis, a tree with drooping foliage and brilliant red flowers (photo below left). This plant is known as Weeping Bottlebrush and often grows along watercourses in its native NSW and Queensland.

plants.name: Veronica derwentiana subsp. derwentiana
plants.context: 13. Turn right along the road above the Rock Garden to see, on your left, Veronica derwentiana subsp. derwentiana with terminal sprays of white flowers on lacy bright green foliage (photo above right). This plant is native to the coast of eastern Australia from Queensland to South Australia, including Tasmania.

plants.name: Verticordia galeata
plants.context: 14. Bear right into the Rock Garden to see ahead in a pot, Verticordia galeata with bright gold, honey-scented flowers in profusion (photo above). This plant is native to the area near Geraldton, WA. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the depot, cut

plants.name: Grevillea whiteana
plants.context: 15. On your left is Grevillea whiteana, a tall, rangy bush with dark-green linear leaves and creamy-white racemes of flowers (photo above). This plant is native to southeastern Queensland.

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, along the road above the Rock Garden and turn left uphill towards the Red Centre Garden

plants.name: Brachychiton 'Jerilderie Red'
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre, on your right, in pots, are two Brachychiton ‘Jerilderie Red’, a small tree with a dense canopy of large lobed leaves, a bloated trunk and many powdery-red bell flowers (photo above).

plants.name: Brachychiton 'Griffith Pink'
plants.context: 2. Also on your right, in a pot is Brachychiton ‘Griffith Pink’ a shade tree with glossy, lobed foliage and clusters of pink bell flowers that appear in summer, a hybrid of B. populneus x discolor. Flowers are attractive to birds (photo next page top left).

plants.name: Eucalyptus langleyi
plants.context: 3. Look down the steps to your right to see Eucalyptus langleyi, or Green Mountain Ash or Albatross Mallee, which is native to a restricted area near Nowra, NSW and considered vulnerable in the wild (photo above right). This tree has glossy-green, ovate leaves and fluffy white flowers on long stalks.

plants.name: Grevillea leptobotrys
plants.context: 4. Also on your right, in a pot, is Grevillea leptobotrys, or Tangled Grevillea, with small racemes of lilac-pink flowers buried in prickly, dark-green foliage with red new growth (photo above). Grevillea leptobotrys is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Clerodendron floribundum var. attenuatum
plants.context: 5. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, on your left, Clerodendron floribundum var. attenuatum or Lolly Bush, a small rainforest tree with dark-green foliage and fluffy white flowers (photo above). This plant is native across the northern half of Australia.

plants.name: Melaleuca bracteate 'Revolution Green'
plants.context: 6. Further on your right is Melaleuca bracteate ‘Revolution Green’, a tree with dark green foliage and white blooms, endemic to northern Australia (photo below). The flowers have a slight honey scent and are very popular with insects.

plants.name: Hibiscus divaricatus
plants.context: 7. Further on your left is Hibiscus divaricatus with pure yellow flowers contrasting with maroon centres and stamens on a straggly bush (photo below). This hibiscus is native to Queensland, the NT and northern parts of WA.

plants.name: Cordyline stricta
plants.context: 8. On your right is Cordyline stricta, or Narrow-leaved Palm Lily, with long sprays of violet flowers and glossy, green linear foliage up to half a metre long (photo below). This plant is native to coastal northeastern NSW and southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Anigozanthos 'Landscape Pastel Pink'
plants.context: 9. Turn right along the road above the Rock Garden to see, on your right, Anigozanthos ‘Landscape Pastel Pink’ one of the ‘Landscape Line’ bred by Angus Stewart from Anigozanthos flavidus, or Tall Kangaroo Paw (photo below).

plants.name: Anigozanthos flavidus
plants.context: 10. On your left is Anigozanthos flavidus or Tall Kangaroo Paw in shades of green (photo below). All Kangaroo Paws are native to WA and the flowers are bird pollinated.

plants.name: Veronica derwentiana subsp. derwentiana
plants.context: 11. On your left is Veronica derwentiana subsp. derwentiana with terminal sprays of white flowers on lacy, bright-green foliage (photo below). This plant is native to the coast of eastern Australia from Queensland to South Australia, including Tasmania.

plants.name: Acacia dangarensis
plants.context: 12. Also on your left is Acacia dangarensis, a small tree with dense, frond-like phyllodes and attractive seed pods, endemic to NSW and confined to the summit and surrounding slopes of Mount Dangar south of Merriwa, within Goulburn River National Park (photo below left0. The total population size of this endangered wattled is esti- mated to be between 13,000 to 40,000 plants, ex- tending over an area of about 112 hectares.

plants.name: Grevillea whiteana
plants.context: 13. On your right is Grevillea whiteana, a tall rangy bush with dark green linear leaves and creamy-white racemes of flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Leptospermum polygalifolium subsp. montanum
plants.context: 14. Turn left uphill towards the Red Centre Garden to see, on your left, Leptospermum polygalifolium ssp. montanum, also known as Tantoon Tea Tree or Mountain Tea Tree, a small tree covered in white, five petalled-flowers with green centres (photo below left). This tree is native from the south coast of NSW to Cape York in far north Queensland. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. W

plants.name: Triplarina nowraensis
plants.context: 15. On your right is Triplarina nowraensis, or Nowra Heath Myrtle, a small, drooping bush with creamy-white tea-tree flowers which occur in pairs (photo above right). This plant is listed as endangered in the wild and only occurs in the Nowra area, NSW.

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, along the road behind the depot, then up the hill again, ending along the road above the Rock Garden

plants.name: Pandorea jasminoides
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre look up to your left to see Pandorea jasminoides covered in scented, pink, trumpet flowers with attractive mid-green foliage (photo above). This woody vine, also known as Bower of Beauty, is native to NSW and Queensland, and develops large, pointed pods filled with papery seeds.

plants.name: Banksia serrata
plants.context: 2. Further on your right is Banksia serrata, a small tree with large greenish flowers, ovate serrated leaves and a wrinkled trunk (photo next page top left). The trunk wrinkles more with age leading to its common name of Old Man Banksia. Banksia serrata is a widespread species in eastern Australia, as far inland as the Great Dividing Range.

plants.name: Spyridium burragorang
plants.context: 3. Also on your right is Spyridium burragorang, a long-flowering shrub with unusual white bracts surrounding a central cluster of flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to the Lake Burragorang district in the Blue Mountains, NSW and is considered rare in the wild.

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia 'Dwarf Orange'
plants.context: 4. Up to your left is Corymbia ficifolia ‘Dwarf Orange’, a small tree with dark green foliage and arrays of pink buds (photo above). This grafted gum, originally from the southern WA flowering gum, Corymbia ficifolia, is one of the most spectacular when in full flower.

plants.name: Melaleuca nesophila 'Narrow Nessy'
plants.context: 5. Bear left up the hill behind the café, then right along the road behind the depot to see, on your right, Melaleuca nesophila ‘Narrow Nessy’, an upright shrub with purplish-pink pom-pom flowers fading to white, giving it a two-tone appearance (photo above). The narrow habit makes it suitable for smaller gardens.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Lana Maree'
plants.context: 6. Turn left uphill to see on your left Grevillea ‘Lana Maree’, a shrub with divided foliage and rich pink, bird-attracting flowers bred by Richard Tomkin, Changers Green Nursery, Gin Gin, Queensland from the same cross as ‘Billy Bonkers’ – G. nana ssp. abbreviata x G. ‘Majestic’ (photo below left).

plants.name: Prostanthera lasianthos
plants.context: 7. Turn right along the road before the waterfall to see, on your left, Prostanthera lasianthos, with dense, dark-green foliage and white flowers with dark pink centres (photo above right). This plant is native to southeastern Australia, including eastern Tasmania.

plants.name: Brachychiton populneus subsp. populneus
plants.context: 8. On your right is Brachychiton populneus ssp. populneus, a drought-tolerant tree with neat, pointed green foliage and cream flowers with speckled dark red throats, native to a diversity of habitats in the eastern states, Queensland, NSW and Victoria (photo above).

plants.name: Stenocarpus angustifolius
plants.context: 9. On your left is Stenocarpus angustifolius, a bush with clusters of creamy umbel flowers opening from green buds in attractive contrast to the lance-shaped light green foliage (photos below). This plant is native to the Townsville area of coastal Queensland.

plants.name: Grevillea asteriscosa
plants.context: 10. Turn left up the hill to see, on your left, Grevillea asteriscosa or Star-leaf Grevillea with small, dark-green, prickly foliage and lipstick red flowers with long styles (photo below). This plant is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Grevillea triloba
plants.context: 11. Turn left along the road above the Rock Garden to see, on your left, Grevillea triloba, a spreading shrub with grey-green foliage and white starburst flowers (photo below). This grevillea is native to the Geraldton, WA area.

plants.name: Callistemon brachyandrus
plants.context: 12. On your right is Callistemon brachyandrus, with grey-green linear foliage and red flowers with gold tipped stamens (photo below left). The common name of this plant is Prickly Bottlebrush and it does live up to its name. This species is native to western NSW, Victoria and SA.

plants.name: Calothamnus tuberosus
plants.context: 13. On your left is Calothamnus tuberosus, a stiff, upright bush with spiky grey-green linear foliage and a few bright-red fluffy flowers appearing, endemic to southwestern WA (photo above right).

plants.name: Grevillea albiflora
plants.context: 14. Go left down the gravel path into the Rock Garden to see, on your left, Grevillea albiflora or White Spider Flower, a large sweet-smelling bush with long, grey needle-like foliage and white flowers with prominent styles, which develops smooth, velvety furred pinkish-beige fruits (photo below left). This plant is native to the drier inland parts of Australia and can be found in two distinct regions, one near Uluru and the other near the Queensland/NSW border near Bourke. A publication of the

plants.name: Anigozanthos flavidus
plants.context: 15. High on your right is Anigozanthos flavidus or Tall Kangaroo Paw in rusty orange shades (photo above right). All Kangaroo Paws are native to WA and the flowers are bird pollinated.

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre up to the Ian Potter National Conservatory under construction

plants.name: Rhododendron (viriosum) lochiae
plants.context: 1. On your left as you approach the Visitor Centre is Rhododendron (viriosum) lochiae with magnificent coral bells on shiny dark green leaves (photo above). This is one of the few representatives of the genus Rhododendron in Australia and is native to the high mountains of tropical northern Queensland.

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia sp
plants.context: 2. Further on your left Is Corymbia ficifolia sp., a small tree, with dark red, fluffy blooms and dark green, leathery foliage (photo next page top left). This grafted gum, native to Western Australia, is one of the most spectacular when in full flower.

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia 'Precious Pearl'
plants.context: 3. On your right is Corymbia ficifolia ‘Precious Pearl’ with masses of pink buds opening to pale pink fluffy flowers mobbed by bees (photo above right). This small and compact cultivar is a grafted form of the West Australian flowering gum.

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia 'Dwarf Orange'
plants.context: 4. High on your left is a row of Corymbia ficifolia ‘Dwarf Orange’, small trees, with dark green foliage, pink buds, brilliant orange, fluffy blooms and very attractive gumnuts (photo above). This grafted gum, originally from the southern West Australian flowering gum is one of the most spectacular when in full flower.

plants.name: Crinum pedunculatum
plants.context: 5. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, on your left, Crinum pedunculatum with long, green, strappy leaves and striking terminal clusters of white perfumed flowers (photo above). This plant is native to the tidal flats of coastal Queensland and New South Wales.

plants.name: Dicksonia antartica
plants.context: 6. Also on your left is Dicksonia antartica or Soft Tree Fern, with magnificent, bright green, ferny foliage which unfurls from the chocolate brown, hairy base (photo below). This iconic plant is native to southeastern Australia, including Tasmania.

plants.name: Callistemon subulatus 'Brogo Overflow'
plants.context: 7. Bear right behind the depot to see, on your left, Callistemon subulatus ‘Brogo Overflow’ with bright red flowers and a low spreading habit (photo below). This species is native to NSW and Victoria where it grows along the banks of watercourses.

plants.name: Babingtonia 'Howie's Feathertips'
plants.context: 8. Also on your left is Babingtonia ‘Howie’s Feathertips’, a large bush of dense, light green foliage with masses of tiny creamy-white flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Westringia fruticosa 'Wunderbar'
plants.context: 9. As you turn left up the hill, see on your left Westringia fruticosa ‘Wunderbar’ or ‘Double Wonder’, a small, dense shrub with grey-green foliage and pale mauve or pink semi-double flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Legacy Flame'
plants.context: 10. Also on your left is Grevillea ‘Legacy Flame’, a small grevillea, bred locally by Bywong Nursery, which commemorates 100 years of Legacy Australia with flame-like, orange-red flowers which resemble the Legacy torch (photo below).

plants.name: Scaevola albida 'Blue Skies'
plants.context: 11. Still on your left is Scaevola albida ‘Blue Skies’ (‘Blue Mist’), a prostrate shrub with small blue/mauve fan flowers on bright green foliage (photo below).

plants.name: Pelargonium littorale
plants.context: 12. Further back on your left is Pelargonium littorale, with bright pink flowers with darker pink markings on green, lobed ‘geranium’ leaves, native to southern coastal Australia, including Tasmania (photo below).

plants.name: Crowea 'Little Rockstar'
plants.context: 13. On your left is Crowea ‘Little Rockstar’, a compact form of Crowea from a seedling variant growing at the ANBG. This plant is covered in pink star flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Bloodline'
plants.context: 14. On your left is Grevillea ‘Bloodline’, bred at Bywong Nursery by Peter Ollerenshaw, similar to the long-flowering variety Grevillea ‘Lady O’, but with a slightly arching habit (photo below left). A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre up to the Ian Potter National Conse

plants.name: Grevillea 'Metal Red'
plants.context: 15. Once again on your left is Grevillea ‘Metal Red’, a hardy shrub with metallic-red flowers held above soft, divided green foliage. a hybrid between G. banksii 'prostrate' x G. 'Bronze Rambler' (photo above right).

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, across the bridge, past the cafe and along the road above the Banksia Garden to the Pomaderris Garden

plants.name: Blandfordia nobilis
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre, on your right, in a pot, is Blandfordia nobilis, or Christmas Bells, with large fluted red bells, tipped with yellow, on thin stems above linear foliage (photo above). Named blandfordia after George Spencer- Churchill (1766-1840), Marquis of Blandford, this plant is native to the sandstone country of southeastern NSW.

plants.name: Lepidozamia peroffskyana
plants.context: 2. On your left, in a pot, is Lepidozamia peroffskyana, or Pineapple Zamia, one of the tallest cycads, with long arching stems of shiny, dark green foliage (photo next page top left). This palm-like cycad is native to the wet open forests of southeastern Queensland and northeastern NSW. These plants do not produce flowers but have large cones on separate female and male plants.

plants.name: Banksia serrata
plants.context: 3. On your right is Banksia serrata, a small tree with large, greenish flowers, ovate serrated leaves and a wrinkled trunk (photo above right). The trunk wrinkles more with age leading to its common name of Old Man Banksia. Banksia serrata is a widespread species in eastern Australia, as far inland as the Great Dividing Range.

plants.name: Callistemon subulatus 'Brogo Overflow'
plants.context: 4. Go over the bridge and bear right, to see on your right, Callistemon subulatus ‘Brogo Overflow’ with bright red flowers and a low spreading habit (photo above). This species is native to NSW and Victoria where it grows along the banks of watercourses.

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia 'Dwarf Orange'
plants.context: 5. Again on your right is Corymbia ficifolia ‘Dwarf Orange’, a small tree, with dark green foliage, pink buds, brilliant orange, fluffy blooms and very attractive gumnuts (photo above).

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia
plants.context: 6. Also on your right is Corymbia ficifolia, a small tree, with dark-red, fluffy blooms and dark green leathery foliage (photo below). This grafted gum, originally from Western Australia, is one of the most spectacular when in full flower.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Wendy Sunshine'
plants.context: 7. On your left is Grevillea ‘Wendy Sunshine’, a small shrub with fine, divided, grey-green foliage and many pinkish-red spider flowers (photo below). This plant, a hybrid between Grevillea bipinnati- fida (Chittering Valley) x Grevillea thyr- soides ssp. pustulata was developed by Neil Marriott and is a great native bird and bee attractor.

plants.name: Banksia epica
plants.context: 8. Continue along the road above the Banksia Garden to see, on your right, Banksia epica, a bushy shrub without a lignotuber, with large creamy-yellow flowers and iridescent lime-green buds (photo below). This species is native to the Great Australian Bight, WA.

plants.name: Leptospermum juniperinum
plants.context: 9. On your left is Leptospermum juniperinum, a shrub with arching branches, white ‘tea=tree’ flowers and rough bark (photo below). This plant has a wide distribution along the entire NSW coast extending as far north as Fraser Island in Queensland and scattered through Victoria with some records in SA.

plants.name: Banksia prionotes
plants.context: 10. On your right is Banksia prionotes, commonly known as Acorn Banksia or Orange Banksia, which has toothed, grey-green linear foliage and white felty cones which develop a pale orange colour when mature (photo below left). This plant is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Banksia burdettii
plants.context: 11. Also on your right is Banksia burdettii, or Burdett’s Banksia, a tall shrub with grey-green oblong leaves, showy white buds turning to bright orange flowers as they open (photo above right). This plant is native to the area near Perth, WA

plants.name: Banksia media
plants.context: 12. Again on your right is Banksia media, or Southern Plains Banksia, with broad, toothed, leathery leaves and bright yellow flowers with brown tips (photo below left). This plant is native to the south coast of WA.

plants.name: Beaufortia sparsa
plants.context: 13. Turn left into the Pomaderris Garden to see, on your left, Beaufortia sparsa, a small bush with neat green foliage and luminous red/orange ‘bottlebrush’ flowers native to the extreme southwestern corner of WA (photo above right).

plants.name: Banksia baxteri
plants.context: 14. Turn left uphill, to see on your left, in a pot, Banksia baxteri, or Bird’s Nest Banksia, with tall spires of stiff, triangular, pink-tipped foliage and yellow flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to southwestern WA between Albany and Esperance. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Today we will wa

plants.name: Banksia aemula
plants.context: 15. Turn back to the road to see, on your left Banksia aemula or Wallum Banksia, a small, gnarled tree with knobby bark and large squat green flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to Queensland and NSW, from Bundaberg to Sydney, in coastal, heath, and sandy soil areas.

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, along the road above the Rock Garden, then downhill into the Grevillea section

plants.name: Corymbia 'Summer Red'
plants.context: 1. On your right is Corymbia ‘Summer Red’, a grafted eucalypt with dark green leathery foliage, attractive new red foliage and beautiful bud formations (photo above).

plants.name: Crowea 'Little Rockstar'
plants.context: 2. Also on your right is Crowea ‘Little Rockstar’, a compact form of Crowea from a seedling variant growing at the ANBG (photo next page top left). This plant is covered in pink star flowers.

plants.name: Crinum pedunculatum
plants.context: 3. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, on your left and right, Crinum pedunculatum with long green strappy leaves and striking terminal clusters of white perfumed flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to the tidal flats of coastal Queensland and NSW.

plants.name: Eucryphia moorei
plants.context: 4. Further on your right is Eucryphia moorei or Plumwood, a slow-growing tree with dark green, pinnate leaves and fragrant, white, four-petalled flowers, native to southeastern NSW and northeastern Victoria (photo above).

plants.name: Leptospermum petersonii
plants.context: 5. Also on your right is Leptospermum petersonii or Lemon-scented Tea-tree with narrow green foliage with a strong lemon scent and white flowers with green centres, native to the coastal areas of northern NSW and southern Queensland (photo above).

plants.name: Wollemia nobilis
plants.context: 6. Turn right along the road above the Rock Garden to see, on your right, Wollemia nobilis, or Wollemi Pine, which is related to Kauri, Hoop, Norfolk Island and Bunya Pines. Previously thought extinct, this species was discovered in 1994 growing in the Wollemi National Park northwest of Sydney, and can grow up to 40m high with bubbly brown bark (photo below left). Each plant has both male, (brown tassels) and female, (green circular) reproductive cones. Fewer than 100 Wollemi Pines remain in nat

plants.name: Grevillea 'Mason's Hybrid'
plants.context: 7. Also on your right is Grevillea ‘Mason’s Hybrid’, a spreading bush with large spider blooms of pink, red and orange (photo above right). This hybrid arose from seed collected from an upright glaucous form of Grevillea bipinnatifida while the other parent is presumed to be G. banksii.

plants.name: Calothamnus tuberosus
plants.context: 8. Again on your right is Calothamnus tuberosus, a stiff upright bush endemic to southwestern WA, with spiky grey-green linear foliage and a few bright red fluffy flowers remaining (photo above).

plants.name: Hakea constablei
plants.context: 9. Further on your right is Hakea constablei, a small tree with very large, brown, warty nuts which remain unopened on the tree (photo below left). This plant is endemic to the Blue Mountains near Sydney and was named after Ernest Constable, a plant collector for the Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney.

plants.name: Hakea megadenia
plants.context: 10. Also on your right is Hakea megadenia, or Autumn Hakea, a bushy shrub to 5m tall with dull green prickly leaves and creamy axillary flowers (photo above right). This plant is endemic to Tasmania where it grows along the east coast and the Furnaux Islands.

plants.name: Grevillea triloba
plants.context: 11. Further on your right is Grevillea triloba, a spreading shrub with grey green foliage and white starburst flowers (photo above). This grevillea is native to the Geraldton area in Western Australia.

plants.name: Grevillea aspleniifolia
plants.context: 12. Turn right downhill, then right along the road to see Grevillea aspleniifolia, a large sprawling shrub with long, linear, toothed green foliage and red toothbrush flowers, endemic to southern NSW (photo below left). 13.On your left is Lambertia formosa, or Mountain Devil, with red flowers with long stamens and sepals (photo above right). The common name comes from the horned woody seed follicles, which were used to make small devil-figures. This plant is endemic to the coast and ranges of NS

plants.name: Lambertia formosa
plants.context: 12. Turn right downhill, then right along the road to see Grevillea aspleniifolia, a large sprawling shrub with long, linear, toothed green foliage and red toothbrush flowers, endemic to southern NSW (photo below left). 13.On your left is Lambertia formosa, or Mountain Devil, with red flowers with long stamens and sepals (photo above right). The common name comes from the horned woody seed follicles, which were used to make small devil-figures. This plant is endemic to the coast and ranges of NS

plants.name: Grevillea 'Lady O'
plants.context: 14. On your right is Grevillea ‘Lady O’, a long blooming shrub with red flowers and bright green foliage (photo below left). ‘Lady O’ is a cross between a Grevillea victoriae hybrid x Grevillea rhyolitica made by local plant breeder Peter Ollerenshaw and named for his mother. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott T

plants.name: Grevillea rhyolitica subsp. rhyolitica
plants.context: 15. On your left is Grevillea rhyolitica subsp. rhyolitica, or Deua Grevillea, a spreading shrub with coral red spider flowers, endemic to the south coast of NSW near Moruya (photo above right).

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will take a short walk from the Visitor Centre up the hill behind the café, towards the waterfall

plants.name: Pandorea jasminoides
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre look up to your left to see Pandorea jasminoides covered in scented, pink, trumpet flowers with attractive mid-green foliage (photo above). This woody vine, also known as Bower of Beauty, is native to NSW and Queensland, and displays large, pointed pods filled with papery seeds.

plants.name: Pilidiostigma rhytispermum
plants.context: 2. .On your right, in a pot, is Pilidiostigma rhytispermum, or Small-leaved Plum Myrtle, a woody shrub with small leaves and cream cup flowers with prominent yellow stamens (photo next page top left). This plant has black fruits which are attractive to many fruit eating birds and is native to the coast of southeastern Queensland.

plants.name: Crowea saligna
plants.context: 3. Also on your right, in a pot, is Crowea saligna, a small shrub with large, pink flowers and aromatic foliage (photo above right). Native bees and butterflies are attracted to this plant which is native to the central coastal area of NSW.

plants.name: Eremophila cuneifolia × E. fraseri
plants.context: 4. Across to your right, in a pot, is Eremophila cuneifolia x E. fraseri, the most spectacular of all the E. cuneifolia hybrids, forming a shrub 2m high and wide with large green leaves, purple flowers with spotted throats, and very large pink sepals (photo above).

plants.name: Kunzea baxteri 'Scarlet Jack'
plants.context: 5. Further down to your right is Kunzea baxteri ‘Scarlet Jack’, a compact bush with light green-grey foliage and profuse red bottlebrush flowers with gold tips (photo above).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Peaches and Cream'
plants.context: 6. Down to your right again is Grevillea ‘Peaches and Cream’ with deeply divided green leaves and large flower heads of pink and cream (photo below). This hybrid was developed in Queensland by Jan Glazebrook and Dennis Cox and patented in 2006.

plants.name: Epacris longiflora 'Nectar Pink'
plants.context: 7. On your left is Epacris longiflora ‘Nectar Pink’, a very floriferous small shrub covered in slender pink bells with white tips (photo below).

plants.name: Corymbia 'Summer Red'
plants.context: 8. On your right is Corymbia ‘Summer Red’, a grafted eucalypt with dark-green, leathery foliage, attractive new red foliage, red fluffy flowers with yellow centres just opening and beautiful bud formations (photo below).

plants.name: Viola sp
plants.context: 9. Also on your right is Viola sp., a close groundcover with fresh green foliage and bright blue flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Legacy Flame'
plants.context: 10. Bear left up the hill behind the café then right along the road above the depot to see, on your left, Grevillea ‘Legacy Flame’, a small grevillea, bred locally by Bywong Nursery, which commemorates 100 years of Legacy Australia with flame-like orange-red flowers which resemble the Legacy torch (photo below).

plants.name: Westringia fruticosa 'Wunderbar'
plants.context: 11. On the corner, to your left as you turn up the hill, is Westringia fruticosa ‘Wunderbar’ or ‘Double Wonder’, a small dense shrub with grey-green foliage and pale mauve or pink semi-double flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Crowea 'Little Rockstar'
plants.context: 12. Still on your left is Crowea ‘Little Rockstar’, a compact form of Crowea, reaching only 60-80cm high, from a seedling variant growing at the ANBG (photo below left). This plant has many pink star flowers.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Bloodline'
plants.context: 13. On your left again is Grevillea ‘Bloodline’, bred at Bywong Nursery by Peter Ollerenshaw, similar to the long-flowering variety Grevillea ‘Lady O’, but with a slightly arching habit (photo above right)

plants.name: Grevillea 'Bush Lemons'
plants.context: 14. To the back on your left in a pot is Grevillea ‘Bush Lemons’ with lemon toothbrush flowers on grey-green divided foliage (photo above). A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Today we will take a short walk from the Visitor Centre up the hill behind the café, towards the waterfall

plants.name: Phebalium woombye
plants.context: 15. Further on your left is Phebalium woombye, a bushy shrub with slender leaves, silver on the reverse, and clusters of starry, pink flowers, native to southeastern Queensland and northeastern NSW coastal regions (photo above).

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will take a short walk from the Visitor Centre, over the bridge, past the café into the Banksia Garden

plants.name: Corymbia 'Summer Red'
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre, on your right is Corymbia ‘Summer Red’, a grafted eucalypt with dark-green, leathery foliage, attractive new red foliage, red fluffy flowers and beautiful bud formations (photo above).

plants.name: Anigozanthos 'Bush Pearl'
plants.context: 2. .Also on your right is Anigozanthos ‘Bush Pearl’, a hybrid Kangaroo Paw with long- blooming bright-pink flowers developed by Angus Stewart (photo next page top left).

plants.name: Corymbia 'Summer Beauty'
plants.context: 3. Cross the bridge, and bear right, to see on your right Corymbia ‘Summer Beauty’, a small, bushy tree with dark-green, glossy foliage, attractive bud formations and spectacular pink fluffy flowers (photo above right).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Metal Red'
plants.context: 4. On your left is Grevillea ‘Metal Red’, a hardy shrub with metallic-red flowers held above soft, divided green foliage. a hybrid between G. banksii 'prostrate' x G. 'Bronze Rambler' (photo above).

plants.name: Banksia menziesii
plants.context: 5. Continue into the Banksia Garden to see, on your right, Banksia menziesii, Firewood Banksia or Menzies Banksia, a small tree or shrub with oblong, toothed, green leaves and deep pink to red flowers (photo above). This plant is native to the west coast of WA, around Perth.

plants.name: Banksia epica
plants.context: 6. On your left is Banksia epica, a bushy shrub without a lignotuber, with large yellow flowers and iridescent lime-green buds (photo below left). This species is native to the Great Australian Bight, WA.

plants.name: Banksia grandis
plants.context: 7. Also on your left is Banksia grandis, or Bull Banksia, which varies from spreading shrub to a tree with rough grey bark, dark green, toothed leaves and large, dense, yellow cylindrical flowers (photo above right). The new growth can be bright red. This plant is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Banksia speciosa
plants.context: 8. Again on your left is Banksia speciosa, or Showy Banksia, with green, triangular leaves and pale-yellow flowers (photo above). This tall shrub is native to the area around Esperance, WA.

plants.name: Banksia brownii
plants.context: 9. On your right is Banksia brownii or Feather-leaved Banksia, named after Robert Brown, (1773-1858), Scottish born botanist who accompanied Flinders to Australia in 1801 (photo below left). This shrub with soft, linear, whorled leaves and gold flowers is native to the south coast of WA from Albany to the Stirling Ranges.

plants.name: Banksia spinulosa 'Birthday Candles'
plants.context: 10. Low on your right is Banksia spinulosa ‘Birthday Candles’ a dense, bright-green bush with attractive needle foliage and short, yellow cones with reddish styles (photo above right). ‘Birthday Candles’ is a dwarf cultivar of Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa developed by Bill Molyneux of Austraflora Nurseries in Montrose, Victoria.

plants.name: Banksia baxteri
plants.context: 11. Bear left to see, on your left, Banksia baxteri or Bird’s Nest Banksia, with tall spires of stiff, triangular, pink-tipped foliage and yellow flowers (photo above). This plant is native to southwestern WA between Albany and Esperance.

plants.name: Banksia integrifolia subsp. integrifolia
plants.context: 12. On your right is Banksia integrifolia subsp. integrifolia or Coast Banksia, a vigorous mound of foliage and flowers, with dark green leaves with silver backs and plenty of short greenish-yellow cones (photo below left). This plant is native to the coast of eastern mainland Australia.

plants.name: Banksia tricuspis
plants.context: 13. On your left is Banksia tricuspis or Pine Banksia, a stunted tree or shrub, with a wrinkled trunk, pine-like needle foliage and large gold flowers, native to the central west coast of WA (photo above right).

plants.name: Banksia occidentalis
plants.context: 14. On your right is Banksia occidentalis, or Red Swamp Banksia, a tall shrub or small tree with whorled, linear, green leaves and lime-green buds developing into golden flowers with prominent red styles (photo below left). This plant is native to the south coast of WA. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. Written and illustrated by ANBG Friends Rosalind and Benjamin Walcott Today w

plants.name: Banksia plagiocarpa
plants.context: 15. On your left is Banksia plagiocarpa, or Blue Banksia, a tall shrub with long, narrow leaves and grey to mauve flowers, aging to dull yellow (photo above right). The attractive new growth seen here is velvety rusty brown. This plant is native to Hinchinbrook Island and the adjacent mainland in Queensland.

plants.name: Crowea saligna
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre, on your right, in a pot, is Crowea saligna, a small shrub with large pink flowers and aromatic foliage (photo above). Native bees and butterflies are attracted to this plant which is native to the central coast of NSW.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Peaches and Cream'
plants.context: 2. Down the steps, on your right is Grevillea ‘Peaches and Cream’ with deeply divided green leaves and large flower heads of pink and cream (photo next page top left). This hybrid was developed in Queensland by Jan Glazebrook and Dennis Cox and patented in 2006.

plants.name: Epacris longiflora 'Nectar Pink'
plants.context: 3. On your left is Epacris longiflora ‘Nectar Pink’, a very floriferous small shrub covered in slender pink bells with white tips (photo above right).

plants.name: Corymbia 'Summer Red'
plants.context: 4. On your right is Corymbia ‘Summer Red’, a grafted eucalypt with dark green leathery foliage, attractive new red foliage, red fluffy flowers with yellow centres and beautiful bud formations (photo above).

plants.name: Banksia ericifolia 'Bird Song'
plants.context: 5. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, on your right, Banksia ericifolia ‘Bird Song’, a small hybrid banksia with fine, bright green foliage and large orange flowers (photo above).

plants.name: Syzygium paniculatum 'Backyard Bliss'
plants.context: 6. Further on your right is Syzygium paniculatum ‘Backyard Bliss’, a fast growing, dense, evergreen shrub with dark green, glossy leaves and red new growth that shades to bronze (photo below). The flowers are cream and borne terminally and the berries are pink to red.

plants.name: Acronychia littoralis
plants.context: 7. On your left is Acronychia littoralis, an endangered small tree with shiny leaves and strongly scented greenish-cream flowers mobbed by butterflies (photo below). The Scented Acronychia or Beach Acronychia is native to northeastern coastal NSW and a few areas in adjacent Queensland.

plants.name: Stenocarpus sinuatus
plants.context: 8. Look up to your left to see Stenocarpus sinuatus, or Fire Wheel Tree, a tall tree with leathery, lobed leaves and bright red ‘wheel’ flowers (photo below). This plant is native to the coastal rainforest regions of NSW and Queensland, north of Nambucca River.

plants.name: Davidsonia jerseyana
plants.context: 9. Also on your left is Davidsonia jerseyana, or Davidson’s Plum, a rainforest tree native to the northern NSW coast and listed as endangered (photo below left). This tree has pinkish flowers along the trunk followed by edible, sour, dark-burgundy fruit. This tree has hairy, compound leaves with red new growth and the fruit can be made into jams and tarts.

plants.name: Hibiscus divaricatus
plants.context: 10. Still on your left is Hibiscus divaricatus with pure yellow flowers contrasting with maroon centres and stamens on a straggly bush (photo above right). This hibiscus is native to Queensland, the NT and northern parts of WA.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Mason's Hybrid'
plants.context: 11. Turn right along the road above the Rock Garden to see, on your right, Grevillea ‘Mason’s Hybrid’, a spreading bush with large spider blooms of pink, red and orange (photo above). This hybrid arose from seed of an upright glaucous form of Grevillea bipinnatifida with the other parent presumed to be G. banksii.

plants.name: Hakea lissocarpha
plants.context: 12. On your right is Hakea lissocarpha, or Honeybush, a small shrub with intricate foliage covered in buds which will develop into sweet-scented white or pale pink flowers, native to southwestern WA (photo below left).

plants.name: Grevillea corrugata
plants.context: 14. Turn right downhill to see, on your right, Grevillea corrugata, a shrub with deeply lobed leaves endemic to southwestern WA (photo below left). This bush has prominent white buds which will soon open to white flowers. A publication of the Friends of the Australian National Botanic Gardens Featuring the plants of the Australian National Botanic Gardens, Canberra, ACT. plants.name: Banksia neoanglica
plants.context: 15. Turn right at the next road to see, on your right, Banksia neoanglica, or New England Banksia, with silver-backed, dark green foliage and gold flowers held upright (photo above right). This shrub is native to eastern tablelands of Queensland and NSW.

author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, right behind the depot, then up the hill along the Main Path

plants.name: Eustrephus latifolius
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre look up to your left to see Eustrephus latifolius, or Wombat Berry, a vigorous vine, with lance-shaped leaves and orange berries containing many shiny, black seeds, which persist on the plant for many months (photo above). This plant is native to the entire east coast of Australia, excepting Tasmania.

plants.name: Buckinghamia celsissima
plants.context: 3. On your left look up to see Buckinghamia celsissima, or Ivory Curl, a small tree with fragrant, dense, terminal clusters of cylindrical ivory flower spikes, native to the ‘wet tropics’ rainforest areas of northeastern Queensland (photo above right).

plants.name: Epacris longiflora 'Nectar Pink'
plants.context: 4. Further on your left is Epacris longiflora ‘Nectar Pink’, a very floriferous small shrub covered in slender pink bells with white tips (photo above).

plants.name: Banksia spinulosa 'Birthday Candles'
plants.context: 5. Look down to your right to see Banksia spinulosa ‘Birthday Candles’, a dense, bright green bush with attractive needle foliage and short, yellow flowers with rusty red styles (photo above). ‘Birthday Candles’ is a dwarf cultivar of Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa developed by Bill Molyneux of Austraflora Nurseries in Montrose, Victoria.

plants.name: Callistemon subulatus 'Brogo Overflow'
plants.context: 6. Bear left uphill behind the café, then right behind the depot, to see on your left Callistemon subulatus ‘Brogo Overflow’ with bright red flowers and a low spreading habit (photo below).

plants.name: Scaevola 'Pink Fusion'
plants.context: 7. On your right is Scaevola ‘Pink Fusion’, a low-growing, wide-spreading, cushion-like plant with many pink, fan flowers over a long period (photo below).

plants.name: Brachyscome sp
plants.context: 8. Also on your right is Brachyscome sp., a close groundcover of ferny, green leaves with mauve flowers with gold centres (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Legacy Flame'
plants.context: 9. As you turn left uphill on your left is Grevillea ‘Legacy Flame’, a small grevillea, bred locally by Bywong Nursery, which commemorates 100 years of Legacy Australia with flame-like orange-red flowers which resemble the Legacy torch (photo below).

plants.name: Correa 'Snowbelle'
plants.context: 10. Also on your left is Correa 'Snowbelle', a small spreading shrub with grey-green foliage and white bell-shaped flowers with upturned petals bred by Peter Ollerenshaw at Bywong Nursery, near Canberra (photo below).

plants.name: Correa alba
plants.context: 11. Again on your left is Correa alba, or White Correa, with grey-green leaves with silver backs and white star flowers (photo below). This correa is a popular and reliable plant in the garden, native to eastern coastal regions of Australia, first formally described by Henry Cranke Andrews in 1798.

plants.name: Eucalyptus macrocarpa
plants.context: 12. Bear right in front of the waterfall to see, on your left, Eucalyptus macrocarpa, or Mottlecah, with magnificent, silver- grey, sword-like foliage (photo below). This sprawling mallee is native to southwestern WA and has the largest eucalypt flower.

plants.name: Brachyscome multifida 'Amethyst'
plants.context: 13. On your right is Brachyscome multifida ‘Amethyst’, a small daisy with fine green foliage and purple flowers with gold centres (photo above right). Many of the Brachyscome cultivars make excellent garden plants.

plants.name: Grevillea leptobotrys 'Lilac Tangles'
plants.context: 14. On your left, in a pot, is Grevillea leptobotrys ‘Lilac Tangles’ with small racemes of lilac-pink flowers buried in prickly, dark-green growth (photo above). Grevillea leptobotrys is known as the Tangled Grevillea and is native to southwestern WA. plants.name: Hakea drupacea
plants.context: 15. On your right is Hakea drupacea, commonly known as Sweet Hakea, an open tree or shrub with sharp-pointed, green leaves and white pincushion flowers, native to southwestern WA (photo above).

plants.name: Acronychia littoralis
plants.context: 3. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, on your left, Acronychia littoralis, an endangered small tree with shiny leaves and strongly scented greenish-cream flowers much visited by butterflies (photo above right). The Scented Acronychia or Beach Acronychia is native to northeastern coastal NSW and a few areas in adjacent Queensland.

plants.name: Stenocarpus sinuatus
plants.context: 4. Look up to your left to see Stenocarpus sinuatus, or Fire Wheel Tree, a tall tree with leathery lobed leaves and bright red ‘wheel’ flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to the coastal rainforest regions of NSW and Queensland north of Nambucca River.

plants.name: Elaeodendron australe var. integrifolium
plants.context: 5. On your right is Elaeodendron australe var. integrifolium, or Narrow-leaved Red Olive Plum, native to central-eastern Queensland and as far south as Narrabri, NSW. with weeping foliage, and green berries which ripen to red-orange (photo above right). This plant grows in dry rain forest and is distinguished from the other variety in this species, E. australe var. australe, by the narrower leaves.

plants.name: Banksia aquilonia
plants.context: 6. As you turn right along the road above the Rock Garden, on your left is Banksia aquilonia, a large shrub or small tree, with lance-shaped leaves with a silvery underside arranged spirally on the branches (photo below). The flowers are pale yellow in colour. The seeds are enclosed in follicles attached to a woody cone and they are released from the cones annually. This banksia is native to northern coastal Queensland.

plants.name: Hakea nodosa
plants.context: 7. On your right is Hakea nodosa, or Yellow Hakea, a shrub with yellow flowers and green needle-shaped leaves, native to southeastern SA, Victoria and northeastern Tasmania in swampy areas and heath (photo below).

plants.name: Hakea archaeoides
plants.context: 8. Again on your right is Hakea archaeoides, a shrub with oblong leaves and clusters of grey woody nuts (photo below). This plant is native to the north coast of NSW and is listed as vulnerable in the wild.

plants.name: Hakea drupacea
plants.context: 9. Still on your right is Hakea drupacea, commonly known as Sweet Hakea, an open tree or shrub with sharp-pointed, green leaves and white pincushion flowers, native to southwestern WA (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea triloba
plants.context: 10. Further on your right is Grevillea triloba, a spreading shrub with grey green foliage and white starburst flowers (photo below). This grevillea is native to the Geraldton area of WA.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Sid Reynolds'
plants.context: 11. Turn right down hill then along the road to see, on your left, Grevillea ‘Sid Reynolds’ which arose as a seedling in the garden of Sid Reynolds and is thought to be a hybrid between G. pinaster and G. commutate (photo below). This shrub has fine green foliage and red and yellow spider flowers.

plants.name: Banksia neoanglica
plants.context: 12. On your right is Banksia neoanglica, or New England Banksia, with silver-backed, dark-green foliage and gold flowers held upright (photo below left). This shrub is native to the eastern tablelands of Queensland and NSW.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Coconut Ice'
plants.context: 13. On your left is Grevillea ‘Coconut Ice’ with large pink/orange spider flowers with long red styles (photo above right). This hybrid plant was grown from seed collected from G. bipinnatifida and the male parent was G. banksii (white flowered form). The seedling was raised by Mr. M. Hodge of Queensland.

plants.name: Banksia paludosa
plants.context: 14. On your left is Banksia paludosa, or Marsh Banksia, with young ginger-coloured cones which develop into gold flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to central and southeastern NSW with an outlying population on the north coast near Kempsey.

plants.name: Banksia conferta
plants.context: 15. On your right is Banksia conferta, an attractive, tall bush with elliptical leaves and yellow-green flowers, native to the Lamington Plateau and Glasshouse Mountains in Queensland and adjacent northeastern NSW (photo above right).

Cross the bridge, go past the café to see, on your left, Banksia spinulosa ‘Stumpy Gold’ with fine, toothed, linear foliage and masses of short gold flowers with rusty red styles (photo above right). This plant is a dwarf cultivar of Banksia spinulosa var. collina that was selected by Richard Anderson of Merricks Nursery in Victoria from material collected on the NSW Central Coast.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Loopy Lou'

plants.name: Banksia epica

plants.name: Banksia solandri
plants.context: 8. On your right is Banksia solandri, or Stirling Range Banksia, a large shrub with tough, dark green deeply lobed leaves and when in flower, brown sweetly scented flowers (photo above). This plant is native to the Stirling Range of southwestern WA.

plants.name: Banksia hookeriana
plants.context: 9. Also on your right is Banksia hookeriana or Hooker’s Banksia with upright, slender, green toothed foliage and developing bright orange flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to the area between Perth and Geraldton in WA.

plants.name: Banksia brownii

This shrub with soft, linear, whorled leaves and gold flowers is native to the south coast of WA from Albany to the Stirling Ranges.

plants.name: Banksia neoanglica
plants.context: 11. Still on your right is Banksia neoanglica, or New England Banksia, with silver-backed, dark green foliage and gold brushes with burgundy styles held upright (photo above). This shrub is native to the eastern tablelands of Queensland and NSW.

plants.name: Banksia ericifolia 'Bird Song'
plants.context: 12. On your left is Banksia ericifolia ‘Bird Song’, a small hybrid banksia with fine, bright green foliage and large orange flowers (photo below left).

plants.name: Banksia oblongifolia
plants.context: 13. On your right is Banksia oblongifolia, a shrub with oblong leaves and yellow flowers (photo above right). This plant grows along the eastern coast of Queensland and NSW between Bundaberg and Ulladulla.

plants.name: Banksia pencillata
plants.context: 14. Also on your right is Banksia pencillata or Newnes Plateau Banksia. a small tree covered in whorled, olive- green foliage and greenish- yellow flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to a restricted area of the Blue Mountains, NSW.

plants.name: Acacia binervia 'Sterling Silver'
plants.context: 1. As you approach the Visitor Centre on your left is Acacia binervia ‘Sterling Silver’, a hardy mounding plant, tolerant of windy sites and almost any well-drained soil, with beautiful silver-grey foliage (photo above). 27 May – 9 June 2026 Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, along the road above the Rock Garden, returning via the Main Path

plants.name: Correa 'Catie Bec'
plants.context: 2. After the Visitor Centre, on your left, is Correa ‘Catie Bec’ a small shrub with pink flowers over a long period which will grow in a wide range of soil types and is frost hardy and drought tolerant (photo next page top left).

plants.name: Templetonia retusa
plants.context: 3. On your right in a pot is Templetonia retusa or Cockies Tongues with rounded greyish-green leaves and red pea flowers (photo above right). These plants, named after John Templeton, an 18th century botanist, are native to the coastal borders of SA and WA and also Flinders Ranges, SA.

plants.name: Acacia beckleri
plants.context: 4. Also on your right is Acacia beckleri, or Barrier Range Wattle, with hard, elliptical grey-green foliage and yellow ball flowers on stalks (photo above). This plant is native to the Barrier Range of NSW, near Cobar and Jerilderie.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Peaches and Cream'
plants.context: 5. Again on your right is Grevillea ‘Peaches and Cream’ with deeply-divided green leaves and large flower heads of pink and cream (photo above). This hybrid was developed in Queensland by Jan Glazebrook and Dennis Cox and patented in 2006.

plants.name: Crinum pedunculatum
plants.context: 6. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, on your left, Crinum pedunculatum with long green strappy leaves and clusters of large green seed pods (photo below). This plant is native to the tidal flats of coastal Queensland and NSW.

plants.name: Syzygium (Acmena) smithii
plants.context: 7. Further up the hill, on your right is Syzygium (Acmena) smithii, or Lilly Pilly, a small tree with a dense crown of shiny green leaves covered in clusters of pinkish berries (photo above). Syzygium smithii is the best-known member of the lilly pillies and is widespread in east coast rainforests from north Queensland to Victoria, also found on King Island.

plants.name: Acronychia littoralis
plants.context: 8. On your left is Acronychia littoralis, an endangered small tree with shiny leaves and strongly scented greenish-cream flowers much visited by butterflies (photo above). The Scented Acronychia or Beach Acronychia is native to northeastern coastal NSW and a few areas in adjacent Queensland.

plants.name: Stenocarpus sinuatus
plants.context: 9. Look up to your left to see Stenocarpus sinuatus, or Fire Wheel Tree, a tall tree with leathery, lobed leaves and bright red ‘wheel’ flowers (photo below). This plant is native to the coastal rainforest regions of NSW and Queensland north of Nambucca River.

plants.name: Epacris calvertiana var. calvertiana
plants.context: 10. On your right as you turn right along the road above the Rock Garden is Epacris calvertiana var. calvertiana, with cream bells on dark green foliage, native to coastal NSW near Pigeon House Mountain (photo below).

plants.name: Hakea nodosa
plants.context: 11. On your right is Hakea nodosa, or Yellow Hakea, a shrub with yellow flowers and green needle-like leaves, native to south eastern South Australia, Victoria and northeastern Tasmania in swampy areas and heath (photo below).

plants.name: Hakea drupacea
plants.context: 12. Also on your right is Hakea drupacea commonly known as Sweet Hakea, an open tree or shrub with green, sharp-pointed leaves and white pincushion flowers (photo below left) This plant is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Hakea varia
plants.context: 13. Again on your right is Hakea varia with hard, prickly, drooping variable foliage and small white starburst flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Grevillea manglesii subsp. ornithopoda
plants.context: 14. Turn right downhill to see, on your right, Grevillea manglesii subsp. ornithopoda, or Birdsfoot Grevillea, a large bush with frothy, white terminal clusters of flowers and tripartite ‘birdsfoot’ foliage (photo above). This plant is native to WA near Perth.

plants.name: Banksia tenuis var. reptans
plants.context: 15. Turn right down the Main Path to see, on your left, Banksia tenuis var. reptans, a lax bush with tough lobed leaves and yellow brown flowers, native to the south coast of WA (photo above).

intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the depot, then uphill again towards the Rock Garden 13.

plants.name: Lepidozamia peroffskyana
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre on your left is Lepidozamia peroffskyana, or Pineapple Zamia, one of the tallest cycads, with long arching stems of shiny, dark green foliage(photo above). This palm-like cycad is native to the wet open forests of southeastern Queensland and northeastern NSW. These plants do not produce flowers but have large cones on separate female and male plants. 10 – 23 June 2026 Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the depot, then uphill again to

plants.name: Phebalium woombye
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre on your left is Lepidozamia peroffskyana, or Pineapple Zamia, one of the tallest cycads, with long arching stems of shiny, dark green foliage(photo above). This palm-like cycad is native to the wet open forests of southeastern Queensland and northeastern NSW. plants.name: Isopogon cuneatus
plants.context: 2. On your right is Isopogon cuneatus, an upright shrub with floppy branches of flat, bright green leaves, often tinged with red, and large pink heads of drumstick flowers (photo next page top left). This plant is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Lechenaultia formosa
plants.context: 3. Also on your right, in a pot, is Lechenaultia formosa, a small, attractive plant with close grey-green foliage and bright gold flowers (photo above right). The genus Lechenaultia is named after the naturalist Leschenault de la Tour, 1773- 1826. This plant is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Anigozanthos 'Bush Pearl'
plants.context: 4. Further on your right is Anigozanthos ‘Bush Pearl’, a hybrid Kangaroo Paw with long-blooming, bright pink flowers developed by Angus Stewart (photo above).

plants.name: Hakea laurina × petiolaris 'Pin Ball'
plants.context: 5. Also on your right is Hakea laurina x petiolaris ‘Pin Ball’, a tall shrub or small tree with leathery, green leaves and ball-like red flowers with creamy white styles (photo above). The flowers attract nectar feeding birds.

plants.name: Templetonia retusa
plants.context: 6. Still on your right, in a pot, is Templetonia retusa or Cockies Tongues with rounded, greyish-green leaves and red pea flowers (photo below). These plants, named after John Templeton, an 18th century botanist, are native to the coastal borders of SA and WA, also Flinders Ranges, SA.

plants.name: Acacia beckleri
plants.context: 7. On your right is Acacia beckleri, or Barrier Range Wattle, with hard, elliptical grey-green foliage and yellow ball flowers on stalks (photo above). This plant is native to the Barrier Range of NSW, near Cobar and Jerilderie.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Peaches and Cream'
plants.context: 8. Also on your right is Grevillea ‘Peaches and Cream’ with deeply-divided green leaves and large flower heads of pink and cream (photo above). This hybrid was developed in Queensland by Jan Glazebrook and Dennis Cox and patented in 2006.

plants.name: Banksia ericifolia 'Bird Song'
plants.context: 9. Bear left uphill past the café, then right behind the depot to see, on your left, Banksia ericifolia ‘Bird Song’, a small hybrid banksia with fine, bright green foliage and large orange flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Scaevola 'Pink Fusion'
plants.context: 10. On your right is Scaevola ‘Pink Fusion’, a low-growing, wide-spreading, cushion-like plant with many pink, fan flowers over a long period (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Legacy Flame'
plants.context: 11. As you turn left uphill notice on your left Grevillea ‘Legacy Flame’, a small grevillea, bred locally by Bywong Nursery, which commemorates 100 years of Legacy Australia with flame-like orange-red flowers which resemble the Legacy torch.

plants.name: Correa 'Lemon Twist'
plants.context: 12. On your left is Correa ‘Lemon Twist’, a hybrid between C. reflexa var. nummularia and C. alba which occurred in the gardens of Native Plant Wholesalers in Mount Gambier (photo below left). ‘Lemon Twist’ is a small, spreading shrub with attractive shiny foliage and well displayed lemon flowers.

plants.name: Banksia neoanglica
plants.context: 14. Behind on your left is Banksia neoanglica, or New England Banksia, with silver-backed, dark green foliage and gold flowers with black styles held upright. This shrub is native to the eastern tablelands of Queensland and NSW (photo below left).

plants.name: Correa 'Snowbelle'
plants.context: 15. On your left is Correa 'Snowbelle', a small, spreading shrub with grey-green foliage and white bell-shaped flowers with upturned petals bred by Peter Ollerenshaw at Bywong Nursery, near Canberra (photo above right).

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk straight up the hill behind the café and return to the Visitor Centre along the road near the Rainforest Gully

plants.name: Isopogon cuneatus
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre, on your right, down the steps, is Isopogon cuneatus, an upright shrub with floppy branches of flat, bright-green leaves, often tinged with red, and large pink heads of drumstick flowers (photo above). This plant is native to southwestern WA. 24 Jun – 7 Jul 2026 Today we will walk straight up the hill behind the café and return to the Visitor Centre along the road near the Rainforest Gully

plants.name: Guichenotia ledifolia
plants.context: 2. Also on your right is Guichenotia ledifolia, a small shrub with grey-green foliage covered in drooping, dusty pink, 5-petalled flowers with maroon centres (photo next page top left). This plant is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Pimelea physodes
plants.context: 3. Further on your right, in a pot, is Pimelea physodes, or Qualup Bell, with grey-green foliage close to reddish stems with pendant, green bracts enclosing the small flowers and dark-red outer bracts (photo above right) This plant is native to southwestern WA and is considered the most outstanding of the genus.

plants.name: Actinotus helianthi
plants.context: 4. Also on your right, in a pot, is Actinotus helianthi or Flannel Flower, with white, star flowers with yellow-grey centres and silver-grey divided foliage (photo below left). These plants are native to the coast and mountains of NSW and southern Queensland.

plants.name: Banksia aquilonia
plants.context: 5. Bear left uphill to see on your left Banksia aquilonia, a large shrub or small tree, with lance-shaped leaves with a silvery underside arranged spirally on the branches (photo above right). The flowers are pale yellow in colour. The seeds are enclosed in follicles attached to a woody cone and they are released from the cones annually. This banksia is native to northern coastal Queensland.

plants.name: Banksia neoanglica
plants.context: 6. On your right is Banksia neoanglica, or New England Banksia, showing silver- backed, dark green foliage with gold flowers with black styles held upright (photo below). This shrub is native to the eastern tablelands of Queensland and NSW.

plants.name: Banksia oblongifolia
plants.context: 7. Also on your right is Banksia oblongifolia, a small shrub with oblong leaves and yellow flowers (photo below). This plant grows along the eastern coast of Queensland and NSW between Bundaberg and Ulladulla.

plants.name: Acacia boormanii 'Gold Tips'
plants.context: 8. Further on your right is Acacia boormanii ‘Gold Tips’ a fast-growing, evergreen shrub with profuse gold ball flowers in bud and gold-tinted new foliage (photo below).

plants.name: Callitris baileyi
plants.context: 9. Also on your right is Callitris baileyi, a conifer native to southeast Queensland, a slender tree with rough, greyish bark and a green crown (photo below). Both male and female cones form on the same tree. The common name is Bailey's Cypress-pine after Australian botanist Frederick Manson Bailey, who was the first to collect specimens of this tree.

plants.name: Xanthorrhoea glauca subsp. glauca
plants.context: 10. Bear left and turn downhill to see, on your left, several Xanthorrhoea glauca subsp. glauca, large grass trees with rippling grey- green linear foliage native to coastal NSW and Queensland (photo below).

plants.name: Gymnostoma australianum
plants.context: 11. Also on your left is Gymnostoma australianum, or Daintree Pine, a small, conical pine tree with bright-green, ferny foliage, tiny red flowers and prickly brown fruit (photo below). This plant is native to the tropical rainforest of northern Queensland and dates back 300 million years to the Gondwanan period.

plants.name: Livistona fulva
plants.context: 12. On your right is a group of Livistona fulva, tall, solitary palms restricted in distribution to the Blackdown Tablelands in central Queensland (photo below left).

plants.name: Psychotria daphnoides
plants.context: 13. Also on your right is Psychotria daphnoides, commonly known as Smooth Psychotria or Turkey Bush, a small tree with narrow, glossy green leaves, fragrant white flowers, and edible, white berries that attract birds, native to coastal northern NSW, Queensland and NT (photo above right).

plants.name: Tabernaemontana pandacaqui
plants.context: 14. On your left is Tabernaemontana pandacaqui, Windmill bush or Banana bush, a tall shrub or tree with white or pale-yellow flowers and orange fruit with paired follicles, each up to 7 cm (3 in) in diameter, native to China, Taiwan, Thailand,Melesia, Papua New Guinea, Australia and many Pacific islands (photo below left).

plants.name: Streblus pendulinus
plants.context: 15. Also on your left is Streblus pendulinus a tree, usually dioecious, without spines, exuding a white latex when damaged with a common name of Isaac Wood or Siah's or Sia's Backbone (photo above right). This tree is native to Norfolk Island, also to New Guinea, Micronesia, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Rapa and Hawai'i.

plants.name: Pimelea physodes

After you leave the Visitor Centre on your right, in a pot, is Pimelea physodes, or Qualup Bell, with grey-green foliage close to reddish stems with pendant green bracts enclosing the small flowers and dark red outer bracts (photo above). This plant is native to southwestern WA and is considered the most outstanding of the genus. 8 – 21 July 2026 Today we will walk up the hill behind the café and along the road past the Ian Potter Consevatory construction site

plants.name: Anigozanthos 'Bush Pearl'
plants.context: 2. Also on your right is Anigozanthos ‘Bush Pearl’, a hybrid Kangaroo Paw with long- blooming, bright pink flowers developed by Angus Stewart (photo next page top left).

plants.name: Chorizema cordatum
plants.context: 3. Again on your right is Chorizema cordatum or Heart-leaved Flame Pea, a showy plant with vivid pink and orange flowers on a weeping shrub with bright-green prickly foliage, native to the moist southwestern parts of WA (photo above right).

plants.name: Banksia ericifolia 'Bird Song'
plants.context: 4. Bear left behind the café and right behind the depot to see, on your left Banksia ericifolia ‘Bird Song’, a small hybrid banksia with fine, bright green foliage and large orange flowers (photo above).

plants.name: Banksia spinulosa
plants.context: 5. On your right is Banksia spinulosa, a bush with large pale-yellow flowers held upright on toothed linear grey-green foliage (photo above). Sometimes known as the Hairpin Banksia, this plant is native to the three eastern states extending along the coast from Victoria to Cairns.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Legacy Flame'
plants.context: 6. As you turn left uphill, on your left is Grevillea ‘Legacy Flame’, a small grevillea, bred locally by Bywong Nursery, which commemorates 100 years of Legacy Australia with flame-like, orange-red flowers which resemble the Legacy torch (photo below).

plants.name: Westringia fruticosa 'Wunderbar'
plants.context: 7. Also on your left is Westringia fruticosa ‘Wunderbar’ or ‘Double Wonder’, a small dense shrub with grey-green foliage and pale mauve or pink semi-double flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Crowea 'Little Rockstar'
plants.context: 8. Still on your left is Crowea ‘Little Rockstar’, a compact form of Crowea, reaching only 60-80cm high, from a seedling variant growing at the ANBG. This plant has many pink star flowers (photo below)..

plants.name: Grevillea 'Bloodline'
plants.context: 9. Again on your left is Grevillea ‘Bloodline’, bred at Bywong Nursery by Peter Ollerenshaw, similar to the long flowering variety Grevillea ‘Lady O’, but with a slightly arching habit (photo below).

plants.name: Brachychiton rupestris
plants.context: 10. On your right is Brachychiton rupestris, or Queensland Bottle Tree, a small tree with a trunk swollen with water, endemic to central Queensland and northern NSW (photo below).

plants.name: Callistemon subulatus 'Brogo Overflow'
plants.context: 12. Also on your left is Callistemon subulatus ‘Brogo Overflow’ with bright red flowers and a low spreading habit (photo below left). This species is native to NSW and Victoria where it grows along the banks of watercourses. Bear right along the road with the Ian Potter Conservatory site.

plants.name: Banksia pencillata
plants.context: 13. On your right is Banksia pencillata or Newnes Plateau Banksia, a small tree covered in whorled, olive- green foliage and greenish-yellow flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to a restricted area of the Blue Mountains, NSW.

plants.name: Isopogon cuneatus
plants.context: 14. Also on your right is Isopogon cuneatus, an upright shrub with floppy branches of flat bright green leaves, often tinged with red, and large pink heads of drumstick flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Banksia neoanglica
plants.context: 15. Again on your right is Banksia neoanglica, or New England Banksia, with silver-backed, green foliage and gold flowers with dark-red styles held upright (photo above right). This shrub is native to the eastern tablelands of Queensland and NSW.
