intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, across the bridge, past the café, to the Banksia Garden

plants.name: Lechenaultia formosa
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre, on your right, in a pot, is Lechenaultia formosa, a small attractive plant with close, grey-green foliage and bright gold flowers (photo above). The genus Lechenaultia is named after the naturalist Leschenault de la Tour, 1773-1826 and is native to southwestern WA. 22 Jul – 4 Aug 2026 Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, across the bridge, past the café, to the Banksia Garden

plants.name: Isopogon cuneatus
plants.context: 2. Also on your right is Isopogon cuneatus, an upright shrub with floppy branches of flat, bright-green leaves, often tinged with red, and large pink heads of drumstick flowers (photo next page top left). This plant is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Guichenotia ledifolia
plants.context: 3. Again on your right is Guichenotia ledifolia, a small shrub with grey-green foliage covered in drooping, dusty-pink, 5-petalled flowers with maroon centres (photo above right). This plant is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Pimelea physodes
plants.context: 4. Further on your right, in a pot, is Pimelea physodes, or Qualup Bell, with grey-green foliage close to reddish stems with pendant green bracts enclosing the small flowers and dark-red outer bracts (photo above). This plant is native to southwestern WA and is considered the most outstanding of the genus.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Metal Red'
plants.context: 5. On your right is Grevillea ‘Metal Red’, a hardy shrub with metallic-red flowers held above soft, divided green foliage. a hybrid between G. banksii 'prostrate' x G. 'Bronze Rambler’ (photo above).

plants.name: Banksia spinulosa 'Stumpy Gold'
plants.context: 6. Cross the bridge, go past the café to see, on your left, Banksia spinulosa ‘Stumpy Gold’ with fine, toothed, linear foliage and masses of short, gold flowers with rusty-red styles (photo below). This plant is a dwarf cultivar of Banksia spinulosa var. collina that was selected by Richard Anderson of Merricks Nursery in Victoria from material collected on the NSW Central Coast.

plants.name: Banksia menziesii
plants.context: 7. As you enter the Banksia Garden on your right is Banksia menziesii, Firewood Banksia or Menzies Banksia, a small tree or shrub with oblong, toothed, green leaves and deep pink to red flowers (photo below). This plant is native to the west coast of WA, around Perth.

plants.name: Banksia baueri
plants.context: 8. Low on your right is Banksia baueri, or Possum Banksia, with dark-green, toothed foliage and grey furry flowers (photo below). These flowers can be very large when the plant is mature and can age to orange. This plant is native to the south coast of WA.

plants.name: Banksia solandri
plants.context: 9. Again, on your right is Banksia solandri, or Stirling Range Banksia, a large shrub with tough, dark-green, deeply-lobed leaves and brown, sweetly scented flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to the Stirling Range of southwestern WA.

plants.name: Banksia hookeriana
plants.context: 10. Also on your right is Banksia hookeriana or Hooker’s Banksia with upright, slender, green toothed foliage and bright orange flowers (photo above right). This plant is native to the area between Perth and Geraldton in WA.

plants.name: Banksia ericifolia 'Little Eric'
plants.context: 11. On your far right is Banksia ericifolia ‘Little Eric’ with dark green heath-like foliage and orange brushes with maroon styles (photo above).

plants.name: Banksia spinulosa 'Birthday Candles'
plants.context: 12. Low on your right is Banksia spinulosa ‘Birthday Candles’ a dense, bright-green bush with attractive needle foliage and short yellow cones with reddish styles (photo below left). ‘Birthday Candles’ is a dwarf cultivar of Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa developed by Bill Molyneux of Austraflora Nurseries in Montrose, Victoria.

plants.name: Banksia neoanglica
plants.context: 13. On your right is Banksia neoanglica, or New England Banksia, with silver-backed, dark green foliage and gold flowers with prominent black styles held upright (photo above right). This shrub is native to the eastern tablelands of Queensland and NSW.

plants.name: Banksia ericifolia 'Bird Song'
plants.context: 14. On your left is Banksia ericifolia ‘Bird Song’, a small hybrid banksia with fine, bright green foliage and large orange flowers (photo below left).

plants.name: Banksia robur
plants.context: 15. Further on your right is Banksia robur, or Swamp Banksia, with long egg-shaped leaves which are shiny on top and dull underneath (photo above right). This plant is native to the eastern mainland coast of Australia usually in sandy or swampy conditions. The flowers are bluish green when young, developing into yellow green and then rusty brown as they age.

intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, along the road above the Rock Garden, returning via the lower road to the café

plants.name: Eucalyptus caesia 'Silver Princess'
plants.context: 1. As you approach the Visitor Centre, on your left, in a pot, is Eucalyptus caesia ‘Silver Princess’ with large, heart-shaped leaves and dark red stems and new growth (photo above). This ornamental tree has a weeping habit, white buds opening to large red flowers and will develop white branches and minni-ritchi bark with peeling curls. 5 – 18 August 2026 Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, along the road above the Rock Garden, returning via the lower road to

plants.name: Dracophyllum macranthum
plants.context: 2. Further on your left, in a pot, is Dracophyllum macranthum with long, spiky leaves and bright pink flowers (photo next page top left). This plant is native to the north coast of NSW and is listed as vulnerable in the wild.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Scarlet King'
plants.context: 3. On your right is Grevillea ‘Scarlet King’, an attractive cultivar with dark-red, toothbrush flowers contrasting with white stems and grey- green divided foliage (photo above right).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Peaches and Cream'
plants.context: 4. Also on your right is Grevillea ‘Peaches and Cream’ with deeply-divided, green leaves and large flower heads of pink and cream (photo above). This hybrid was developed in Queensland by Jan Glazebrook and Dennis Cox and patented in 2006.

plants.name: Epacris calvertiana var. calvertiana
plants.context: 5. Bear left behind the café and continue uphill to see, on your right, Epacris calvertiana var. calvertiana, with cream bells on dark-green foliage, native to coastal southern NSW near Pigeon House Mountain (photo above).

plants.name: Chamelaucium 'Cascade Brook'
plants.context: 6. As you turn right along the road above the Rock Garden, on your right is Chamelaucium ‘Cascade Brook’, or Geraldton Wax, an open airy bush with masses of purplish-pink 5 petalled flowers with darker centres which is endemic to coastal areas of WA between Perth and Geraldton (photo below).

plants.name: Acacia aphylla
plants.context: 7. Also on your right is Acacia aphylla, or Leafless Rock Wattle, with large gold ball flowers on leathery, leafless, grey-green stems (photo below). This plant is native to the area around Perth, WA.

plants.name: Acacia barringtonensis
plants.context: 8. On your left is Acacia barringtonensis, known as Barrington Wattle, with long, elliptical green phyllodes and gold ball flowers (photo below). This plant is native to northeastern NSW.

plants.name: Hakea recurva
plants.context: 9. Further on your right is Hakea recurva, a large shrub with fearsomely prickly, grey-green needle foliage and many pinkish-yellow fragrant flowers (photo below). This plant is native to east of an area between Perth and Geraldton, WA.

plants.name: Hakea archaeoides
plants.context: 10. Also on your right is Hakea archaeoides, a shrub with oblong leaves and clusters of grey, woody nuts (photo below). This plant is native to the north coast of NSW and is listed as vulnerable in the wild.

plants.name: Grevillea sp
plants.context: 11. Again on your right is Grevillea sp., a tangled bush with short, green, needle foliage and clusters of white flowers with yellow buds (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea wilsonii × tripartita
plants.context: 12. Turn right downhill to see, on your right, Grevillea wilsonii x tripartita, a tall, rangy bush with prickly foliage, white buds and large, pink spider flowers with red styles (photo below left).

plants.name: Grevillea asteriscosa
plants.context: 13. Also on your right is Grevillea asteriscosa or Star-leaf Grevillea with small, dark green, prickly foliage and lipstick red flowers with long styles (photo above right). This plant is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Grevillea 'Sid Reynolds'
plants.context: 14. Turn right along the next road to see, on your left, Grevillea ‘Sid Reynolds’ which arose as a seedling in the garden of Sid Reynolds and is thought to be a hybrid between G. pinaster and G. commutate (photo below left). This shrub has fine green foliage and red and yellow spider flowers.

plants.name: Banksia neoanglica
plants.context: 15. On your right is Banksia neoanglica, or New England Banksia, with silver-backed, dark green foliage with gold flowers held upright (poto above right). This shrub is native to the eastern tablelands of Queensland and NSW..

plants.name: Acacia boormanii
plants.context: 2. High on your left is Acacia boormanii, or Snowy River Wattle, with fine, needle foliage and masses of golden ball flowers (photo next page top left). This shrub is a suckering, multi-stemmed, copse-forming plant, native to the alpine country of southeastern Australia.

plants.name: Corymbia ficifolia 'Dwarf Orange'
plants.context: 4. High on your left is Corymbia ficifolia ‘Dwarf Orange’, a small tree, with dark-green foliage and very attractive gumnuts (photo below left). This grafted gum, originally bred from the southern West Australian flowering gum, Corymbia ficifolia, is one of the most spectacular when in full flower.

plants.name: Rhodanthe anthemoides
plants.context: 5. On your right is Rhodanthe anthemoides, known as Chamomile Sunray, a mound of grey-green foliage almost covered with maroon buds opening to white daisy flowers with gold centres (photo above right). This plant is widespread on the mainland but listed as rare in Tasmania.

plants.name: Acacia leprosa 'Scarlet Blaze'
plants.context: 6. On your right is Acacia leprosa ‘Scarlet Blaze’ with weeping green foliage and many striking, reddish, fluffy balls of flowers (photo below left). The cultivar ‘Scarlet Blaze’ attracts attention because of its flower colour which is unique among wattles. This cultivar arose from a single, red-flowered specimen discovered by bushwalkers in a Victorian state forest northeast of Melbourne. The original plant has since died.

plants.name: Acacia pycnantha
plants.context: 7. Go up the hill behind the café and turn right along the road above the Rock Garden to see, on your right, Acacia pycnantha or Golden Wattle, the floral emblem of Australia (photo above right). This small tree has curved green phyllodes with large yellow ball flowers and is native to southeastern mainland Australia.

plants.name: Acacia phasmoides
plants.context: 8. Also on your right is Acacia phasmoides, or Phantom Wattle, a spreading wispy wattle, native to Dora Dora State Forest, near Holbrook, with grey-green linear foliage and bright yellow ball flowers (photo above).

plants.name: Acacia ingramii
plants.context: 9. Turn left up hill towards the Red Centre Garden to see, on your right, Acacia ingramii, a small tree with fine linear foliage and masses of gold ball flowers (photo below left). This plant is native to areas near Armidale in northern NSW.

plants.name: Acacia ulicifolia
plants.context: 10. On your right again is Acacia ulicifolia, or Prickly Moses, with many pale-yellow, ball flowers on fine, dark green, prickly foliage (photo above right). This wattle is native to the eastern part of Australia from Queensland to Tasmania.

plants.name: Aluta maisonneuvei subsp. maisonneuvei
plants.context: 11. Turn right, then left to enter the Red Centre Garden to see, on your right, in a pot, Aluta maisonneuvei ssp. maisonneuvei, known as Desert Heath Myrtle, a dense, woody shrub with tiny, crowded leaves and small white or pink flowers, native to arid regions in WA, SA, and the NT (photo above).

plants.name: Triodia scariosa
plants.context: 12. Bear right to see, on your left, Triodia scariosa, or Porcupine Grass which is native to southern, inland, mainland Australia, forming very prickly hummocks of dark-green, grass-like foliage with attractive seed heads (photo below left).

plants.name: Hakea leucoptera subsp. leucoptera
plants.context: 13. On your right is Hakea leucoptera ssp. leucoptera, known as Needlewood, a tall, erect, very prickly shrub with silvery grey leaves and showy cream flowers in axillary racemes (photo above right). Fruits are mainly smooth with a sharp beak, native to Queensland, NSW, SA, Victoria and the NT.

plants.name: Acacia ammobia
plants.context: 14. Also on your right, Acacia ammobia or Mt. Connor Wattle, a rare wattle from central Australia (photo below left). This plant has short golden flower spikes and grey-green linear foliage.

plants.name: Livistona mariae subsp. rigida
plants.context: 15. Back on your right are four Livistona mariae subsp. rigida, or Red Cabbage Palm, with beautiful drooping fronds (photo above right). This palm grows in central Australia, mostly in Finke Gorge National Park, and recent genetic research shows that it arrived there only 15,000 years ago.

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, along the road behind the depot, then up hill to the waterfall

plants.name: Pandorea pandorana 'Golden Showers'
plants.context: 1. As you leave the Visitor Centre look up to your left to see Pandorea pandorana ‘Golden Showers’, a vigorous twining vine with masses of tubular brown and gold flowers (photo above). 2 – 15 September 2026 Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, up the hill behind the café, along the road behind the depot, then up hill to the waterfall

plants.name: Acacia boormanii
plants.context: 3. On your left is Acacia boormanii, or Snowy River Wattle, with fine, needle foliage and masses of golden ball flowers (photo above right). This shrub is a suckering, multi-stemmed, copse-forming plant, with a native range in the alpine country of southeastern Australia.

plants.name: Grevillea petrophiloides subsp. remota
plants.context: 4. On your right, in a pot, is Grevillea petrophiloides ssp. remota, an erect, open shrub with long stems of pink flowers held above the divided foliage, native to southwestern WA (photo above).

plants.name: Olearia homolepsis 'Pretty Pops'
plants.context: 5. Low on your right is Olearia homolepsis ‘Pretty Pops’, a small upright shrub with bright- green leaves and profuse mauve, well-displayed, daisy-like flowers with gold centres (photo above).

plants.name: Acacia leprosa 'Scarlet Blaze'
plants.context: 6. Also on your right is Acacia leprosa ‘Scarlet Blaze’ with weeping green foliage and many striking, reddish, fluffy balls of flowers (photo below left). The cultivar ‘Scarlet Blaze’ attracts attention because of its flower colour unique among wattles. This cultivar arose from a single, red-flowered specimen discovered by bushwalkers in a Victorian state forest northeast of Melbourne. The original plant has since died.

plants.name: Acacia myrtifolia
plants.context: 7. On your right again is Acacia myrtifolia, an unusual wattle with bright-red new growth and stems, green elliptical phyllodes and globular cream flower clusters, often called the Red- stemmed Wattle or Myrtle Wattle (photo above right). This wattle is native to all six Australian states.

plants.name: Acacia covenyi
plants.context: 8. Bear left up the hill behind the café to see, on your right, Acacia covenyi, commonly known as Blue Bush, with magnificent silver- grey foliage and masses of contrasting bright lemon flower balls (photo above). This plant is rare in the wild and is confined to Deua National Park in southeastern NSW.

plants.name: Westringia fruticosa 'Wunderbar'
plants.context: 9. Continue behind the depot, then turn left up hill, to see on your left Westringia fruticosa ‘Wunderbar’, a small dense shrub with grey-green foliage and pale mauve or pink semi-double flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Philotheca myoporoides 'Winter Rouge'
plants.context: 10. On your left again is Philotheca myoporoides ‘Winter Rouge’, a small shrub with green aromatic foliage, bright pink buds and white star flowers (photo below).

plants.name: Grevillea 'Bloodline'
plants.context: 11. Also on your left is Grevillea ‘Bloodline’, bred at Bywong Nursery by Peter Ollerenshaw, similar to the long flowering variety Grevillea ‘Lady O’, but with a slightly arching habit (photo below).

plants.name: Hardenbergia comptoniana
plants.context: 12. Back to your left, along the path, on the wall is Hardenbergia comptoniana, or Native Wisteria, a vigorous, climbing vine with purple pea flowers and dark green three-lobed leaves (photo below left). This plant is native to southwestern WA.

plants.name: Phebalium woombye
plants.context: 13. Still on your left is Phebalium woombye, a bushy shrub with slender leaves, silver on the reverse, and clusters of starry, pink flowers, aging to white, native to southeastern Queensland and northeastern NSW coastal regions (photo above right).

plants.name: Acacia pycnantha
plants.context: 14. On your left is Acacia pycnantha or Golden Wattle, the floral emblem of Australia (photo below left). This small tree has curved green phyllodes with large yellow ball flowers and is native to southeastern mainland Australia.

plants.name: Indigofera australis
plants.context: 15. Bear right in front of the waterfall to see, on your left Indigofera australis, or Austral Indigo, a straggly bush with pinnate, blue- green leaves and pink flowers (photo above right). This member of the pea family is native from northern Queensland to Tasmania, also west to SA and WA. On your right, in a pot, is Commersonia (Rulingia) magniflora ssp. magniflora native to central and western Australia, an open bush with oblong, grey-green foliage and pink buds that open to pink, then white

plants.name: Commersonia (Rulingia) magniflora subsp. magniflora
plants.context: 15. Bear right in front of the waterfall to see, on your left Indigofera australis, or Austral Indigo, a straggly bush with pinnate, blue- green leaves and pink flowers (photo above right). This member of the pea family is native from northern Queensland to Tasmania, also west to SA and WA. On your right, in a pot, is Commersonia (Rulingia) magniflora ssp. magniflora native to central and western Australia, an open bush with oblong, grey-green foliage and pink buds that open to pink, then white

title: Flowers, Fruit & Foliage
author: Rosalind & Benjamin Walcott
intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, uphill behind the café and along the road above the Rock Garden

plants.name: Acacia pubescens
plants.context: 1. After you leave the Visitor Centre look right, down the steps, to see Acacia pubescens or Downy Wattle, with gold ball flowers on soft, fringed foliage (photo above). This endangered wattle is native to the Sydney Basin in central NSW and much of its habitat has vanished with the growth of the city of Sydney. 16 – 29 September 2026 Today we will walk from the Visitor Centre, uphill behind the café and along the road above the Rock Garden

plants.name: Coronidium sp
plants.context: 2. Further on your right is Coronidium sp., commonly known as the White Paper Daisy or Tall Everlasting, a compact shrub with silvery leaves and many white paper daisies with gold centres, native to open forests in eastern Australia (photo next page top left).

plants.name: Asterolasia elegans
plants.context: 3. In a pot, on your right is Asterolasia elegans, an open shrub with lance-shaped leaves and prominent white flowers, native to an area north of Sydney, growing on Hawkesbury sandstone (photo above right).

plants.name: Prostanthera ovalifolia 'Brundah Candy'
plants.context: 4. On your right again is Prostanthera ovalifolia ‘Brundah Candy’, a medium sized shrub with highly aromatic leaves and masses of pink flowers (photo above). This plant was found by Noel and Sharon Cartwright at North Brundah School site, Brundah Hills, east of Grenfell, NSW.

plants.name: Asterolasia 'Lemon Essence'
plants.context: 5. Still on your right is Asterolasia ‘Lemon Essence’, a compact shrub with many lemon- yellow star flowers, developed at the ANBG (photo above).

plants.name: Acacia cognata
plants.context: 6. Bear left, uphill behind the café to see on your right, Acacia cognata, or Bower Wattle, a graceful, weeping tree with green linear leaves and plenty of flowers, native to southeastern mainland Australia (photo below).

plants.name: Acacia aphylla
plants.context: 7. As you turn right along the road above the Rock Garden, on your left is Acacia aphylla, or Leafless Rock Wattle, with large gold ball flowers on leathery, leafless, grey-green stems, native to the area around Perth, WA (photo below).

plants.name: Olearia viscidula
plants.context: 8. On your left is Olearia viscidula, or Wallaby Weed, a large open bush covered in small white daisy flowers with a strong scent, native to coastal NSW and Victoria (photo below).

plants.name: Acacia filicifolia
plants.context: 9. Look up to your left to see Acacia filicifolia or Fern-leaf Wattle, a large tree with dark-green, ferny foliage with pale-yellow ball flowers. native to southern Queensland and NSW (photo below left).

plants.name: Acacia longifolia var. sophorae hybrid
plants.context: 10. On your left is Acacia longifolia var. sophorae hybrid, or Coastal Wattle, with lemon rod flowers well displayed on leathery dark green phyllodes. This plant is widespread along the eastern and southeastern coast of Australia (photo above right).

plants.name: Acacia leprosa 'Scarlet Blaze'
plants.context: 11. Also on your left is Acacia leprosa ‘Scarlet Blaze’ with weeping green foliage and many striking, reddish, fluffy ball flowers (photo above). The cultivar ‘Scarlet Blaze’ attracts attention because of its flower colour unique among wattles. This cultivar arose from a single, red- flowered specimen discovered by bushwalkers in a Victorian state forest northeast of Melbourne. The original plant has since died.

plants.name: Pimelea cremnophila
plants.context: 12. On your right is Pimelea cremnophila, or Gorge Rice-flower, an erect shrub with cream flowers and red-brown stems with white, rigid, bristly hairs which become hairless with age (photo below left). The pale green fruit is egg- shaped and dry. This critically endangered plant is endemic to a restricted area of northern NSW near Armidale and Tamworth.

plants.name: Hakea macraeana
plants.context: 13. Further on your right is Hakea macraeana, or Needlewood, a small tree with fine, drooping foliage and white flowers along the stems, native to eastern mainland Australia (photo above right).

plants.name: Hakea horrida
plants.context: 14. On your right again is Hakea horrida, a stiff shrub with extremely prickly, intricate needle foliage and strongly scented creamy white fluffy flowers, native to southwestern WA (photo below left).

plants.name: Grevillea corrugata
plants.context: 15. Turn right downhill to see, on your right, Grevillea corrugata, a shrub with deeply- lobed leaves and white flowers, endemic to southwestern WA (photo above right).
